items.location: Dallas, Texas · University of Texas at Dallas

items.fullDescription: Call for Papers From its inception, cinema has transcended borders through the movement of people, capital, narratives, and visual technology. However, over the past two decades, the term transnational cinema has evolved into one of the most influential and contested frameworks in film studies. Scholars such as Elizabeth Ezra, Terry Rowden, Deborah Shaw, Will Higbee, and Song Hwee Lim have variously expanded, critiqued, and redefined the concept, emphasizing its aesthetic, political, and industrial dimensions and prompting new questions about its theoretical and pedagogical implications. While these approaches have illuminated the circulation of films, filmmakers, and spectators across borders, they have also raised questions about the continuing relevance of the national cinema framework and the analytical boundaries of the transnational itself. This symposium revisits the concept of transnational cinema at a moment when two distinct currents seem bound for collision. On the one hand, global migration, digital media, the global climate catastrophe, geopolitical conflicts, and transregional collaborations have blurred distinctions between the local and the global, as well as the national and the transnational. On the other hand, isolationism, authoritarianism, and protectionism have re-erected physical and ideological borders across the globe. Is the world more or less transnational as a result of these competing impulses? We invite proposals that address theoretical, historical, or pedagogical questions, such as: How can the familiar concept of transnational cinema elucidate emergent and unfamiliar problems in the contemporary landscape? How do we define and teach transnational cinema now? Is transnational cinema best understood as a framework, an approach, a mode of filmmaking, or a category of world cinema? How does transnational cinema intersect with, or diverge from, national, world, and global cinema theories? What are the political, aesthetic, or ethical stakes of emphasizing transnationality in film studies today? We welcome both theoretical interventions and case studies from diverse regions and traditions. Possible topics include, but are not limited to: • Theories and definitions of transnational cinema • Pedagogical approaches to transnational cinema • Feminist, queer, and trans approaches to transnational cinema • Transnational authorship and stardom • Memory, trauma, and postmemory in transnational film • Digital technologies and virtual transnational spaces • Streaming platforms and global distribution • Cinemas of diaspora, exile, and migration • Cross-border activism and solidarity through film • Environmental and ecological transnationalism • Film policy, censorship, and cultural diplomacy • Transnational labor, precarity, and creative economies • International film festivals and global circulation • Archival and historiographical approaches to transnational film • Politics of translation, dubbing, and subtitling • Regional and transregional filmmaking practices • Anti-colonial, postcolonial, and de-colonial aesthetics and narratives • Global Hollywood and transnational co-productions• Transnational spectatorship and global audiences • State, statelessness, and belonging in transnational cinema • Borders, border-crossings, and redefinitions of home • Transnational genres • De-Westernizing film studies Presenters will be invited to submit completed papers for consideration in an edited collection or special issue developed from the symposium. Proposals (250-300 words) and short bios (100 words) should be submitted by June 1st, 2026, using this Google Form: https://forms.gle/R7Jw98KpMEc7BAHo6 For questions, please contact the organizing committee at ahtfilmstudies@utdallas.edu.

items.excerpt: Tentative Title- Beyond the Ocean: Maritime Infrastructure and Hydro-Narratives of Indians under the Raj Concept Note The imperial ships of the British Raj bore millions of Indian migrants across waterways just the way Charon ferried souls across the river Styx to an irreversible fate. items.fullDescription: Tentative Title- Beyond the Ocean: Maritime Infrastructure and Hydro-Narratives of Indians under the Raj Concept Note The imperial ships of the British Raj bore millions of Indian migrants across waterways just the way Charon ferried souls across the river Styx to an irreversible fate. Nonetheless, the Indians transformed the vicious vessels into spaces of radical rebirth and enduring kinship. While the first volume in this series geographically mapped the global representations of Indian migration under the British Empire, Volume 2 moves into a critical interrogation of colonial history through ports, maritime framework, and waterways. Moving away from land-bound histories, this volume initiates an intensive interrogation of colonial history through its maritime infrastructures: ports, dockyards, maritime records, and waterways. This book adopts a hydrocolonial and aqua-centric hermeneutic to explore how subaltern narratives were historically erased from official imperial records, shipping registers, and mainstream historiography. It will examine the ports, vessels, inland rivers, and vast oceans that witnessed the diverse, turbulent flows of Indian populations across the globe. We invite chapter proposals that explore how literary depictions illustrate the ways the British Empire transformed global waterways into networks of imperial power, capital, and radical identity transformation. The psychological and structural undoing of native culture began long before the ship reached the open ocean. In the liminal, high-stress spaces of the colonial dockyards and ports, social hierarchies began to collapse. Diaspora literature, folk traditions, travelogues, and ship logs frequently evoke the immediate and profound breakdown of caste and religious boundaries the moment emigrants set foot on the regimented ports. Sudden intermixing occurred in these crowded transit camps as we witnessed Brahmins consuming food prepared by lower-caste hands, Hindus and Muslims shared sleeping quarters, and sacred visual markers of identity (turbans, sacred threads, prayer beads, religious caps, and tilaks) were stripped or voluntarily discarded to avoid surveillance, standing out, or segregation upon reaching destination ports. Once aboard, the ship itself became a volatile micro-world, sort of floating world suspended between an old life and an uncertain future. Significantly, many post-slavery labour migrations repurposed slave ships to transport new, freer workforce alongside other cargo. Textual representations from this middle passage vividly capture the horrors of overcrowding, disease, and racial prejudice. Yet, the vessel can be read as a site of profound subaltern resilience. Indian migrants forged deep, enduring bonds that acted as vital substitutes for the blood relations left behind, helping them survive the culture shock and grief of displacement. The songs, stories, and archives of this passage are filled with narratives of maritime resistance, shipboard revolts, and haunting tragedies that demand our critical attention. Book II of the Beyond the Ocean series invites proposals that capture the Indian migrant experience from port to port during the British Raj. Echoing Kamau Brathwaite's conceptualization of the tidal experience, we welcome essays that explore the large-scale, long-term dispersion of Indians across the global maritime network, starting from the Gulf nations and the African continent to Southeast Asia, American states, and the archipelagic Caribbean islands. Suggested areas for submission, including, but not limited to: Literary depictions of port architecture, custom houses, dockyards, and the initial dismantling of caste/religious identities. Ship as a total institution, the legacy of repurposed slave ships, and narratives of disease, discipline, and imperial surveillance at sea. Textual and musical representations of shipboard kinship, solidarity, and emotional survival among diverse migrant groups. Songs, oral histories, and literary accounts of maritime mutinies, escapes, sabotage, and shipboard tragedies. How the crossing of the Kala Pani (black waters) fractured and reshaped languages, creating creolized idioms, plantation songs, and hybrid oral traditions. Comparative literary readings of different aquatic journeys- including indentured labourers, penal convicts, Lascar sailors, Kangani System, Maistry System, Sepoys, and Colonial Constabularies, and free passage merchants. Literary representation of Indian ocean, Atlantic Ocean, Pacific Ocean, Bay of Bengal, Arabian Sea, Red Sea, and other water bodies. Literary representation of ship and its infrastructure. Literary representation of the ocean as repository of forgotten/suppressed history and marginalized culture. Comparative study of the Middle Passage and the Kala Pani crossing or other hydro-crossings and its literary representation. Abstract submission deadline: 31st July 2026 Word limit: 250- 350 words with 4-5 keywords Submissions in a word document along with a brief bio-note to be sent to: shubhankukochar@outlook.com You can find Book I (Beyond the Ocean: Literature, History and the British Empire) via this link https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-981-95-2137-1. Note: As Book I was published by Springer, the editors have submitted the proposal for Book II to Springer as well, aiming to establish this as a long-running series. Editors: Dr. Shubhanku Kochar (Associate Professor, University School of Humanities and Social Sciences at Guru Gobind Singh Indraprastha University, Delhi) Dr. Shehnaz Kabir (Research and Development Officer, Loreto College, Kolkata)

items.title: CFP: 3rd International Interdisciplinary Conference of the Department of English, University of Zululand 28-30 September 2026 Re-imagining Language, W
items.location: University of Zululand, Ongoye, KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa · University of Zululand
items.excerpt: CFP: 3rd International Interdisciplinary Conference of the Department of English, University of Zululand 28-30 September 2026 Re-imagining Language, Writing, and Literature in English in a Fast-Changing World In an era that has been labelled by scholars as the age of technocracy, AI and post-truth, the spheres of literature and the channels of creative an...
items.fullDescription: CFP: 3rd International Interdisciplinary Conference of the Department of English, University of Zululand 28-30 September 2026 Re-imagining Language, Writing, and Literature in English in a Fast-Changing World In an era that has been labelled by scholars as the age of technocracy, AI and post-truth, the spheres of literature and the channels of creative and critical discourses seem to face a dire future. Society globally is becoming entrapped within an accelerated spiral comprising lowest common denominator discourse, the loss of autonomy, the dissipation of embodied social networks and the forceful commodification of imagination and creativity. Considering these threats, it is vital to create radical acts of imagining and reimagining. These should be rooted not only in the hegemonic technocratic traditions and orthodoxies imposed from the Global North, but also, and more urgently, in the lived textures of local language, memory, and survival. The need to re-imagine language, writing and literature is not only an aesthetic necessity, but a desperate need for the future of meaning and society. In the context of AI for example, there are thriving, often cacophonous discourses debating the extent to which the technological deployment of large language models (LLMs) either enhance or curtail individual expression whether in private contexts of self-articulation or in the more public spheres of formal education. In the sphere of formal education, the issue of ethics has assumed a significant role as reliance on, or use of largely predictive AI-enabled or AI-generated content challenges previously stable notions of academic integrity and authentic authorship. While there seems to be consensus on the need for the 'ethical' use of AI in these contexts, the question that continues to divide commentators is: What exactly constitutes 'ethical' use of content or material that is generated or curated in full or part by another party? What exactly is ethical these days? Other vital questions relate to the dominance of certain languages (European) and what seems to be the increased sidelining of others (African in particular) as well as the unsubtly hidden market-centric orientation of the current drive towards AI in academic writing. These are only a few of the significant puzzles posed by the new forms of language-use inaugurated, imposed and valorised by new forms of technology. This invites scrutiny of the more traditional roles that language plays in embodying culture, collective identity, knowledge-creation and transmission as well as in the codification of epistemologies. Given the marginalisation of indigenous languages and knowledge systems in contemporary Africa over the centuries of colonial domination, reclaiming language as a medium to address unabating local dilemmas is proving to be more daunting than ever. Yet, the rise of social media as de-facto sites of imagination and new forms of expression represent possibilities for cultural expression and practices of literature and knowledge production. Furthermore, the increasing diversity of social platforms spawned by technology has a variety of positive and negative implications for, among other things, the re-imagination of fiction, redefining realism, generating alternate currents of speculation, enforcing modes of stereotyping, unforeseen ontological hallucinations, and even contributing towards the current vivification of propaganda. All in all, there is no simple reductionist approach to interpret the current moment. Considering the urgency of the above, the Department of English at the University of Zululand issues the following call for papers: Re-imagining Language, Writing, and Literature in English in a Fast-Changing World Themes and sub-themes which are encouraged (but not limited to) include: The future of language and literature. Imagination and conflicts/interfaces with reality. Academic ethics, authorship and linguistic agency in the age of AI. Ghost Writing and Co-creation Home, homelessness, journeys and writing. Dreaming and language. Multilingualism and Integration Imaginations in literature as forms of resistance and rebellion. Postcolonial literatures, planetarity and the global technocratic order. Imagination and the narrating of already lived (possibly forgotten) histories. Fading/submerged names of nations, peoples, and things, and the (non)realms of departed/buried ontologies. Cracks in reality and meaning. Re-telling and translations Lost childhoods and lost generational mandates/missions. Non-existence as an outcome of personal and social life. Survival and language. Ecological imaginations and environmental futures. The death of nature/ecological unravellings in literary texts Extinctions and disappearances of forms of literature and narratives. Otherness, adaptation and change Possible subversive/creative uses of AI and technology as imagination tools. Slavery, Exploitation, and AI. Slow writing and slow reading as forms of accelerationist resistance and critique. Furthermore, we open the call to other interpretations of the theme which weave academic insights with creative interpretations, including: Short presentations of lived practice of language imaginings, writers' reflections upon their own creative practice(s) which may blur lines between creative and academic spaces. Approaches to creative writing which may enhance imaginative possibilities. Presentations of short pieces of creative writing which directly respond to the theme/sub-themes. Performances of language reimagining or embodied writing. Provocations/perturbations of the possibilities/impossibilities of language and meaning when situated within structured genres/spaces/histories. Literary manifestoes of a "decline to participate" (in the mode of Lesego Rampolokeng, in 2014) in the dominant futurity narrative (challenging the hegemonic rhetoric, adapt to 4IR or be irrelevant) with an insistence on alternative unlived narratives and subversive explorations of change. We invite all interested parties to submit abstracts of approximately 250 words, with five keywords, by 31 July 2026, to the following three email addresses: allank@unizulu.ac.za / phakathib@unizulu.ac.za / ndlovua@unizulu.ac.za If accepted, a member of the organising team will contact you prior to 31 July 2026. The Organising Team, 3rd International Interdisciplinary Conference of the Department of English, University of Zululand.

items.fullDescription: About the Organiser Durgapur Institute of Legal Studies (DILS), Durgapur, West Bengal, is an institution dedicated to legal education and professional training. The Institute is affiliated with Kazi Nazrul University and approved by the Bar Council of India. DILS offers 5-year B.A. LL.B. (Hons.) and 3-year LL.B. (Hons.) programmes and seeks to integrate doctrinal legal education with practical exposure, research, critical thinking, and professional development. The seminar is being organised by Durgapur Institute of Legal Studies (DILS) in collaboration with its Research & Development Committee, as an IQAC Initiative. About the Seminar Durgapur Institute of Legal Studies is organising a National Level Seminar titled: "Questing the Horizon of International Law and New World Order: Jurisprudential Aspects, Contemporary Challenges, and Emerging Perspectives" The contemporary global order is witnessing significant transformation due to shifting geopolitical dynamics, evolving governance structures, technological developments, and emerging legal challenges. Against this background, the seminar seeks to explore the changing horizons of legal systems at both international and domestic levels. The seminar aims to provide a platform for academicians, practitioners, researchers, professionals, and students to engage in meaningful academic deliberations on jurisprudential developments, contemporary challenges, and emerging perspectives concerning law and governance. The seminar will be conducted in Hybrid Mode, enabling both physical and virtual participation. Themes for Paper Presentation The broad themes are: Evolving Legal Orders in a Changing Global and Domestic Landscape Law, Governance, and the Crisis of Legitimacy in Contemporary Societies Sovereignty, Federalism, and Decentralised Governance Justice Systems in Transition: Courts, Tribunals, and ADR Human Rights, Social Justice, and Constitutional Values Law and Public Policy: Bridging Theory and Practice Economic Regulation, Trade, and Developmental Challenges Environmental Governance and Sustainable Development Technology, Digital Regulation, and Emerging Legal Challenges Crime, Security, and Accountability in Modern Legal Systems Maritime Law, Space Law, and Emerging Global Commons Gender Justice and Intersectionality in Legal Systems The themes are indicative and not exhaustive. Authors are encouraged to explore interdisciplinary and contemporary issues connected with the broader theme of the seminar. Who is it For? Paper submissions and participation are invited from: Academicians and Faculty Members Legal Practitioners and Professionals Research Scholars Students Policy Experts Interdisciplinary Researchers Submission Guidelines Authors are required to submit an abstract of 300 words with 5-6 keywords in MS Word format (.doc/.docx). The full paper should contain a minimum of 5,000 words, inclusive of references. All submissions must follow the APA 7th Edition citation style. The manuscript should be in Times New Roman, font size 12, 1.5 line spacing, with footnotes in size 10. Submissions must be original, unpublished, and not under consideration elsewhere. A maximum of two authors per paper is permitted. The co-author is required to register separately. Authors must submit a plagiarism report with the full paper. A maximum similarity of 10% is permissible, excluding references and properly cited quotations. Only authors whose abstracts are accepted will be permitted to present their papers. Papers presented during the seminar may be considered for publication, subject to peer review. Mode and Venue Mode: Hybrid - Physical/Offline and Virtual/Online Physical Venue: Seminar Hall Durgapur Institute of Legal Studies (DILS) City Center, Phase II, Surya Sen Sarani Near Gandhi More Durgapur, West Bengal - 713208 Registration Procedure Interested participants are required to complete the registration form and pay the applicable registration fee. Registration Form: Register for the Seminar Registration is mandatory. Spot registration may be permitted subject to availability. Registration Fee Category Fee Academicians & Professionals - Paper Presentation ?1,500 Research Scholars & Students (except DILS students) - Paper Presentation ?1,000 DILS Students & Alumni - Paper Presentation ?800 Paper Presentation in Virtual/Online Mode - All Categories ?800 Participation Only - Physical/Offline ?800 Participation Only - Virtual/Online ?500 DILS Students & Alumni - Physical Participation ?500 DILS Students & Alumni - Virtual Participation ?250 Local hospitality, tea/coffee, snacks, seminar lunch, and seminar kits will be provided to participants. Travelling allowance and accommodation will not be provided. Certificates will be provided for paper presentation and participation. Submissions reflecting on how AI corporations and Generative AI models are reshaping life writing practices across textual, digital, and visual formats, or on the consequences of such practices for a...
items.fullDescription: Abstract: This panel reexamines life writing in the age of Generative AI, asking who controls the conditions under which individuals narrate their own lives. Submissions reflecting on how AI corporations and Generative AI models are reshaping life writing practices across textual, digital, and visual formats, or on the consequences of such practices for authorship, equity, and cultural power, are especially welcome. Full CFP: Generative AI has fundamentally changed how we think, articulate, and write. However, access to AI is not equitable, and its outputs frequently fail to account for diverse lived experiences and reflect biases. The corporations developing AI models are agents actively reshaping how we perceive, think, interpret, and articulate our identities and experiences. This panel examines what that means for Life Writing - defined broadly to include textual, digital, and visual formats - where individuals reflect, narrativize, and present their lived experiences in public-facing contexts. Submissions engaging the conference theme, "Our Ruling Classes: Culture, Power and Conflict," are especially welcome. The panel welcomes submissions that explore (but are not limited to): a) Questions of authorship for AI-assisted/AI-mediated life writings b) The aesthetics and formal transformations in the practice of Life Writing in the age of Generative AI c) Life Writings produced by or attributed to Generative AI models d) The 'Author' Persona in AI-generated/AI-mediated Life Writing e) Autoethnographic explorations of writing life with AI f) Reader/Audience response to AI-mediated/AI-generated life writings g) Questions of ethics, trust, and safety, when narrating life with AI h) Impacts of AI-mediated life writing on individuals from vulnerable and marginalized communities, diverse gender identities, racial, and cultural communities i) "Permanent Memory" of AI models and archival of individual identities j) Translation, multilingualism, and cultural limitations of Generative AI in supporting Life Writing activities Note: > Please submit your proposals only via the link: https://pamla.ballastacademic. com/Home/S/20174 > Extended Deadline to submit proposals is June 30, 2026 ; early submissions are encouraged. > The 2026 PAMLA Conference is entirely in person , in Seattle, WA, with no provision for virtual or hybrid presentations . > Please check the PAMLA website for dates and additional information

items.fullDescription: "Rhetorical Theory" (Standing Session) Seattle, WA, Nov. 20-23 Chair: Dr. Ryan Leack (USC) Email: leack@usc.edu Abstract This panel will explore recent movements in rhetorical theory writ large, either in connection with or apart from composition theory and practice. Special attention will be given to proposals that engage with the conference's theme. Description In addition to expanding rhetoric's disciplinary relations, this panel hopes to push rhetoric beyond persuasion-beyond rhetoric as purposeful action toward some given end, but also as reception, listening, responsivity, relationality, resonance, presence, aurality, and the like. In this way, the panel hopes to push rhetoric's boundaries and find kinship in new frontiers beyond its disciplinary and historically sanctioned borders. This panel invites papers which explore rhetorical theory in general, but prefers papers which relate rhetoric, specifically or generally, to the below topics: o Rhetorical listening o Orality and/vs. aurality o Rhetorical new materialisms o Sound studies o Sonic rhetoric o New/materialisms o Quantum/physics o Agential realism o Posthumanism o Empiricism o Object-oriented rhetoric o Object-oriented ontology o Affect theory Abstract Length : 150-200 words Abstract Deadline : May 25, 2026 Please Submit Abstract through PAMLA website : https://pamla.ballastacademic.com/Home/S/19615

items.excerpt: Italian Teaching Symposium 2026 - II edition "Creative Pathways in Italian Language and Culture Teaching" September 25-26, 2026 St. Jerome's University (University of Waterloo) & online Inspired by the theme chosen for the XXVI Week of the Italian Language in the World, "Lingua geniale: ideare, progettare, creare con l'italiano", we are pleased to announc...
items.fullDescription: Italian Teaching Symposium 2026 - II edition "Creative Pathways in Italian Language and Culture Teaching" September 25-26, 2026 St. Jerome's University (University of Waterloo) & online Inspired by the theme chosen for the XXVI Week of the Italian Language in the World, "Lingua geniale: ideare, progettare, creare con l'italiano", we are pleased to announce the second edition of the Italian Teaching Symposium, once again endorsed by the Canadian Association for Italian Studies (CAIS). Building on the success of its inaugural 2025 edition, which welcomed more than fifty participants - including presenters, chairs, and attendees from both academia and cultural institutions - this year's symposium will take place on September 25-26, 2026, at St. Jerome's University, federated with the University of Waterloo (Ontario, Canada). While primarily designed as an in-person event, limited opportunities for remote participation may be available. The second edition of the Italian Teaching Symposium, Creative Pathways in Italian Language and Culture Teaching, aims to bring together scholars, researchers, language educators, teacher trainers, graduate students, and practitioners interested in exploring three interconnected dimensions of Italian language education: imagine, design, and create. As Marcel Danesi (2025) observes, "the study of creativity crosses all disciplinary boundaries", making creativity a particularly productive lens through which to examine the teaching and learning of Italian language and culture. This resonates well with the theme of the XXVI Week of the Italian Language in the World, inspired by the newly established Directorate General for Growth and Export Promotion of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, which highlights the creative potential of Italian as a language capable of fostering ideas, innovation, and intercultural dialogue. In this sense, teaching Italian extends beyond the transmission of grammar and pronunciation to encompass cultural mediation, collaboration, and engagement with diverse forms of expression. In this context, we invite proposals that reflect on how this perspective inspires - or challenges - instructors to adopt creative and unconventional approaches to course design, including content, activities, teaching methods, and assessment. In addition to traditional paper presentations, the 2026 edition of the Italian Teaching Symposium will introduce a new hands-on session format designed to foster practical exchange, experimentation, and collaborative learning. These interactive sessions will give participants the opportunity to showcase classroom activities, digital tools and apps, pedagogical resources, multimodal projects, creative assignments, community-engaged initiatives, assessment tools, or other innovative practices implemented in Italian language and culture courses. This format is intended to encourage active engagement and discussion, allowing attendees to learn directly from colleagues' experiences and to leave the symposium with practical ideas and materials that can be adapted to their own teaching contexts. Suggested?topics:?? Imagine? Exploring how Italian language and culture can be reimagined as spaces for creativity, identity formation, intercultural dialogue, and social engagement -new perspectives on Italian language, culture, and identity? -intercultural competence and global citizenship through Italian studies? -new imaginaries of Italy,?Italianness, and Italian-speaking communities? -heritage learners, multilingualism, and transnational Italian identities -the future of Italian studies and language programs in changing educational landscapes -reimagining the role of Italian language education in contemporary society? ? Design? Examining the pedagogical, technological, and curricular frameworks that shape innovative Italian language education -curriculum development and innovative pedagogical models? -project-based learning in Italian language education? -multilingual and intercultural learning environments? -educational technologies, AI, and digital course design? -assessment design and innovative evaluation practices -Italian for specific purposes (LSP) and professional communication? -international collaborations and virtual exchange projects? ? Create? Investigating creative practices, cultural production, and multimodal forms of expression in Italian language and culture teaching. -creative writing and storytelling in Italian language?pedagogy? -language learning through music, performance, theatre, cinema,?and?visual arts?? -literature in the Italian classroom?as a tool for language acquisition and cultural?awareness? -student-generated content and multimodal?literacy? -digital creativity and media production -community-engaged learning, public humanities projects, digital creativity, and collaborations beyond the classroom? ? Submission Guidelines? We invite proposals for individual papers (15 minutes), thematic panels (90 minutes), and hands-on workshops (approximately 30 minutes) designed to engage participants in innovative pedagogical practices, classroom activities, digital tools and apps, teaching resources, and creative approaches to Italian language and culture education.? Submissions should include the presentation title, author name(s) and affiliation(s), an abstract in English or Italian of no more than 300 words, and a contact e-mail address. Proposals should be submitted via this form by July 25 , 2026. Notification of acceptance will be sent by July 24, 2026. Questions may be addressed to the symposium organizers, Gianmarco Bocchi (gbocchi@uwaterloo.ca) and Alessia Ursella (aursella@uoguelph.ca).?

items.fullDescription: 'Showing Myself, Seeing Myself': Lived Experience in Disabled & Neurodivergent Film A Call for Papers for the Lived Perspectives Film Festival and Conference. Saturday 6th March 2027, University of Winchester, UK Since launching in 2023, the Lived Perspectives film festival has celebrated disabled and neurodivergent filmmakers. By championing their innovative, diverse, and often challenging work, we aim to support them in telling their stories and creating a space for their vision to be shared. This year's event combines film screenings with a one-day conference exploring the importance of creating opportunities for disabled and neurodivergent filmmakers to have their work shared and seen, and the range of representations for these minority groups in mainstream cinema. We invite proposals for 20-minute presentations and interactive workshops from academics, research students, filmmakers, and lived-experience-led organisations. Contributions might, for example, explore: Disabled and neurodivergent representation in mainstream film Audience perspectives on recognition and representation on screen Identity-based film festivals as sites of self-representation Independent lived experience filmmaking Key themes, styles, or case studies in disabled and neurodivergent independent filmmaking Interactive workshops exploring film, accessibility, and community connection Proposals of approximately 250 words are due by Monday 2nd November 2026 through the call for papers form on the website: www.livedperspectives.co.uk/showingmyself2027 Contact for more information or to discuss your ideas email: contact@livedperspectives.co.uk

items.fullDescription: The sea and marine life are often considered as pillars of cultural heritage, identity, and collective memories in Portugal (Lourenço 2001; Lourenço 2014). From the historical milestones of the sixteenth century transoceanic navigation (Cortesão 1978) to literary production (Avelar 2024), the ocean has shaped the national imagination of Portugal (Tomás 2013). As Antonio Barreto writes: "Heritage is a human creation and the results from history and culture. But there are natural realities that are transformed, through history, culture, and technology into heritage. Such is the case of the sea for the Portuguese" (2019: 15). As a form of heritage, this connection extends to gastronomy and, in a particularly profound way, to the musical sphere (Simões 2013: 45-62; Sardo 2013: 44-64). From fado, with its narratives of longing and loss, to the songs that gave rhythm to the the fishermen's daily work, the Portuguese musical repertoire has functioned as a living archive of human interaction with the environment. However, there is nothing natural or essentialist about this Portuguese relationship with the sea, for it is an imaginary that has been constructed and continously negotiated across historical periods, which also bears the imprint of colonialism (João 2015: 119-147; El-Shawan Castelo-Branco et al 2003: 73-142). More dramatically, the transformations driven by climate change and unsustainable industrial fishing in the twenty-first century threaten not only biodiversity (Ramos-Pereira 2004: 26-43), but also the cultural practices linked to it - a topic that still requires greater attention in schoarly research. In any case, beyond its material and economic dimensions, the sea in Portugal remains a space of imagination and transformation. As evoked in the songs of José Afonso, the sea is not just a site of identity and homecoming, but also a place of alterity and utopia. By singing of the sea, we evoke the possibility of a new era, in which culture and nature meet once again in a shared project of humanity - a vision that also resonates with the notion of the Blue Humanities (Mentz 2023; Oppermann 2019: 443-461). This call seeks to explore the intersection between what we have inherited and what we must protect. Therefore, we invite researchers, artists, and cultural practitioners to reflect on how these environmental changes reshape the meaning of the arts and their role as vehicles of identity and resistance. Papers are welcome on the following topics, amongst others: The sea as a cultural construct in Portuguese music and the arts; Music, critique, and resistance to climate crises in Portugal; Intersections between literature, music, and environmental heritage; Representations of the sea and music in literature and written culture; Music, sound, identity, and the politics of ocean memory; Collective memory, local identities, and soundscapes; The sea in film, the media, and popular culture; Folklore, folk groups, and the preservation of intangible cultural heritage; Coloniality and decoloniality of contemporary maritime identity; Transcultural and postcolonial perspectives on the maritime imaginary; Blue Humanities and music as an environmental archive; Resistance, utopia, and sound activism in the face of climate change; Tourism and heritage preservation of coastal musical cultures; Technology, marine sciences, and music; Ocean ethics, music, and maritime imaginaries; Phenomenology, aesthetics, listening, and maritime experience. Submission Guidelines Proposals should be sent to the email: cecc.fch@ucp.pt, and include paper title, A 300-word abstract in Portuguese or in English should be submitted for a 20-minute presentation, including a provisional title, a brief biographical note (max. 150 words) and contact details. Contributions may be in Portuguese or English. Abstract submission deadline: July 31, 2026 Notification of acceptance: September 15, 2026 After acceptance of abstracts, participants must register for the conference. Registration Fees and Deadlines The registration fee includes coffee breaks and conference materials. Early bird registration (September 16-30): €75 (student) | €100 (non-student) Regular registration (October 1-20): €100 (student) | €150 (non-student) Keynote Speakers Diana Gonçalves, Catholic University of Portugal Susana Sardo, University of Aveiro Organizers Alyse Kaweng Fan e Thales Reis Alecrim Scientific Committee Ana Matoso, CECC Ana Margarida Abrantes, CECC Carla Ganito, CECC Joana Moura, CECC Mário Avelar, CECC Nuno Amado, CECC Patrícia Anzini, CECC Pedro A. Mendes, INET-md Rita Bueno Maia, CECC Sofia Vieira Lopes, INET-md This activity is part of the 4ELEMENTS project, representing the element Water, funded by the Transform4Europe (T4EU) alliance, in a strategic collaboration between the Catholic University of Portugal, the University of Sofia (Bulgaria) and the University of Silesia (Poland).

items.excerpt: Abstract : This roundtable explores contemporary directions in life writing, biography, and memoir, with a particular interest in how we narrate the self amidst evolving issues of identity, culture, and power. We welcome both traditional scholarly essays and creative nonfiction/memoir submissions accompanied by a brief meta-analysis. Potential topics incl...
items.fullDescription: Abstract : This roundtable explores contemporary directions in life writing, biography, and memoir, with a particular interest in how we narrate the self amidst evolving issues of identity, culture, and power. We welcome both traditional scholarly essays and creative nonfiction/memoir submissions accompanied by a brief meta-analysis. Potential topics include, but are not limited to, autoethnography, digital self-representation, intersectional approaches to life writing, and the emerging impacts of technological shifts-such as generative AI-on authorship and equity. Desctription : How do we articulate, preserve, and present our lived experiences in an era marked by rapid cultural and technological change? Aligning with the conference theme, "Our Ruling Classes: Culture, Power and Conflict," this roundtable invites participants to investigate the shifting landscape of life writing across textual, digital, and visual formats. To foster a vibrant, multi-voiced dialogue, we encourage submissions from a wide range of perspectives, including traditional literary criticism, biographical studies, and creative pieces that feature a reflective or meta-analytical component. Presenters will deliver brief, 10-to-12-minute talks to maximize time for collective discussion. Link for submissions: https://pamla.ballastacademic.com/Home/S/20174 Submission Deadline: June 30, 2026 Conference format: In Person, in Seattle. No provision for virtual presentations If you have any queries, please reach out to the undersigned: Dr. Meghna Gangadharan Presiding Officer, "Narrating the Self Today" Email: phd1901261010@alum.iiti.ac.in

items.fullDescription: Building Bridges: Preparing for Global Business (39th Annual IATEFL BESIG Conference) When : Friday, November 20, 2026 (13.00 CET / 12.00 UK time) - Sunday, November 22, 2026 (14.00 CET / 13.00 UK time) Venue : Hotel Flemings Wien Stadthalle in Vienna, Austria. Call for Proposals Business English education sits at the intersection of education, professional communication, and global social change. In a world shaped by geopolitical tensions, economic inequalities, technological disruption, and cultural polarization, communication across cultural contexts is both more necessary and more complex than ever. Business English therefore involves more than teaching linguistic skills for the workplace; it also prepares learners to deal with cultural diversity, power structures, and ethical decision-making in international professional contexts. Effective professional communication today requires not only exchanging information but also negotiating meaning, building trust, and collaborating across cultures and perspectives. Business English courses support university students, vocational learners, and professionals in developing communicative competence, intercultural awareness, and confidence in multilingual workplaces. In many contexts, this work involves collaboration with corporate partners and engagement with current workplace practices, while also encouraging critical reflection on whose voices are heard in professional communication. The role of the business English educator is therefore to help learners bridge multiple gaps: between education and professional practice, between various cultures, and between local experiences and global systems. In a fragmented and rapidly changing world, business English education can help create spaces for inclusive, responsible, and effective professional communication. This year's conference invites contributions that explore how business English education can respond to these challenges and build the bridges needed for meaningful intercultural understanding. We particularly welcome contributions that combine practical experience, innovative teaching approaches, and reflective insights from educational and professional contexts. ----------------- Thank you for your interest in submitting a speaker proposal for the 39th IATEFL BESIG Conference. Only members of IATEFL BESIG can present at the conference. You may submit a proposal if you are not a member; however, if your proposal is accepted, you will be required to join IATEFL BESIG in order to be included in the programme. The call for proposals is open until 30 June 2026 at 16:00 (UK time). Click here for more information: https://www.iateflbesig.org/events/annual-conference

items.fullDescription: The Centre for Research on Language and Culture Contact invites you to submit an abstract for Resisting Abandonment: Language, Culture, and Ecology, an interdisciplinary conference that will explore the ways in which ecology intersects with language contact, cultural transformation, and pedagogical practice. Conference Dates: October 15-16, 2026 Location: Glendon College -York University (Toronto, Canada) Keynote Speaker: Daniel Frost, Professor of Spanish and of Latin American, Latinx, and Caribbean Studies, College of the Holy Cross Abstracts Due: June 15, 2026 - - - - - - - - - - - - - Le Centre de recherche sur le contact des langues et des cultures vous invite à soumettre un résumé pour Résister à l'abandon : langue, culture et écologie, un colloque interdisciplinaire qui explorera les liens entre l'écologie, le contact linguistique, la transformation culturelle et les pratiques pédagogiques. Dates du colloque : 15-16 octobre 2026 Lieu : Collège universitaire Glendon - Université York (Toronto, Canada) Conférencier principal : Daniel Frost, professeur d'espagnol et d'études latino-américaines, latinx et caribéennes, College of the Holy Cross Date limite de soumission des résumés : 15 juin 2026 - - - - - - - - - - - - - International Conference Resisting Abandonment: Language, Culture, and Ecology Centre for Research on Language and Culture Contact Glendon College, York University (Toronto, Canada) October 15-16, 2026 The Centre for Research on Language and Culture Contact invites you to an interdisciplinary conference that will explore the ways in which ecology intersects with language contact, cultural transformation, and pedagogical practice. Resisting Abandonment is inspired by Sunaura Taylor's groundbreaking book Disabled Ecologies: Lessons from a Wounded Desert (2024), which challenges dominant environmental narratives by centring disability, care, and interdependence. The conference aims to build on Taylor's theorization of abandonment - material and ideological - which manifests in polluted landscapes, dispossessed communities, endangered languages, and marginalized bodies. Ecological degradation and linguistic erosion often unfold together, shaped by colonialism, extractivism, migration, and neoliberal restructuring. In Ecolinguistics: Language, Ecology, and the Stories We Live By (2020), Arran Stibbe articulates the ways in which ecolinguistic inquiry - including language-contact studies - reveals how knowledges of living sustainably in the local environment are embedded in endangered languages and are vulnerable to the global spread of dominant languages. Threats to linguistic diversity can be correlated to diminished biodiversity. Resisting Abandonment will foreground the idea that languages, like ecosystems, are sites of relationality and care. When communities are displaced by climate crises, economic dispossession, or other factors, their linguistic practices shift, hybridize, or face erasure. Yet contact zones also generate creative survivance: new vernaculars, embodied knowledges, and solidarities across difference. The conference convenes scholars, educators, translators, artists, and community advocates to examine how practices of naming, storytelling, teaching, and translating can resist ecological, linguistic, and cultural abandonment. How do metaphors of purity and contamination shape both environmental and linguistic policy? What can disability justice teach us about sustaining multilingual ecologies of access? How might translation function as a form of environmental care work? Participants will explore the ethical and political stakes of attending to fragile ecologies - human and more-than-human - without reproducing narratives of loss that justify further neglect. Resisting Abandonment invites collective reflection on care as method, contact as creativity, and interdependence as a framework for ecological and linguistic futures. Examples of subtopics by discipline: Cultural Studies : analyzing representations of ecological and linguistic wastelands - including their recuperation and adaptation - in media and literature of former and current power sites and/or in post/neocolonial texts. Linguistics : examining how ecological loss accelerates language endangerment or, conversely, how language erosion facilitates ecological loss; reflecting on whether documentation practices themselves risk reproducing extractive models Sociolinguistics : studies of language contact in climate-displaced communities; examining codeswitching as ecological adaptation Translation Studies : translating environmental knowledge across Indigenous and minoritized languages without epistemic extraction Pedagogy : designing care-centred, place-based curricula that link environmental justice with multilingual education Communication Studies : analyzing how environmental crises and linguistic marginalization are framed across media, policy discourse, and digital platforms; probing how choice of language used in the media influences how communities think about ecological issues and/or manufactures consent Second-Language Teaching : incorporating local ecological narratives into L2 classrooms to foster environmental and intercultural care Minority-Language Advocacy : examining how environmental policy, urban planning, and disaster response frequently neglect linguistic accessibility, thereby compounding abandonment or proposing strategies for integrating language justice into climate-resilience planning Those interested in contributing to the conference with a 20-minute paper should send a title, 200-word abstract, and short biography to crlcc@glendon.yorku.ca by June 15, 2026. Keynote speaker: Daniel Frost, Professor of Spanish and Latin American, Latinx, and Caribbean Studies, College of the Holy Cross Scientific Committee: Sibo Chen, Associate Professor & Associate Chair, School of Professional Communication, Toronto Metropolitan University Bruce Connell, Professor of Linguistics, Language, and Society, York University's Glendon College Maryanne L. Leone, Professor of Spanish, Assumption University Shanna Lino, Associate Professor of Spanish and Latin American Cultures & Societies; Director of the Centre for Research on Language and Culture Contact, York University's Glendon College Timeline: June 15: Abstracts Due July 1: Participants Notified of Acceptance July 1-31: Early-Bird Registration August 1-31: Regular Registration September 1: Registration Closes Registration Fees: Tenure & Tenure-Track Professors: $150 / early-bird $130 Tenure & Tenure-Track Professors (York University): $100 / early-bird $85 Sessional and Contract Faculty: $90 / early-bird $80 Sessional and Contract Faculty (York University): $60 / early-bird $50 Postdoctoral Fellows & Graduate Students: $75 / early-bird $65 Postdoctoral Fellows & Graduate Students (York University): $50 / early-bird $45 Include 3 coffee breaks + 2 lunches Options: Dinner Reception on Thursday Evening - Details and Fee TBD Eco-Cultural Excursion - Details and Fee TBD Languages of the Conference: French English Accommodations: York University's Glendon College is located in mid-town Toronto, about 30-40 minutes via public transit or car from the city's downtown, where many lodging options are available close to cultural attractions. Rooms in the College's residence will also be available at affordable rates for conference participants (single dorm rooms with shared bath, WiFi, linens). Colloque international Résister à l'abandon: langue, culture et écologie Centre de recherche sur le contact des langues et des cultures Collège universitaire Glendon, Université York (Toronto, Canada) 15 et 16 octobre 2026 Le Centre de recherche sur le contact des langues et des cultures vous invite à un colloque interdisciplinaire qui explorera les manières dont l'écologie interagit avec le contact entre les langues, avec les transformations culturelles et avec les pratiques pédagogiques. Résister à l'abandon s'inspire de l'ouvrage marquant de Sunaura Taylor, Disabled Ecologies: Lessons from a Wounded Desert (2024), qui remet en question les récits environnementaux dominants à la lumière du handicap, du respect et de l'interdépendance. Le colloque vise à approfondir la théorisation de l'abandon, à la fois matériel et idéologique, proposée par Taylor, qui se manifeste dans des paysages pollués, des communautés dépossédées, des langues en voie de disparition et des corps marginalisés. La dégradation écologique et l'érosion linguistique évoluent souvent conjointement, façonnées par le colonialisme, l'extractivisme, les migrations et les restructurations néolibérales. Dans Ecolinguistics: Language, Ecology, and the Stories We Live By (2020), Arran Stibbe met en lumière la manière dont les approches écolinguistiques, y compris les études sur le contact entre les langues, permettent de mieux comprendre les liens entre langue et environnement. Les menaces qui pèsent sur la diversité linguistique peuvent ainsi être reliées à l'appauvrissement de la biodiversité. Résister à l'abandon mettra en avant l'idée que les langues, à l'instar des écosystèmes, constituent des espaces de relation et de respect. Lorsque des communautés sont déplacées par des crises climatiques, la dépossession économique ou d'autres facteurs, leurs pratiques linguistiques se transforment, s'hybrident ou risquent de disparaître. Pourtant, les zones de contact engendrent également des formes créatives de survie: de nouveaux vernaculaires, des savoirs incarnés et des solidarités au-delà des différences. Le colloque réunit des chercheur·e·s, enseignant·e·s, traducteurs/trices, artistes et militant·e·s communautaires afin d'examiner comment les pratiques de nomination, de narration, d'enseignement et de traduction peuvent résister à l'abandon écologique, linguistique et culturel. Comment les métaphores de pureté et de contamination influencent-elles les politiques environnementales et linguistiques? Que peut nous apprendre la justice du handicap sur le maintien d'écologies multilingues accessibles? De quelle manière la traduction peut-elle fonctionner comme une forme de soin environnemental? Les participant·e·s réfléchiront aux enjeux éthiques et politiques liés à l'attention portée aux écologies fragiles, humaines et plus qu'humaines, sans reproduire des récits de perte qui justifient davantage de négligence. Résister à l'abandon invite à une réflexion collective sur le respect en tant que méthode, sur le contact comme créativité et sur l'interdépendance comme cadre pour penser les futurs écologiques et linguistiques. Exemples de sous-thèmes par discipline : Études culturelles : analyser les représentations des déserts écologiques et linguistiques, y compris leur récupération et leur adaptation, dans les médias et la littérature issus de centres de pouvoir, anciens ou actuels, et/ou dans des textes post/néocoloniaux Linguistique : examiner comment la perte écologique accélère la disparition des langues ou, inversement, comment l'érosion linguistique facilite la perte écologique; réfléchir à la possibilité que les pratiques de documentation elles-mêmes reproduisent des modèles extractivistes Sociolinguistique : étudier le contact entre les langues dans des communautés déplacées par les changements climatiques; analyser l'alternance codique comme forme d'adaptation écologique Traductologie : traduire les connaissances environnementales dans les langues autochtones et minoritaires sans extraction épistémique Pédagogie et didactique : concevoir des programmes axés sur les soins et ancrés dans le territoire, qui associent la justice environnementale à l'éducation multilingue Études en communication : analyser la manière dont les crises environnementales et la marginalisation linguistique sont représentées dans les médias, les discours politiques et les plateformes numériques; examiner comment les choix linguistiques dans les médias influencent la manière dont les communautés pensent les enjeux écologiques et contribuent à fabriquer le consentement Enseignement d'une langue seconde : intégrer des récits écologiques locaux dans les cours de langue seconde afin de promouvoir le respect de l'environnement et l'ouverture interculturelle Promotion des langues minoritaires : examiner comment les politiques environnementales, l'urbanisme et les interventions en cas de catastrophe négligent souvent l'accessibilité linguistique, ce qui accentue l'abandon de ces communautés, ou proposer des stratégies visant à intégrer la justice linguistique dans la planification de la résilience climatique Si vous souhaitez contribuer au colloque avec une communication de 20 minutes, veuillez envoyer un titre, un résumé de 200 mots et une courte biographie à crlcc@glendon.yorku.ca avant le 15 juin 2026. items.fullDescription: Call for Papers: Of Pods and Pages: Rare Books and the Human-Insect/Human-Mollusk Relationship Deadline for submissions: 1st June 2026 From the Tamamushi Shrine to enconchado missal stands; from Maria Sibylla Merian to the codex purpureus, and from cochineal to wasp larvae to bookworms, this symposium seeks to showcase research on human-arthropod/gastropod entanglements in the history of the book. Papers (15-20 minutes) on insects and shelled organisms as materials, subjects, or as uninvited or unwilling participants in book and art history are welcome. They may include art and architectural objects intended for housing books. The aim is to view the materiality of texts from an insect's or mollusk's point of view, bringing the human-beyond-human/organism-organism relationship to the foreground. Please send an abstract (max. 1200 characters), title, and bio to yeidy.rosa@upr.edu. SUBMISSION DEADLINE: June 1st, 2026. Organized by the History of Art Program at the University of Puerto Rico-Río Piedras and the Andrew W. Mellon Society of Fellows in Critical Bibliography at the Rare Book School-University of Virginia. To be held in-person at UPRRP and online, Friday, September 18th, 2026

items.fullDescription: CALL FOR PAPERS, ABSTRACTS, AND PANEL PROPOSALS Midwest Popular Culture Association/Midwest American Culture Association Annual Conference Friday-Sunday, October 9-11, 2026 Horizon Convention Center | Muncie, Indiana The Midwest Popular Culture Association/American Culture Association is accepting proposals for the organization's 50th annual conference this October in Muncie, Indiana. Submit paper, abstract, or panel proposals (including the title of each presentation within the panel) with the appropriate keywords via the submissions website at https://www.mpcaaca.org/submit-panels. Individuals may only submit one paper. The deadline for receipt of proposals is May 15, 2026. Please include your name, affiliation, and e-mail address of each author/participant. A preliminary version of the schedule will be posted on our website in August 2026. The final version will be posted online prior to the conference. Special Notes Regarding Proposal Submissions: (1) AV equipment will be provided. The Association does not provide laptops, cords, or speakers. (2) If necessary, indicate and submit potential scheduling conflicts along with your proposal. (3) If you wish your presentation to be listed as MACA (rather than MPCA), please include this request with your proposal. Please plan to attend the entire conference. Panels will run at the following approximate times: Friday 9:00 a.m.-6:00 p.m., Saturday 9:00 a.m.-5:30 p.m., and Sunday 9:00 a.m.-2:00 p.m. Special events may include game night on Thursday evening, featured speakers and awards ceremony on Friday evening, and a keynote speaker and pub quiz on Saturday evening. These events will be free for conference registrants. A membership meeting will be held on Saturday. All attendees are encouraged to attend. Hotel & Lodging: Courtyard by Marriott Muncie at Horizon Convention Center MPCA Room block price: $129/night 601 S High St Muncie, Indiana 47305 Attached to the Horizon Convention Center Membership Dues & Registration Fees: Membership renewal forms for the 2026 calendar year and 2026 conference registration forms are now available on our website. All participants must register for the conference. Early bird combined membership/registration tiers: ? Full-Time Faculty: $150 ? Part-Time Faculty, Independent Scholars, Graduate Students: $125 ? Undergraduate Students: $50 Early bird registration ends on August 1, 2026. Any unregistered presenters will be dropped from the program after September 1, 2026. Payment on-site will be by cash, check, or via credit card on Square. To pre-register, send a check anytime to Julia Kuttler, McPherson College, 1600 E Euclid, McPherson, Kansas 67460. Make a check payable to the Midwest Popular Culture Association. A registration-membership form may be printed from our website. Day passes will be available for guests of the conference who are not presenting a paper. Student Travel Grants & Awards: MPCA/MACA encourages students to apply to our competitive awards. Select undergraduate students will be honored with the Pat Browne Paper Award. Select graduate students, meanwhile, will be awarded the Gary Burns Travel Awards. More details on these opportunities are available here. Cancellation Policy: If you submit a proposal (or if you accept an invitation to appear on a panel), you are promising to attend the conference if your proposal is accepted, and you are promising to pay the conference registration fee, the Association membership fee, and a late fee of $15 if applicable. If your proposal is accepted and you do not attend the conference, it is expected that you will (1) notify all members of your panel and the MPCA/MACA President (president@mpcaaca.org) of your cancellation; (2) provide such notification as early as possible; (3) arrange to have your paper distributed at the panel; (4) arrange for somebody else to carry out any other duties you may have; and (5) pay your membership and registration fees (plus late fee if applicable). If conditions 1-5 are met, you may file a written request, after the conference, for a refund of half your registration fee. For co-authored papers, all authors are welcome and encouraged to attend, but only one author is required to attend.

items.title: In Case of Emergency: Catastrophe, Climate, and Capitalism
items.excerpt: When we trace the genealogy of crisis, it can seem as if we've always been surrounded by catastrophe. items.fullDescription: When we trace the genealogy of crisis, it can seem as if we've always been surrounded by catastrophe. Different factions of the ruling class tell us that we need to be prepared, but also that preparation may be fruitless. Crises shift and expand, strengthening their hold on us through their very instability. The state of emergency, after all, "is not the exception but the rule," as Walter Benjamin theorized. It is not a single event but what Lauren Berlant called a norm "embedded" in the everyday. In the zones of crisis and in daily life, the emergency overwhelms the senses, requiring constant self-governance and limiting our political imagination. The urgent threat of climate change, though often disavowed, is at the center of today's general atmosphere of crisis. Walls hold back displaced populations and rising seas. Earth systems sustain lasting damage. Species are devastated. And with apocalyptic alacrity, capitalist-imperialist competition crosses terrains that were once uninviting and hostile, from deserts to the polar regions and outer space. So far, discourses of risk and emergency have mostly been a boon for the racist right and anti-democratic technocrats, rather than contributing to a genuine project of planetary stewardship. The quest for "energy sovereignty" has unleashed a wave of extractive interventions in the Global South amid the collapse of the postwar international order, creating new sacrifice zones and colonial resource frontiers. Amid widespread doubts about electoral institutions' ability to deliver systemic transformation, some environmentalists have even embraced climate doomerism or the technosolutionism of geoengineering. We see how climate crisis is increasingly governed through biopolitical management, securitized borders, and technocratic forms of environmental control-and how the emergency becomes yet another opportunity for further administration. Crisis discourse often privileges spectacular catastrophe while obscuring the slow, uneven, and racialized forms of ecological violence embedded in everyday life. Unlike the "fevered immediacy that governs the society of the catastrophe-as-spectacle," as Rob Nixon writes, unspectacular "slow violence" is dispersed over time. With the sirens blaring, it is easy to lose sight of the material impacts of the ideology of crisis across time and space. We can also miss the ways in which the permanent emergency warps our cultural production and social relations, concealing the most pressing contradictions of capitalism today. How might we map the cartography of crisis? In doing so, might we open space for alternative ways of thinking and living within and against crisis? How do we hold crisis at bay long enough to bring about a "real state of emergency," as Benjamin says is our task? Jason W. Moore (Binghamton) and Gökçe Günel (Rice) will deliver keynote addresses at the conference, which will also feature a curated program of poetry readings and film screenings. In Case of Emergency is organized by Aditi Kini, Tadhg Larabee, Ernest Lee, and Yolian Ogbu in collaboration with the Chicago Center for Contemporary Theory, and with support from the Committee on Environment, Geography, and Urbanization. To apply, submit an abstract (max. 300 words) and a CV via this Google form by June 30, 2026: https://forms.gle/Fj4r9oAk5r8b6Q5K6 We want to investigate how crisis is produced, circulated, and inhabited across domains, including climate, culture, political economy, media, and governance. Through this cartography of crisis, we hope to understand how we might countermap and counteract this state of ecological and social emergency. We invite proposals from graduate students in the humanities and social sciences, as well as artists, writers, and other practitioners. Our goal is to create space for imagination and speculation with people of varied backgrounds, interests, and praxes. We welcome interdisciplinary scholarship and cultural criticism attentive to the cultural, aesthetic, historical, and political dimensions of crisis. We imagine submissions might discuss: Technosolutionism and the dilemmas of growth Speculation, commodities, and disaster capitalism Fossil life as economy and desire Green neoliberalism as a political and cultural form Enclosure and destruction of the commons: water, forests, air and more Hydrocolonialism, oceanic crisis, and blue humanities Border ecologies, displacement, and the production of space State-making, world-making, and the remaking of political, social and ecological orders Toxic temporalities, slow violence, and "post"-colonial precarity Apocalypse and new worlds in literature and culture Climate pessimisms and the politics of fear and hope in crisis Resistance, strikes, and land back: movements and solidarity Community, care, and affective ecologies of crisis Participants without access to institutional funding will have the opportunity to request travel support, though we cannot guarantee it. Questions for the organizers can be sent to ccct@uchicago.edu.

How have spiritualized visions of nature shaped elite cultural production, countercultural movements, or alternative political communities? What conflicts emerge when e...
items.fullDescription: Engaging with PAMLA's 2026 theme, "Our Ruling Classes: Culture, Power, Conflict," this panel asks: How do esoteric ecological imaginaries reinforce, negotiate, or resist ruling ideologies? How have spiritualized visions of nature shaped elite cultural production, countercultural movements, or alternative political communities? What conflicts emerge when esoteric environmental ethics confront institutional religion, scientific rationalism, or capitalist extraction? Topics of interest include, but are not limited to, literary representations of enchanted ecologies, spiritual ecologies in travel writing or poetic form, occult environmental metaphysics, and the role of esoteric belief in shaping ecological imaginaries. We welcome historically grounded and theoretically informed approaches to literature, art, travel writing, popular culture, and critical theory. Topics may include ecospirituality, occult environmentalism, esoteric dimensions of deep ecology, and aesthetic practices that envision enchanted or spiritually animated landscapes as sites of cultural struggle and renewal. To submit a paper and present, you must become a PAMLA member by paying the member fee and the conference fee. For graduate students, there are scholarships available to help with the conference fee in exchange for some volunteer hours.

items.fullDescription: full name / name of organization: Marc A. Ouellette, Old Dominion University; Peter Pericles Trifonas, University of Toronto contact email: ouellema@gmail.com CFP: Handbook of the Cultural Legacy of 9/11. (under contract with Springer) Edited by: Marc A. Ouellette, Old Dominion University, (mouellet@odu.edu) and Peter Pericles Trifonas, University of Toronto From the instant the first news reports appeared, the events of 11 September 2001 changed the way texts are created, produced, shared, and received and with them the way we read, speak, think and understand our day-to-day existence changed, as well. Winston Wheeler Dixon's early collection, Post-9/11 Film & Television (2004) attempted to capture the initials changes, as did Lynn Spiegel's (2004) field defining essay. However, "9/11" has had and indeed continues to have a thorough and lasting impact on American culture, writ large. Here, we take an important cue from Susan Jeffords' studies of what she calls "Vietnam representation" (1989, 1992), which includes "films, novels, personal accounts, collections of observations and experiences, and political and social analyses" (1989, p. 1). Importantly, the texts need not deal directly with the events; rather, they bear the traces, archetypes, themes, and images that invoke the germinal event and its outcomes. It is no mistake that the American Movie Classics network ran Red Dawn (1984) in heavy rotation in late 2001 and early 2002, nor is it an accident that the film was remade in 2012, with the plot altered to include a member of the "axis of evil. No episode of Friends, with its stock images of the "twin towers," will be the same. Moreover, the presence lingers in other forms and other texts, particularly given the Trump regime's threats of "Gitmo," deportations, and the return to Bagram. As we reach the twenty-fifth anniversary of the attacks, we invite scholars in a host of disciplines to think through how "9/11" conditions the production, distribution, and reception of texts. Here, we mean texts in the truest sense, from the tiniest representation to works of art, poetry, novels, film, television, music, games, and other media. Moreover, 9/11 functions both centrifugally and centripetally, changing how texts produced both prior to and after the attacks are perceived and interpreted. Thus, we also invite scholars to theorize and consider whether post-9/11 representation has become a distinct mode or whether the weight of Vietnam representation lingers, particularly in the valourization of veterans, as the hagiography of American Sniper clearly suggests. We are still living with and experiencing the consequences of that day and the immediate responses to it. Indeed, such was the response to an earlier special issue of a journal that the project on the cultural legacies of 9/11 has grown into this handbook. Topics might include but should not be limited to the cultural productions and constructions of Allegories of 9/11 and/or the war on terror Artefacts and productions that changed after 9/11 (e.g., Red Dawn and 1990s action movies, reinterpretation of the Vietnam era and experience) Sci-fi/fantasy and themes of the war on terror (e.g., Battlestar Galactica) Ideas of cities and "fly over America." Music, popular music, and musical forms Zombies, vampires, and the post-9/11 shaping of monsters Social media, podcasts, and other emerging forms War poetry, war elegies, and other poetic interventions Sport and games as surrogates for war, the projection of nationalism and patriotism Popular culture for children, including toys, TV, apps and games Education and pedagogy Cultural memory, cultural geographies, space and place The culture and representation of veterans, "POGS" and others Journalism, editorial, and the production of "news" Language and semiotics, particularly the reshaping of what can and cannot be said. History and popular histories Memes, gifs, images, and other short digital media forms Cultural resistance and activism, including slow activism Political extremism and the return of right-wing populism The cultural play and performance of patriotism Post-9/11 games and gaming, whether video, table top, and card games The reshaping of the gender order in post-9/11 cultural productions Genre and/or genre theory, including industrial, audience and institutional expectations Ethnography and the multiple layers of community Cult media productions, their fans and their producers The limits of populism and of media effects Paratexts and user-developed content and digital memorials Again, this is only a list of suggestions and the editors welcome other topics that explore the ways in which 11 September 2001 has become an inflection point for considerations of popular culture for the last twenty-five years. Proposals (roughly 500 word abstracts) are sought by 15 Aug. 2026. Completed papers are due by 1 Dec. 2026 and no later than 1 Jan. 2027. Please send proposals, papers, and queries to Marc A. Ouellette, mouellet@odu.edu; ouellema@gmail.com

items.title: Dalit Women and the Politics of Labour: Caste, Gender and Invisibility
items.location: Saundarya and Durba, Jawaharlal Nehru University, New Delhi
items.excerpt: Labour is deeply intertwined with caste, gender and class in the socioeconomic fabric of India. However, caste and gender are the two factors that remain ignored in this discourse. In the Hindu social order, the caste system assigns vocations through arbitrary hierarchy, producing pernicious structures of marginalisation. Labour performed by Dalits is oft...
items.fullDescription: Labour is deeply intertwined with caste, gender and class in the socioeconomic fabric of India. However, caste and gender are the two factors that remain ignored in this discourse. In the Hindu social order, the caste system assigns vocations through arbitrary hierarchy, producing pernicious structures of marginalisation. Labour performed by Dalits is often stereotyped through casteist assumptions that naturalise certain kinds of work as “belonging” to these peripheral communities. These stereotypes that are perpetuated historically, culturally and socio-politically, are furthered through mechanisms of caste that operate in the material and affective realms.

Young people in the region occupy a dynamic space where tradition, globalization, technological transformation, and regional aspirations intersect.

items.title: [SCMS 2027 CFP] High-Tech / Low-Tech: Rethinking Labor, Materiality, and Scale in Media Technologies
items.excerpt: Technological systems are routinely narrated through a rhetoric of the “high-tech”: futuristic, frictionless, dematerialized, and planetary in scale. Such rhetoric directs the attention of media technologies toward the newest platform, the most advanced infrastructure, the most spectacular feat of engineering. items.fullDescription: Technological systems are routinely narrated through a rhetoric of the “high-tech”: futuristic, frictionless, dematerialized, and planetary in scale. Such rhetoric directs the attention of media technologies toward the newest platform, the most advanced infrastructure, the most spectacular feat of engineering. Yet every high-tech system is sustained by processes that are decidedly low-tech: extraction of raw materials, energy consumption at industrial scale, manual and low-wage labor, informal repair and maintenance, grassroots appropriation, and amateur practice operating at the margins of official technological narratives. The “high” is never self-sufficient; it is built on, and constantly obscures, the “low.”

items.fullDescription: Human machine interfacing can be as simple as pressing a button or as complex and entangled (also entangling) as inserting a brain chip into the skull. science fiction. Humans with implants, prosthetic and hybrid humans with electronic and mechanical extensions are yet another level are no longer science fiction. Yet, human-machine interfacing has started long before the invention of these technologies. Machines did communicate with us and tell us about themselves even before chatbots were invented. The clanking of a hammer on the anvil tells us that it is old and dull. The whistle of a microwave tells us that dinner is ready. The process of interfacing is not a one-way process. Through it, humans also communicate with the machine.
