items.fullDescription: Call for Contributors Into the Fog: Essays on Dead by Daylight The call for papers has been extended to August 21st, 2026. While we are particularly interested in submissions dealing with lore and worldbuilding, survival horror, fandom, online discourse, anime and horror, and transmedia ventures and shared worlds of horror, we welcome all topics. Dead by Daylight (DBD) is an asymmetric four versus one online horror game where a team of survivors must work together to escape from a brutal killer, developed and published by Behavior Interactive. From its debut in 2016 the game has risen to become one of the most popular horror gaming experiences. As a live-service game with frequent updates, the game has developed a notable community following with prominent streamers, content creators, and popular memes. The game has inspired fans to cosplay, stream their matches, and develop fanart and fanfiction. The game is also known for its frequent collaborations with classic and emerging horror franchises, including Halloween , Nightmare on Elm Street , Alien , Stranger Things , Five Nights at Freddy's , and drag performers The Boulet Brothers. The game has also had different versions and spinoffs including Dead By Daylight Mobile (Behavior Interactive 2020) and The Casting of Frank Stone (Supermassive Games 2024). In November 2023, the gaming site Polygon reported Dead by Daylight reached 60 million players, and the game is celebrating its tenth anniversary in 2026. We invite proposals for original, unpublished essays that explore the different facets of horror and gaming in Dead by Daylight for an edited volume under contract with McFarland. We welcome interdisciplinary submissions from all career stages, including independent scholars and graduate students. Submissions should be scholarly but accessible to a general audience. The collection will be published in English, but we welcome submissions from and are eager to work with scholars working in other languages who are interested in publishing new work on the game in English. Suggested topics with DBD may include, but are not limited to, the following: · Lore and worldbuilding · Fan culture and community · Horror in video games and the survival horror genre · Transmedia ventures and shared worlds of horror - Anime and horror · Toxicity and online discourse · World horror, folk horror, internet horror, and transnational dimensions of horror · LGBTQ+ representation and community · Race, horror, and survival · The monstrous feminine, final girls, and women in horror · Cosplay and fan work · Embodiment and avatars · Accessibility and horror games · Interfaces and game menus · Ruins, rust, and history in horror · Game mechanics, balancing updates, and fairness · Affect and abjection · Player sentiment and experiences · Licensing, collaborations, and merchandising Submission Guidelines Abstracts of 300 words, as well as brief author bios, should be submitted to Daniel Fandino (Daniel.Fandino@ucf.edu) & Cody Mejeur (codymeje@buffalo.edu) by our extended deadline of August 21, 2026 . The editors will review all submitted proposals and notify applicants by the end of August 2026. Chapters should be approximately between 5000-8000 words, and first drafts of completed manuscripts will be due December 15, 2026. The expected publication date will be 2027-2028. Note: Acceptance of a proposed abstract does not guarantee the acceptance of the full chapter. Chapters will undergo both editor and peer review. About the Editors Daniel Fandino (PhD) is the coordinator of the Digital Exploration Center at the University of Central Florida. He has previously co-edited a book on the Marvel cinematic universe for McFarland and has written articles on EVE Online and the history of computer gaming. Cody Mejeur (They/them, PhD) is Assistant Professor of Media Study at University at Buffalo, SUNY, and Director of the Amatryx Gaming Lab & Studio there. They are currently the game director for Trans Folks Walking , a narrative game about trans experiences. They are an editor of Historiographies of Game Studies (punctum 2025), co-editor of the trans narratology special issue of the Narrative journal (2024) and have published numerous articles and book chapters in Games & Culture , Digital Humanities Quarterly , and Resilience: A Journal of the Environmental Humanities , among others. Contact Email Daniel Fandino: daniel.fandino@ucf.edu Cody Mejeur: codymeje@buffalo.edu

items.fullDescription: “It is worse, much worse, than you think” states David Wallace-Wells at the opening of his The Uninhabitable Earth: Life After Warming (2019). “When do we start physically attacking the things that consume our planet and destroy them with our own hands?” asks Andreas Malm in How to Blow Up a Pipeline (2021). “I don’t think about hope much anymore. But I do think about imagination,” writes Terry Tempest Williams in an interview contained in A voice in the Wilderness: Conversations with Terry Tempest Williams (2006). In the spaces between these statements we encounter a range of reactions to our warming condition, from blunt pessimism, to righteous anger, to nuanced reframing.

items.fullDescription: CALL FOR PAPERS / CALL FOR PRESENTATIONS EUROPEAN HEBREW JOURNAL INTERNATIONAL SCHOLARLY ONLINE ZOOM CONFERENCE New Discoveries and New Directions in Biblical, Hebrew, and Theological Studies 6-8 November 2026 Live Online via Zoom ABSTRACT SUBMISSION DEADLINE: 20 AUGUST 2026 Present Your Research at an International Scholarly Conference The European Hebrew Journal invites scholars, researchers, university professors, postdoctoral researchers, doctoral candidates, graduate students, independent scholars, and other qualified researchers from around the world to submit proposals for presentations at the European Hebrew Journal International Scholarly Online Zoom Conference, taking place on 6-8 November 2026. This three-day international academic conference brings together scholars working across biblical studies, Hebrew language and linguistics, Jewish studies, theology, religious studies, history, archaeology, textual studies, and related disciplines. The conference is organized in support of the Diamond Open Access mission of the European Hebrew Journal, promoting international scholarly exchange and wider accessibility and visibility of academic research. Join an Expanding International Programme The conference programme already includes distinguished scholars and researchers from universities and academic institutions around the world. Confirmed speakers include, among others: Prof. em. Dr. Dr. h.c. Eckart Otto Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München / Hochschule für Philosophie München Prof. Dr. Aaron Koller Regius Professor of Hebrew, University of Cambridge Prof. Dr. Avraham Faust Bar-Ilan University Prof. Joshua Schwartz Chair, Board of Directors, Israel Antiquities Authority Professor Emeritus, Bar-Ilan University Prof. Gabriele Boccaccini Professor Emeritus, University of Michigan Founding Director, Enoch Seminar Prof. Rivka Halevy Professor Emerita of Hebrew Language, The Hebrew University of Jerusalem Prof. Dr. Yigal Levin Bar-Ilan University as well as scholars from the United States, United Kingdom, Israel, Germany, Switzerland, Denmark, Italy, Ethiopia, Nigeria, and other countries. The programme is continuing to expand, and a limited number of additional presentation proposals are now being considered. Areas of Interest We particularly welcome original research related to: Hebrew Bible / Old Testament Biblical Studies Biblical Hebrew Modern Hebrew Mishnaic and Rabbinic Hebrew Medieval Hebrew Hebrew Linguistics Semitic Linguistics Historical Linguistics Philology Lexicography Hebrew Grammar and Syntax Textual Criticism Dead Sea Scrolls Qumran Studies Second Temple Judaism Rabbinic Literature Jewish Studies Jewish History Judaism Theology Religious Studies Early Christianity Christianity and its Jewish Background Biblical Interpretation and Reception Archaeology of Israel Biblical Archaeology Ancient Near Eastern Archaeology Ancient Near Eastern Studies Epigraphy Palaeography Manuscript Studies History of Religion Jewish-Christian Relations Jewish-Muslim Relations Christianity, Judaism, and Islam in comparative perspective Biblical and Religious Literature History and Culture of the Ancient Near East History of Israel Hebrew and Semitic Manuscript Traditions Digital Humanities Computational Linguistics Computational Approaches to Biblical and Historical Research Interdisciplinary approaches connecting language, history, archaeology, religion, theology, and textual studies Research introducing new discoveries, new evidence, new methodologies, reassessments of established interpretations, or genuinely new directions of research is especially welcome. Presentation Format Each accepted presenter will receive an official 30-minute conference presentation slot: 20 minutes - Research Presentation 10 minutes - Questions and Scholarly Discussion Presentations will be delivered live online via Zoom. The online format enables scholars from different countries and academic traditions to participate without the financial and logistical costs of international travel, accommodation, or visas. Who May Submit? Proposals are welcome from: University professors Researchers Postdoctoral researchers Doctoral / PhD candidates Graduate students Early-career scholars Independent researchers Biblical scholars Hebrew specialists Linguists and philologists Historians Archaeologists Theologians Scholars of religion Jewish Studies researchers Scholars working in related interdisciplinary fields Academic affiliation is welcome but is not in itself a requirement. Proposals will be evaluated primarily according to the scholarly quality and relevance of the proposed research. How to Submit a Proposal Please send your application to: office@hebrew.edu.rs Please use the email subject: CFP 2026 - Presentation Proposal Your application should include: Full name Academic title or current academic position Institutional affiliation, if applicable Country Email address Proposed presentation title Abstract of approximately 150-250 words 3-5 keywords Short academic biography Submission Deadline 20 AUGUST 2026 Proposals submitted before the deadline will be evaluated for inclusion in the developing international conference programme. Applicants are encouraged to submit as early as possible while programme slots remain available. Academic Selection Presentation proposals will be considered on the basis of: scholarly quality originality methodological clarity relevance to the conference significance of the research question potential contribution to international scholarly discussion Acceptance is based on academic evaluation and is completely separate from conference payment. Presenter Registration There is no submission fee. Registration is required only after a proposal has been accepted. Submitting an abstract and presentation proposal is completely free of charge. There is no application fee and no abstract submission fee. Only applicants whose presentation proposals have been academically accepted will be invited to complete presenter registration. Accepted Presenter Registration Regular Presenter: €89 Student / PhD Presenter: €49 Presenter registration is payable only after academic acceptance. What Accepted Presenters Receive Accepted presenter registration includes: An official place in the international conference programme A 30-minute presentation session 20 minutes for presentation 10 minutes for questions and scholarly discussion Live access to the complete three-day conference Access to presentations by international scholars Participation in live questions and academic discussions Twelve months of access to the complete conference recording library Digital conference programme Digital certificate of participation Downloadable conference booklet with speaker biographies and abstracts Curated reading lists and bibliographies Digital conference participation badge suitable for LinkedIn and professional portfolios Access to additional conference resources provided to registered participants Complimentary access to two additional live online scholarly Zoom sessions planned for December 2026 Twelve Months of Conference Access Presenters do not need to attend every lecture live. Every registered presenter will receive twelve months of on-demand access to the complete conference recording library, making it possible to follow presentations and scholarly discussions from different time zones and return to important lectures after the conference. One presenter registration provides access to the complete three-day academic programme and twelve months of conference recordings. Scholarly Visibility The conference is designed not only as a live international scholarly meeting but also as a platform for the continuing visibility and dissemination of academic research. Conference proceedings and published presentation materials will receive persistent Crossref-registered DOIs. Eligible scholarly outputs will be structured for scholarly discovery through services such as Google Scholar and OpenAlex. Conference-derived research articles subsequently published in the European Hebrew Journal may additionally benefit from the journal's scholarly dissemination and indexing infrastructure. Supporting Diamond Open Access Scholarship The conference supports the Diamond Open Access mission of the European Hebrew Journal. Diamond Open Access scholarship aims to make academic research available without subscription charges for readers and without publication charges for authors. By participating in the conference, scholars become part of a wider international initiative dedicated to scholarly communication, research visibility, academic exchange, and accessible knowledge. Bring Your Research into the International Conversation Are you working on a new interpretation of a biblical text? Have you identified previously overlooked linguistic evidence? Are you researching Hebrew, Jewish history, theology, religion, archaeology, manuscripts, ancient texts, or the historical world of the Bible? Are you developing a new methodology or challenging an established scholarly interpretation? This conference provides an opportunity to present that research to an international audience and discuss it with researchers working across related disciplines. We especially encourage proposals that introduce new discoveries and new directions - research that can generate discussion, connect disciplines, and contribute meaningfully to contemporary scholarship. SUBMIT YOUR ABSTRACT BY 20 AUGUST 2026 Send your proposal to: office@hebrew.edu.rs European Hebrew Journal International Scholarly Online Zoom Conference 6-8 November 2026 New Discoveries and New Directions in Biblical, Hebrew, and Theological Studies Live Online via Zoom Official Conference Website: https://conference.hebrew.edu.rs/

items.excerpt: Date: October 10-11, 2026 Location: SMU Main Campus, Dallas, TX Theme: Movement & Borderlands Abstract Submission Deadline: August 28, 2026 Keynotes: Dr. Tim Bowman & Dr. Elda María Román Graduate students of Southern Methodist University's Departments of English, History, and Anthropology, in collaboration with the Moody School of Advanced...
items.fullDescription: Date: October 10-11, 2026 Location: SMU Main Campus, Dallas, TX Theme: Movement & Borderlands Abstract Submission Deadline: August 28, 2026 Keynotes: Dr. Tim Bowman & Dr. Elda María Román Graduate students of Southern Methodist University's Departments of English, History, and Anthropology, in collaboration with the Moody School of Advanced Studies, Dedman College Interdisciplinary Institute, and the department of English, have collaborated to hold the third annual Engaging Research Across the Humanities (ERAH) Conference at SMU from October 10-October 11, 2026. ERAH 2026 will prioritize the development of interdisciplinary connections and aims to foster a supportive environment for both graduate students and advanced undergraduates engaged in strong research. There will be special emphasis placed on creating opportunities for participants with limited or no prior conference experience. The theme for ERAH 2026 is Movement & Borderlands. If you have any questions, please email arundhatig@smu.edu. Borders simultaneously construct and limit meaning. By demarcating entities, we hold the power to define space and identity. In the same manner, those entities are restricted to oppositional definitions. What does it mean to occupy borderlands, to move across them and through them? How is the deconstruction of borders, or reconceptualization of definitional demarcation, itself an act of meaning-making that exists without opposition? How do borderlands complicate cultural conceptions rooted in duality? How does movement across and through borderlands produce opportunity for new forms of meaning-making not rooted in hard lines and limitations? This year's theme asks us to think critically about the roles of both movement and borderlands in our respective disciplines by considering these questions and others. We invite you to consider the roles of both movement and borderlands within the works you study-be it literary works, historical archives, etc.-as well as how pervasive disciplinary paradigms shape the ways in which you approach your scholarship. Possible topics may include but are not limited to: Migration, mobility, and displacement Citizenship and belonging Racial, ethnic, national, religious identity Borders as constructs Frontiers Artistic and embodied movement Indigenous perspectives on imposed borders Nationalism and borderlands Environmental and ecological borders Linguistic borders Tourism and global circulation We invite abstracts of 200-250 words for both individual presentations and fully-constructed panels (3-4 speakers). items.excerpt: Ethical questions have become central to museum work, increasingly shaping how institutions acquire, preserve, interpret, and sometimes deaccession collections. Yet discussions around the pedagogy of museum ethics are underdeveloped. This session will convene scholars and practitioners to collaboratively explore best practices for teaching museum ethics a...
items.fullDescription: Ethical questions have become central to museum work, increasingly shaping how institutions acquire, preserve, interpret, and sometimes deaccession collections. Yet discussions around the pedagogy of museum ethics are underdeveloped. This session will convene scholars and practitioners to collaboratively explore best practices for teaching museum ethics across a range of educational contexts. I invite contributions that consider how educators help students enter ethical conversations and develop their own orientations and convictions. Perspectives may address semester-long courses in museum ethics, focused units embedded within other classes, or museum-based training programs. Relevant topics include repatriation and restitution, provenance research, the care and display of human remains, confronting the legacies of colonization, interpreting sites of tragedy, violence, and/or slavery, or the responsibilities of museums towards descendant and source communities. Contributors are encouraged to share case studies, assignments, classroom strategies, or institutional partnerships and reflective assessments of successes and tensions encountered in teaching ethical issues. This session aims to foster dialogue across disciplinary and institutional boundaries to move toward shared frameworks for teaching museum ethics that support emerging practitioners in imagining and enacting ethical futures.

items.fullDescription: Abstract Demanding that student writers maintain an objective, third-person stance when writing academic essays persists in the academy. However, we hold that providing students with strategies that help them develop a hospitable mindset in the writing process, one in which they aim to make a meaningful connection with their readers through the use of both first person and personal experience, does not diminish the scholarly rigor of college-level work. Moreover, by adopting the attitude that student writing is not immediately designed for publication, educators can focus on helping students find ways to connect with readers while cultivating their own writing styles. items.fullDescription: This panel at the SAMLA 97 conference (Nov. 5-7, 2026) examines hospitality as a critical framework within postcolonial studies, attending to the ways literary and cultural texts negotiate welcome, refusal, obligation, and exposure in the aftermath of empire. Within empire studies, hospitality emerges as a fraught ethical and aesthetic relation shaped by colonial histories, uneven mobility, and asymmetrical power. We consider how such texts register these dynamics across postcolonial contexts. Readings across genres and media—including novels, graphic novels, life writing, film, poetry, and theory—deploy hospitality as a vital lens for understanding postcolonial subjectivity, relationality, and the ongoing legacies of colonial governance.

items.fullDescription: Virginia Woolf’s Mrs Dalloway (1925) remains a cornerstone of the modernist literary canon. Often celebrated as Woolf’s greatest novel, the plot is set in post-World War I London and revolves around a single day in the life of its protagonist, Mrs Clarissa Dalloway, as she prepares to host an evening party. Beneath its seemingly simple plot, the novel exemplifies a profound exploration of consciousness, time, and the inner lives of characters through its extensive use of the stream-of-consciousness technique. Although narrated in a third-person omniscient voice, the narrative primarily focuses on the inner consciousness of the characters.

items.title: MICTR 2026 : 7th Marrakech International Conference on Tourism Research (MICTR) THE AI TURN IN TOURISM: NARRATIVE SHIFT OR REAL TRANSFORMATION?
items.location: Nov 10 ABSTRACT Jun 30 DAYS 0 LEFT MICTR 2026 : 7th Marrakech International Conference on Tourism R · UCA
items.excerpt: Overall Conference Theme of the 7th Edition Tourism has never seen the development of artificial intelligence (AI) as fast as we see today. This includes the automation of tourist interaction, use of predictive analytics for their data, and increasing use of personalized systems with the emergence of generative AI (GenAI) that can produce all sorts of con...
items.fullDescription: Overall Conference Theme of the 7th Edition Tourism has never seen the development of artificial intelligence (AI) as fast as we see today. This includes the automation of tourist interaction, use of predictive analytics for their data, and increasing use of personalized systems with the emergence of generative AI (GenAI) that can produce all sorts of content from texts, images, travel itineraries, and even support tourist decision-making processes. An "AI turn" in tourism is now becoming increasingly common with many observers referring to a moment similar to previous digital or platform turn. However, there is one question remaining: Does this shift toward AI truly represent a structural transformation of the industry, or is it simply a change in rhetoric that redefines the way we approach innovation? There has been a growing body of academic research examining how artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into tourists' practices and experiences. However, there remains a limited understanding of the depth and extent of the transformation that AI may bring to the tourism sector. While AI clearly illustrates evolving changes in service delivery and customer interactions-particularly through tools such as large language models like ChatGPT-its applications extend further. AI is now being used for trip planning, customer communication, and the creation of marketing content, among other functions, thereby enhancing and, in some cases, automating service delivery. According to Sigala (2024), the use of generative AI (GenAI) will continue to shape how customers interact with tourism and hospitality products, by transforming value co-creation processes and redefining customer engagement with businesses. Additionally, Bulchand-Gidumal et al. (2024) suggest that AI could significantly alter tourism marketing practices, particularly through hyper-personalization, predictive targeting, and automation. Nevertheless, these emerging applications also pose important challenges for companies, especially in balancing the appropriate level of human involvement with machine-driven interactions in service encounters. On the other hand, many reviews of late have cautioned against associating technological adoption with structural change. In an integrated review of generative AI in tourism management, Li (2025) observes that a great deal of empirical research between 2022 and 2024 has focused on applications and functionalities of generative AI instead of actual organization-wide change. Therefore, the literature remains conceptually fragmented, and robust theoretical frameworks explaining how AI produces sustained managerial change are still emerging. Fouad, Salem, and Fathy (2024) similarly observe that while GenAI is growing fast within tourism and hospitality research, there are also persistent concerns relating to algorithmic bias, governance, transparency, and accountability which will comprise claims of fully realized transformations. The debate becomes even more complex within smart tourism ecosystems. Koo et al. (2025), proposed an "AI-powered smart tourism 2.0" model with the aim of redefining how destinations are governed and resources can be allocated and decisions made in real time by destination management organizations. These changes however appear to have an unevenness and reliance upon several factors including digital maturity, institutional capability and strategic alignment. For these reasons, Buhalis et al. (2024) argue that the adoption of technology in tourism is often incremental, rather than an abrupt change in management. Therefore, it is possible that the AI turn will merely be another form of reinforcing existing structures rather than challenging them. Beyond the efficiency of the operation of AI, it is important to analyze the socio- organizational implications of this technological transition. The reviews on the conversational AI show that there are benefits in terms of increased efficiency and customer satisfaction, yet they also highlight the need for trust, acceptance, and the ethical protections necessary for the use of this technology. In addition, at a policy level, the OECD (2024) has highlighted concerns with respect to the reorganization of work, the need for the reconfiguration of skills, privacy issues, and the need to adapt regulations. Depending on the actions taken by governments, these factors can either accelerate or limit the extent of the transformation associated with the adoption of AI. Overall, this body of research clearly demonstrates that AI has changed both service design and operational practices for tourism. Whereas, it is an empirical and theoretical matter as to whether the "AI turn" will result in the transformation of governance structures, organizational architectures, the professional roles of people working in the industry, and the strategic decisions made by them. As such, the conference theme invites submissions from researchers that provide critical assessments of what is being done with AI in tourism today and whether there is a new form of substantive change in the way the industry is operated, or simply a new form of a powerful narrative about technology. MICTR: Broad Scope of Tourism, Destinations, Heritage, and Hospitality Research While the above topics provide general guidance, MICTR 2026 welcomes all contributions related to tourism, destinations, and hospitality, even if they are not explicitly listed. Multidisciplinary perspectives-including management, economics, sociology, geography, anthropology, law, and information systems-are strongly encouraged. Submissions (in French, English, or Arabic) may take various forms-such as literature reviews, case studies, or empirical research-and may adopt diverse epistemological and methodological approaches, provided that they contribute robust and well- established knowledge. Dates and Submission Guidelines The conference is open to a wide range of topics related to tourism, heritage, and hospitality, and welcomes diverse research perspectives. Abstract Submission Submissions should consist of an abstract of at least 300 words. The abstract must clearly present the theoretical framework, research problem, methodology, and expected results. A concise list of key references should also be included. Full Paper Submission Authors are required to submit their full papers in Microsoft Word (.docx) format. The preferred font is Times New Roman, with the main text set in 12-point size and fully justified for readability. Each paper should be between 6,000 and 8,000 words, including references, tables, and figures. In addition, an abstract of 150-200 words must be provided, along with 4-6 relevant keywords to enhance indexing and visibility. All citations and references should follow the APA (7th edition) style. items.title: Déplacements dans les réseaux transcoloniaux : l'Asie, l’Afrique et l’Europe reliés
items.excerpt: Pendant la période de l'Indochine française, les premiers vietnamiens sont acheminés en Nouvelle-Calédonie en tant que travailleurs sous-contrat dans les mines de nickel. items.fullDescription: Pendant la période de l'Indochine française, les premiers vietnamiens sont acheminés en Nouvelle-Calédonie en tant que travailleurs sous-contrat dans les mines de nickel. Cette période marque en parallèle la rébellion très présente des autochtones de l'île - les Kanak - face à la dépossession territoriale des colons français. Le refus de participer à l'industrie minière d'un groupe favorise l'expatriation de l'autre sur l'archipel en pleine ère de la colonisation française dans plusieurs colonies. Le roi tonkinois Ham Nghi, à l'âge de 18 ans, a été placé en exil en Algérie après des années de mouvements de résistance contre la puissance coloniale française. Son expulsion fait écho à celle de la Reine malgache Ranavalona III, qui a eu lieu après l'annexion de Madagascar par la France en 1896. L'ensemble de l'empire français, étendu de l'Indochine à l'Afrique insulaire, est sujet à la déportation dans la plus grande colonie de peuplement. Ce réseau de déportation des colonies liées met en avant la question des outils de domination employés par le système colonial. Malgré les différentes populations colonisées, la stratégie de domination s'applique d'une certaine façon. **** Dans le cadre académique au sein des études francophones et françaises, nous voyons souvent des pistes de spécialisation distinctes, telles que les études européennes, les études caribéennes, et les études postcoloniales francophones. Les cours d'histoire et de littérature offrent également des réflexions particulières selon une région spécifique ainsi qu'une époque donnée. L'objectif de former les futurs chercheurs dans des domaines précis, faute d'études approfondies sur les caractéristiques transcontinentales, risque de faire oublier qu'au coeur de l'histoire de l'un est tissée celle de l'autre. Cette imbrication transnationale et transcommunautaire, inévitable soit-elle, est due à la fois aux déplacements migratoires, à l'exil d'après-guerre, et à la mobilisation de la force de travail par le système capitaliste et colonial. Lorsque l'on met en évidence ce lien intrinsèque entre des événements, on fait émerger un réseau transcolonial qui lie l'Afrique, l'Asie, et/ou l'Europe. Ce réseau nous oblige à réfléchir à l'interconnexion de l'un à l'autre, d'une communauté spécifique à une autre soi-disant éloignée. Dans le contexte du monde d'aujourd'hui, une telle conscience de l'interconnexion des histoires coloniales peut susciter des réflexions : Peut-on vraiment ignorer le combat de l'autre ? Quels seront les enjeux ? Communications à envoyer soit en anglais, soit en français.

items.fullDescription: Setting the stage: a theatre and performance dissertation writing group Writing a dissertation can be lonely: we want to change that. Many of us first fell in love with theater because — through exploratory rehearsals, late-night tech runs, and joyful opening nights — we found camaraderie and connection, both of which can feel distant in graduate school. If theater is best practiced with others, how can our research and writing processes be shaped by the same commitment to community-building?

The schedule will take shape around readings between Marianne Moore and other writers.

items.title: Inhospitable America: The Confounding Position of African American
items.excerpt: The idea of home is curious concept for African Americans. Though integral to the development and sustainability of the United States, the social death and cultural trauma of slavery render this country inhospitable to Black bodies and the psyches that inhabit them. African Americans are both at home and homeless. This tenuousness places them in a liminal...
items.fullDescription: The idea of home is curious concept for African Americans. Though integral to the development and sustainability of the United States, the social death and cultural trauma of slavery render this country inhospitable to Black bodies and the psyches that inhabit them. African Americans are both at home and homeless. This tenuousness places them in a liminal space in which identity is simultaneously self-asserted and assigned, multifaceted, while limited, a fount of agency and a tool for impotence. The intersectional nature of Black femininity further complicates notions of identity and American hospitality. Black men have unsuccessfully employed patriarchy as an intraracial tool to combat the aforementioned social death.

items.fullDescription: Rome and Capri, 21–28 June, 2027 F. Scott Fitzgerald visited Italy on two distinct occasions: first in the spring of 1921 during his and Zelda’s long-deferred honeymoon trip, and again from late 1924 to early 1925 during his unsuccessful attempt to economize. While the Fitzgeralds made brief stops in Venice, San Remo, Portofino, Savona, Pisa, Fiesole, Florence, and Naples, it was in the two host sites of this conference—Rome and Capri—that he spent the most time. It was here that he found inspiration for some of his most celebrated works, as well as several others that remain underexplored.

Whether it's a literature, documentary, and/or cinema class that focuses on migration, or an activity designed to introduce these topics in language classes at all levels, instructors must be able to navigate difficult conversations, making sure that the discussion remains productive and inclusive even when it creates discomfort. In line with this year's theme of "Hospitality", this roundtable invites short (5- 10-minute) presentations that explore ideas and content related to migrations and diaspora in any language and content classes. What texts do we include in our syllabi to address both hospitality and, more often, inhospitality towards migrants and refugees? What in-class activities, homework, and assessments do we design to elicit students' reflections on such complicated themes? In terms of teaching strategies, which ones can we use to make sure all students feel included in class and in the conversation? What decolonial practices can we utilize to foster both a positive class environment and impactful discussions? Can AI help us with any of these tasks? Presentations may focus on cultural production and primary sources used in L2/LS and content classes related to any languages, migrant communities, or diasporic cultures (including, but not limited to, Afro-Italian, Afro-Brazilian, Italian-American, Asian-American, internal migrations) or on pedagogical aspects, activities, and practices. Please submit a 200- 250-word abstract and a short bio through the SAMLA website by September 1, 2026 (https://samla. ballastacademic.com/Home/S/ 19672). For questions, don't hesitate to contact the roundtable organizers: Giuseppina Gemboni (ggemboni@andrew.cmu.edu) and Francisco (Paco) Chen-López (paco@spelman.edu).

items.fullDescription: The Société Rencesvals, Pan-American Branch, invites proposals from scholars whose research examines Romance-language epics as sites of social discourse. Far from being merely “songs of deeds,” these texts were critical commentaries on contemporary ideologies. They thus speak profoundly to processes of self-conceptualization in far-ranging topics including –but not limited to– regional/national identity, faith, gender, and race. We are interested in the examination of how Romance-language epics use discourse to construct value systems that contribute to conceptions of the self, situating this literature in the larger study of the production of ideologies in the Middle Ages.

items.fullDescription: Plastic / Plasticity Literature and Culture and the Material of a (Bygone?) Era Plastic is a defining material of our era. Its properties—plasticity, durability, the ability to imitate any shape, its toxicity, and indecomposability—are also properties of contemporary culture and literature. The proposed thematic issue begins with the premise that plastic can be read simultaneously as a historical substance and as a "theory machine"—a tool for understanding cultural texts and the experience of contemporary times. "My approach, in this paper, is one of thinking with plastic through its metaphoricity and materiality, its relationality and gestationality; in short, a material mediality.” [R. Gosh]

items.fullDescription: Free of taxes (No APC) - Open Access Journal Academic Journal: Em Tese (ISSN 1982-0739) OA Submission format: .doc or .docx, font 12, spacing 1,5, from 10 to 20 pages long. Submission guidelines : https://periodicos.ufmg.br/index.php/emt/about/submissions Journal homepage: https://periodicos.ufmg.br/index.php/emt/index Questions: lauraribaraujo@gmail.com This special edition will be published in 2027/01 More than four centuries after his death, William Shakespeare (1564-1616) remains one of the most widely read, translated, staged, and reinterpreted authors in the world. His work spans a multitude of media platforms and continues to spark fundamental debates about language, subjectivity, power, gender, history, and performativity. "Our" Shakespeare, as Terry Eagleton suggests, is not the same as that of his contemporaries, and it is precisely the processes of (re)reading and (re)writing that rearticulate his work and ensure its critical and interpretative survival. It is in this sense that this call for papers aims to gather artistic and academic contributions that expand the Shakespearean field of studies. We welcome article submissions that approach his poetic and dramatic production in its multiple facets; from classical to contemporary, including literary analysis, performance, staging and production of Shakespearean texts, issues of translation and adaptation, fan rewritings, comparative and linguistic studies, among other possibilities: Literary and poetic analysis of Shakespeare's works; Textual and editing studies; Literary translation processes; Critical reviews of the state of the art; Studies of the reception of dramatic and poetic works; Comparative readings; Theatre, performance and staging/production; Adaptations and rewritings, including cinematic, literary and intermedial versions of Shakespearean works in modern and post-colonial contexts; Fan studies and productions; Cultural and theoretical studies, including issues of gender, race, politics, ecocriticism, and post-humanism in Shakespeare's texts and receptions; Digital humanities and virtual contexts of the work; Teaching Shakespeare across different levels. For the Resenhas section, we invite submissions of texts that discuss works published in the last three years about the bard, including analyses of theoretical and artistic books and reissues. Up to 15 pages. For the Poéticas section, original artistic works may be submitted, such as texts, photographs, illustrations, stagings, videos, audios, poems, and short stories that engage with the central theme of the dossier, preferably accompanied by a brief introductory note (up to one page) situating the aesthetic gesture and its mediations. Up to 20 pages. Em Tese is a biannual electronic journal of the Postgraduate Program in Literary Studies at the Federal University of Minas Gerais (UFMG) in Brazil dedicated to disseminating productions and research in the areas of Literary Studies and Arts. In addition to the texts in the dossier, the journal accepts, on a continuous basis, unpublished texts that address the areas of Literary Theory, Brazilian Literature, Classical and Medieval Literatures, Modern Foreign Literatures, Literatures from the Anglophone world, and Comparative Literature.

items.fullDescription: Call for Chapters Rhetoric and Communication. Interdisciplinary Studies in the Humanities The intersection of Rhetoric and Communication continues to attract the interest of many scholars, particularly within the fields of the Humanities and Social Sciences. The scope of analysis is wide-ranging, encompassing literature and culture, language studies and advertising, communication studies and politics, among other domains. In this Volume, we aim to bring together a set of studies that focus directly on topics shared by Rhetoric and Communication, from Classical Antiquity to the present, from an interdisciplinary perspective. Scholarly contributions across the Humanities will enhance our understanding of the influence of rhetoric and communication on society, taking into account, on the one hand, there is a vast legacy that merits further study and, on the other, new forms of communication require us to reassess the impact of the rhetorical art. This Volume welcomes contributions of a theoretical or empirical nature, including case studies, from within the field of the Humanities. Possible topics include: · Rhetorical and communication theory applied to discourse; · Treatises on rhetoric and communication; · The presence of rhetorical genres in contemporary forms of communication; · Argumentation techniques and persuasion in literary texts, the media, advertising, or other narrative forms; · The contemporary relevance of teaching rhetoric and communication; · The contemporary application of classical rhetoric in the media; · Rhetoric in political discourse and in literary composition; · Philosophical perspectives on rhetoric and communication; · The role of the audience and the addressee in rhetorical theory and in the communicative process; · Representations of rhetoric and communication in the Arts. Editors: Cristina Santos Pinheiro, Joaquim Pinheiro, Rui Carlos Fonseca, Samuel Mateus, Telmo Reis e Vanessa Cesário Proposals, in Word format, should be submitted by 10 September 2026 to the following email address: retorica.comunicacao@mail.uma.pt The Volume is scheduled for publication in March 2027 by a leading national publisher. All submissions will be subject to scientific evaluation (blind peer review). Authors will be notified of the review decision by 30 November 2026. 1. Accepted languages Submissions will be accepted in Portuguese, French, English, and Spanish. 2. Formatting guidelines 2.1. Length and formatting: main text: maximum of 20 A4 pages and minimum of 12 A4 pages; font: 11 pt, Aptos, 1.5 line spacing; footnotes: 10 pt, Aptos, single spacing. 2.2. Title centred, 12 pt, bold, Aptos. 2.3. Author name(s), affiliation (University, Institute, Research Unit or equivalent), email address, and ORCID should be provided in 11 pt, Aptos. 2.4. Two abstracts (maximum 250 words each) must be included: one in the language of the article and one in English, followed by up to five keywords. 3. General guidelines 3.1. Citations and references should follow APA style (7th ed.); all citations must be properly identified. 3.2. Quotations longer than three lines must be indented 1 cm from the left margin. 3.3. a) Italics should be used for the titles of works, modern monographs, and journals. b) Quotation marks (" ") should be used for quotations from modern texts. c) Italics should not be used for Latin abbreviations (op. cit., loc. cit., cf., ibid., in…). 4. Footnotes Footnotes should be brief. 5. Images/Graphs/Tables 5.1. Any graphical elements must be clearly identified and numbered. 5.2. Images must be submitted in .jpeg format, with a minimum resolution of 300 dpi, be free of copyright fees, and accompanied by official proof of permission or purchase of rights for academic publication. Each submission may include no more than four images (printing will not be in color). 6. Final bibliography The bibliography should be limited to essential works or cited references and must conform to APA style (7th ed.). 7. Publication The Volume will be published by a Portuguese publisher with extensive experience in scientific publishing. It will also be made available as an e-book in institutional repositories. 8. Copyright statement Submissions must be original, and authors grant publication rights upon acceptance.

items.title: Artificial/Ancestral: Black Theatre and the Question of AI
items.excerpt: As artificial intelligence rapidly reshapes cultural, educational, and creative institutions, the field of Black theatre confronts a familiar set of questions in a newly technological register: Who creates knowledge, who benefits from it, who gets remembered, and whose labor remains obscured? Public conversations about AI often proceed as though these tec...
items.fullDescription: As artificial intelligence rapidly reshapes cultural, educational, and creative institutions, the field of Black theatre confronts a familiar set of questions in a newly technological register: Who creates knowledge, who benefits from it, who gets remembered, and whose labor remains obscured? Public conversations about AI often proceed as though these technologies have arrived without history, entering an empty landscape awaiting innovation. Yet Black theatre has long grappled with questions of representation, embodiment, archives, intellectual inheritance, collective memory, labor, and futurity. Rather than asking simply what AI can do for Black theatre, this issue invites contributors to consider what Black theatre reveals about AI itself: its assumptions, limitations, aspirations, and consequences. Volume 4.2 of the Black Theatre Review seeks essays, interviews, case studies, pedagogical interventions, archival investigations, artist statements, and process reflections that place Black theatre and performance studies in critical conversation with artificial intelligence and related technologies. We are particularly interested in work that moves beyond questions of adoption, utility, or rejection toward deeper examinations of power, ethics, governance, memory, embodiment, and knowledge production. We welcome contributions from scholars, artists, archivists, educators, practitioners, dramaturgs, designers, and cultural workers whose engagement with these questions emerges from both theory and practice. The issue is organized around five interrelated areas of inquiry. These themes are offered not as rigid categories, but as points of departure for further investigation. Taken together, these areas encourage contributors to approach AI not simply as a technological development, but as a site through which questions of labor, memory, embodiment, governance, spirituality, and future-making can be reconsidered. AI, Labor and Extraction: The beneficiaries of AI systems, whose labor makes them possible and required forms of accountability when Black creative work becomes data. Possible points of investigation may include: The labor of artists whose knowledge underlies any AI-readable record and what ethical stewardship of that labor requires. Generative AI in dramaturgy, script analysis, and design workflows, and models of artist-led intentional integration. Archives, Memory, and Black Theatre Histories: How do AI systems shape, distort, recover, or fail to capture Black theatrical histories and modes of remembering? Possible points of investigation may include: Digitization and AI-training projects involving Black theatre collections and their assumptions about what counts as trainable data. AI-assisted archival misreadings, flattening, erasure, and historical distortion. Embodiment, Liveness, and Performance: What happens when embodied, communal, and improvisational performance practices encounter technologies built on prediction, simulation, and abstraction? Possible points of investigation may include: Case studies of AI in the classroom, rehearsal hall, or production process. The complementary offerings of embodied, ensemble-based theatre training to university-wide AI adoption. Relatedly, how do such offerings get recognized, funded, or institutionally protected? Ancestral Intelligence, Spiritual Knowledge, and Black Futures: Understanding AI as a knowledge system entering into conversation with much older Black diasporic traditions of intelligence, memory, and futurity Possible points of investigation may include: AI as ancestral intelligence, or Black diasporic traditions of pattern recognition, forecasting, memory, and knowledge transmission. How do Black diasporic understandings of knowledge, memory, inheritance, ritual, and collective survival shape the technological futures we imagine? Refusal, Governance, and Alternative Technological Practices: Forms of resistance, opacity, governance, and the possibilities of misuse Possible points of investigation may include: How Black artists are bending, breaking, or refusing AI against its intended use. Teaching against technological inevitability. Photograph, Visual Media, and Digital Project Documentation tBTR welcomes photographic, visual media, and digital project documentation that illuminates the intersections of Black theatre, performance, and artificial intelligence. We encourage submissions featuring productions, rehearsals, classroom projects, design processes, digital or hybrid performances, archival initiatives, community-based projects, and artistic experiments that engage the themes of this issue. Submissions may include production photography, design renderings, screenshots, interface documentation, archival images, process documentation, and other visual materials that help narrate how artists, scholars, educators, and institutions are critically engaging AI and related technologies. All submissions must include the project or production title, names and roles of key collaborators, location, creator and/or photographer credit, date, and a 2-3 sentence description explaining the work's relationship to the issue's focus on labor, archives, embodiment, pedagogy, artificial intelligence, ancestral knowledge, refusal, governance, or Black futures. Contributors are responsible for securing all necessary permissions and reproduction rights prior to submission. Please contact the managing editor for additional information. Book Reviews, Performance Reviews, and Notes from the Field, and Multimedia Works In addition to scholarly articles, tBTR seeks book reviews, performance reviews, multimedia works, illustrative case studies, and notes from the field that engage the intersections of Black theatre, performance, and artificial intelligence. We are particularly interested in contributions that document pedagogical experimentation, archival initiatives, institution-building efforts, production processes, dramaturgical and design practices, community engagement, and artist-led technological interventions. We also welcome reflections on the ethical, political, and aesthetic questions surrounding AI, including issues of labor, extraction, memory, embodiment, governance, ancestral intelligence, resistance, and alternative technological futures. Submission Guidelines The last date for submissions is September 14, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. EDT. Please refer to the tBTR website for specific article section guidelines. Manuscripts must be submitted in Microsoft Word using standard formatting (1-inch margins, double-spaced, single-column layout, and 12-point Times New Roman font). Please include an abstract and a 150-word author biography with your submission. All submissions must include footnotes and a bibliography and must fully comply with The Chicago Manual of Style (18th ed.), using the notes and bibliography system. Please do not use the author-date citation system or another style guide. Please upload your complete manuscript through the journal's online submission portal via the website. Early submissions will receive preference in the review and publication process.

items.fullDescription: About the Symposium The Weight of Mountains (TWOM) Symposium 2026 is an international academic symposium in film and media studies, with a primary focus on Vietnamese and Southeast Asian screen cultures and on how cinema documents, reimagines, and gives form to the region's landscapes, urban transformations, and contested histories. Co-hosted by RMIT University Vietnam and Fulbright University Vietnam, the symposium brings together scholars from film studies and audiovisual studies, cultural studies, environmental humanities, postcolonial studies, and related fields to examine cinema's engagement with place, memory, and environment in an era of rapid urbanization and ecological change. The symposium underscores the significance of authorial and experimental film practices and of speculative fiction emerging in our region. The symposium is organised in conjunction with the fourth iteration of The Weight of Mountains, a periodic international film residency and research platform whose 2026/2027 program places international filmmakers in residence in Ho Chi Minh City for three months. This urban turn - situating the residency in a city shaped by colonial histories, wartime trauma, ??i M?i transformations, and accelerating development - provides the occasion for a focused scholarly conversation about cinema's relationship to place, history, and environment in Vietnam and the wider Southeast Asian region. The symposium will feature keynote addresses by leading Vietnamese and international scholars, artist presentations by TWOM resident filmmakers, and presentations of selected papers. Partners include: The Weight of Mountains (TWOM) team, RMIT Vietnam (DFV and SCD), Fulbright University Vietnam (Arts & Media Studies), Trigger Film Academy Call for Abstracts: Ho Chi Minh City is a city of layered temporalities - part and contemporary - and Vietnamese cinema has long been one of the most searching instruments for reading those layers. The city itself operates as a cinematic text: its streets and interiors producing divergent spatial imaginaries shaped by who holds the camera and from where they look. Like in Tran Anh Hung's Cyclo, urban space can be a site of the uncanny and memories, the promised land, or the space of autoreflective questions. Drawing on Guy Debord's psychogeography and Timothy Cresswell's understanding of place as practiced and performed, we ask how filmmakers navigate, intervene in, and reimagine the urban and ecological spaces of the region through experimental narratives, tools and future-oriented imaginaries. Contemporary film studies has been decisively shaped by the turn toward critical transnationalism, insisting on interrogating the uneven power relations, industrial infrastructures, and cultural politics that condition the movement of films, filmmakers, and capital across borders. For Vietnamese and Southeast Asian cinemas, this means attending simultaneously to inter-Asian circuits of production and distribution, to festival economies and co-production networks, and to the diasporic communities whose experiences and investments shape what gets made and how it travels. The Weight of Mountains residency operates as what Foucault called a heterotopia - a space of productive dislocation and otherness, deliberately positioned at the margins of dominant film cultures. This symposium extends that heterotopic logic into the academic register, asking what forms of knowledge become possible when international filmmakers and researchers engage seriously with the specific textures of Vietnamese urban life: its soundscapes, its landscapes and ecologies as sites of historical sedimentation and environmental change, and its postcolonial politics of the gaze. The symposium is equally attentive to what cinema can do when it turns toward the nonhuman world - the Mekong Delta, the urban waterways, the forest edges and street ecologies that constitute the lived environment of Vietnam and the wider region, bringing further questions about how film documents landscape, registers environmental change, and attends to the nonhuman dimensions of place. Thematic Strands We invite submissions that engage with one or more of the following strands. Papers should present a clear research question, theoretical framework, and original contribution to the field. STRAND 1. Colonial and Postcolonial Cinemas of Southeast Asia Vietnamese and Southeast Asian cinemas carry the unresolved weight of French colonialism, Cold War intervention, and the ongoing politics of decolonial representation. Papers in this strand might address: • The postcolonial gaze and ethics of representation in Vietnamese documentary and fiction film • French colonial cinema in Indochina and its afterlives in contemporary Vietnamese film culture • Decolonial aesthetics and counter-narratives in Vietnamese, Cambodian, Lao, and Thai cinema • The postcolonial condition of Indochinese cinemas across Vietnam, Cambodia, and Laos, and the shared legacies of French colonialism • Colonial urban space and its cinematic re-inscription in Ho Chi Minh City, Phnom Penh, and Vientiane • The ethics of the outsider filmmaker in Vietnam and Southeast Asia - questions of access, positionality, and the politics of cross-cultural representation STRAND 2. Memory and the Afterlives of 1975 Post-1975 Vietnamese cinema remains one of the most contested sites of historical memory in world cinema. Papers in this strand might address: • Historical voices in post-1975 Vietnamese film • Wartime affect in Vietnamese cinema • Heterogeneous temporalities, colonial haunting, and the fantastic in Southeast Asian cinema • Uncanny urban spaces • Generational shifts in the remembrance of war and revolution across Vietnamese film STRAND 3. Transnational Return Papers in this strand might address: • Transnational desire, mobility, and national belonging • The aesthetics of displacement, longing, and return in film • Insider and outsider representations of Vietnam and the returning gaze • Transnational co-productions and festival circulation • Digital platforms, streaming, and new circuits of Vietnamese film distribution STRAND 4. Urbanism and the Cinematic City Ho Chi Minh City and Hanoi are among the most cinematically rich urban environments in contemporary Southeast Asia, shaped by ??i M?i reforms, rapid development, and the layering of colonial and socialist pasts. Papers in this strand might address: • Ho Chi Minh City as cinematic city-text • Psychogeography, the dérive, and spatial practice in Vietnamese urban cinema • Postcolonial urbanism and the layering of colonial and contemporary temporalities in Vietnamese cityscapes • Rural-urban boundaries and migration narratives in contemporary Vietnamese cinema • Bangkok, Manila, Phnom Penh, and other Southeast Asian cities as sites of cinematic spatial inquiry • Infrastructural development, displacement, and the politics of urban transformation on screen STRAND 5. Independent Cinema and Alternative Exhibition in Southeast Asia Beyond mainstream production, a vital ecosystem of independent and experimental cinema has emerged across the region, creating alternative circuits of production, distribution, and spectatorship. Papers in this strand might address: • Critical transnationalism and the conditions of production, funding, and circulation of Southeast Asian independent film • Alternative film exhibitions • Independent film festivals and independent production circuits across Southeast Asia • The role of digital platforms and transnational funding in enabling independent Southeast Asian filmmaking • Distinct regional independent cinema identities • The sonic and haptic dimensions of place in experimental Southeast Asian films STRAND 6. Landscape, Ecology, and Environmental Cinema This strand invites scholarship on how cinema represents, interprets, and attends to the landscapes, ecologies, and natural environments of Vietnam and Southeast Asia. It encompasses documentary, essay film, and fiction practices that attend to environmental change, rural and riverine life, and the nonhuman world as subjects of serious cinematic inquiry. Papers in this strand might address: • Landscape cinema and ecocinema studies in the Vietnamese and Southeast Asian context - how films document, aestheticise, and bear witness to environments under pressure • The Mekong Delta as cinematic space - rivers, deltas, and rural waterways as subjects of documentary, fiction, and experimental filmmaking • Climate cinema and the Anthropocene in Southeast Asian documentary and fiction film • Sensory and immersive cinema - the use of duration, texture, and ambient sound to render nonhuman environments perceptible • Process cinema and the nonhuman agencies - water, weather, infrastructure, animals - that constitute urban and rural life in Vietnam and the region STRAND 7. Festival Aesthetics, Slow Cinema, and Global Circulation The growing international visibility of Vietnamese and Southeast Asian cinema raises important questions about the institutional and aesthetic conditions of that visibility. Papers in this strand might address: • Transcendental style, slow cinema, and contemplative aesthetics in contemporary Vietnamese film • The construction of "Vietnamese cinema" as a category within global film culture • Co-production networks, international funding, and the shaping of film form for global audiences • The tension between local spectatorship and international festival circuits in Vietnamese and Southeast Asian cinema • Transnational frames for Asian cinema and the risks of Orientalist programming logics • The role of film criticism, academic writing, and scholarly publishing in shaping the international reception of Southeast Asian cinema SUBMISSION GUIDELINES Abstract requirements: - Word count: 300-500 words, excluding references - Language: English Abstracts should include: - Paper title - 3 to 5 keywords - Indication of which thematic strand(s) the paper engages - Author name(s), institutional affiliation(s), bio note and email address(es) should be provided only in the submission form - Please indicate your presentation format: online/face to face in the form Author biography: A short biography of 100-150 words per author should be submitted alongside the abstract Presentation format: A 20-minute academic paper presentation, followed by 10 minutes for questions and discussion Review process: All submissions will undergo blind peer review by an international panel of scholars. Selection criteria include intellectual rigour, theoretical sophistication, methodological clarity, engagement with Vietnamese and Southeast Asian contexts, and relevance to symposium themes. Authors should remove identifying information from the abstract document prior to submission Submission portal: https://cmt3.research.microsoft.com/TWOM2026/Submission/Index Symposium format: The symposium will have a hybrid format. An additional online session will be held for online participants. KEY DATES: Abstract submission deadline: September 15, 2026 Notification of acceptance: October 2026 Full text submission: November 20, 2026 Symposium: December 10, 11, and 12, 2026 Symposium Venues: -December 10, Online -December 11, RMIT Unviersity, Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam -December 12, Fulbright University, Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam Abstract submissions: https://cmt3.research.microsoft.com/TWOM2026/Submission/Index Please submit the abstracts through the submission system. *Some users encountered problems while using Safari browser. If you have problems with registering, please use a different browser. Registration details to be announced. Please contact the organising committee for queries regarding accessibility requirements. The organizers plan to publish an edited monograph containing expanded, selected articles submitted to the symposium. Details to be announced. Enquiries : dfvhub.staff@rmit.edu.vn Organising Committee Khoa Trong Nguyen, Digital Film and Video Program Manager, RMIT Vietnam Dr. Piotr Wajda, Lecturer, Professional Communications, RMIT Vietnam Dr. Agnieszka Kiejziewicz, Design (Games), RMIT Vietnam Tim Marshall, TWOM, Associate Lecturer, RMIT Melbourne Melody Woodnutt, TWOM, Associate Lecturer, RMIT Melbourne Dr. Linda Chen Zhang, Assistant Professor, Fulbright University Vietnam Trinh Dinh Le Minh, Lecturer/Filmmaker, Fulbright University Vietnam Director Lan Nguyen, Trigger Film Academy Le Binh Giang, Trigger Film Academy

items.fullDescription: Historical fiction is generally associated with the novel (see Green [2011] and Young [2018]). Yet the historical short story was significant before WWI: “from 1901 to 1914, over 1200 works of historical fiction were issued, of which nearly a quarter were short-story collections” (Cox and Adrian 1994, xiv). We may wonder if and how the genre has been impacted by the renewed interest in the past and history in fiction over the past 30 years.

items.fullDescription: Transatlantic Connections and the ‘Special Relationship[s]’: BAAS Postgraduate Symposium, 2026 V&A East Storehouse, London 9th November In 1946, Winston Churchill declared the need for a “special relationship between the British Commonwealth and Empire and the United States” in order to maintain world diplomacy, citing our shared language and cultural values as connecting the two countries. Although this ‘special relationship’ has continually been called into question by scholars, there is undoubtedly a channel of cultural and political exchange between the US and the UK, as well as with other countries, which has become even more urgent for discussion in recent years.

items.fullDescription: Tattooing, a form of bodily modification, has existed as a global phenomenon for centuries, persevering within the distant and near past alike. items.excerpt: As some institutions restructure academic priorities in response to various pressures in higher education, the Humanities can face contraction, marginalization, or elimination. These challenges are intensified at specialized universities, meaning institutions oriented toward fields such as STEM, health sciences, business, etc., where Humanities courses ar...
items.fullDescription: As some institutions restructure academic priorities in response to various pressures in higher education, the Humanities can face contraction, marginalization, or elimination. These challenges are intensified at specialized universities, meaning institutions oriented toward fields such as STEM, health sciences, business, etc., where Humanities courses are often kept to general education requirements and could be perceived as peripheral to students’ professional training. Within such environments, Humanities faculty must navigate not only broader disciplinary challenges but also institutional cultures that may misunderstand or underappreciate the field’s contributions.

items.fullDescription: War does not end; it migrates even after the guns fall silent, crawling into bodies, landscapes, archives, and the grammar of storytelling itself. This seminar inquires into how societies of South Asia and the Middle East, so often positioned as sites of conflicts rather than as theorists of their aftermath, have produced their own vocabularies for narrating what survives war. Michael Rothberg (2009) argues that memories of distinct historical violence do not compete for scarce recognition but can be mutually constitutive.

Camera flashes crack as they capture their quarry. By now, these perceptions have become truisms that obscure our own role as consumers in a matrix of violence, spectatorship, and st...
items.fullDescription: If American mass media is an ecosystem, we cast the press as predators, and the celebrity as their prey. We envision the reporters grouped in a posse, arranged for an ambush. Camera flashes crack as they capture their quarry. By now, these perceptions have become truisms that obscure our own role as consumers in a matrix of violence, spectatorship, and stardom. If we condemn the paparazzi for their alleged violence, we also continue to revise and revisit their heyday in the age of print media. This seminar seeks papers that explore how violent desire—of the spectator, the press, the star – shaped the profusion of tabloid and true crime print culture across the Americas.

items.fullDescription: Conference online (via Zoom) CFP: What makes us happy and content in our life? Some people may point to fabulous fame, fortune, or money. Others may argue that interpersonal relationships are the key to happiness. But what if someone is alone? Is loneliness truly disastrous? Are there any benefits of loneliness? Can loneliness become an epidemic? To address these questions, this event focuses on a wide range of specific issues. We are interested in exploring all aspects of loneliness, both in the past and in the present-day world. The conference is intended as an interdisciplinary event. Hence, we invite researchers representing various academic disciplines: sociology, psychology, psychiatry, philosophy, anthropology, gender studies, literary studies, theatre studies, film studies, consciousness studies, social policy, cognitive sciences, and history, among others. The aim of our conference is to provide opportunities for researchers from a range of disciplines and countries to share their research, create an academically challenging and productive space for discussion, and enable them to establish long-lasting, ever-growing scientific networks and contacts with professionals worldwide. We welcome submissions from both experienced scholars and young academics at the beginning of their careers, as well as doctoral and graduate students. We also invite individuals interested in participating in the conference as listeners, without giving a presentation. The topics of the conference include but are not limited to the following suggestions: 1. Loneliness and Society ? loneliness and social relationships (in families, marriages, partnerships, workplaces, etc.)? loneliness and war loneliness and illness loneliness and self-isolation, social distancing loneliness among children loneliness among seniors the lonely crowd loneliness in urban spaces loneliness as an epidemic loneliness and pandemic loneliness and social exclusion (social class, racism, gender factors, educational status) loneliness and social media (Facebook, Instagram, etc.) 2. Loneliness and Culture loneliness in different parts of the world loneliness and religions loneliness and initiation rituals lonely communities abandoned nations expelled minorities loneliness and digital cultures / virtual communities the cultural taboo of solitude vs. hyper-individualism migrant loneliness and diaspora experiences 3. Individual experiences ? loneliness during self-isolation, quarantanne, loneliness as a state of mind loneliness and emotional isolation loneliness and depression loneliness and shame creative loneliness loneliness as a rest situational loneliness existential loneliness loneliness, aloneness, and solitude the commercialization of loneliness (the "rent-a-friend" industry, monetized companion apps, dating algorithms, and AI relationships) synthetic companionship & AI (digital intimacy, dating algorithms, and robotic care) 4. Literature and Arts loneliness in literature, film, theatre and visual arts lonely artists aesthetics, spaces, and narratives of isolation (e.g., in pop culture, life-writing, and architecture) Please submit abstracts (no longer than 300 words) of your proposed 20-minute presentations, together with a short biographical note, by 18 September 2026 to: lonelinessconference@gmail.com

items.title: Entangled Normativities in the Digital Transformation: Technology, Society and the Shaping of Law
items.location: Munich · Constitutional Design Lab, TU Munich
items.excerpt: Poster session at the conference "Entangled Normativities in the Digital Transformation: Technology, Society and the Shaping of Law" Present your research where law, technology and society are being negotiated. How much technological change can normative orders gover? How do law, ethics and social norms change themselves once their creation, mediation and...
items.fullDescription: Poster session at the conference "Entangled Normativities in the Digital Transformation: Technology, Society and the Shaping of Law" Present your research where law, technology and society are being negotiated. How much technological change can normative orders gover? How do law, ethics and social norms change themselves once their creation, mediation and enforcement become digitally mediated? No single discipline settles these questions. With a poster you discuss your project at the centre of the programme, alongside scholars and practitioners working on exactly these questions: Möllers (HU Berlin), Nassehi (LMU Munich), Paulus (former Justice of the German Federal Constitutional Court), Schlögl-Flierl (German Ethics Council), Foblets (MPI for Social Anthropology), Vec (University of Vienna), Hansen (State Data Protection Commissioner of Schleswig-Holstein) and Bubnys (European Commission), among others. What you get:Viisibility in front of leading scholars and practitioners rather than in a parallel session; substantive feedback in conversation plus a short written comment on your abstract; a citable peer-review process; networking with doctoral researchers from across Europe; free attendance on both days. Potential poster publication on our website. Who can apply. Doctoral researchers in law, science and technology studies, sociology, political science, philosophy and ethics, history, computer science and engineering with a societal research question, design, communication and media studies, and further or interdisciplinary fields. What matters is not your disciplinary label but your contribution to the relationship between normativity and technology. Your stage of doctorate is irrelevant: proposals, early outlines and first interim findings are as welcome as work nearing completion, and practitioners pursuing a doctorate alongside their work are invited too. From big picture to concrete cases. We welcome conceptual and foundational contributions (theories of normativity under technological change, legitimacy and the rule of law in digital governance, the interplay of legal, ethical, social and technical norms, automation of norm application, interdisciplinary methodology) as well as specific, applied and empirical work (the AI Act and data protection law in practice, platform regulation, digital administration and courts, predictive policing, health data, technical standardisation, sustainability, and case studies of individual technologies, authorities, decisions or regulatory processes). Please relate your contribution to one of the three guiding questions: (1) To what extent is technological change amenable to normative and in particular legal governance? (2) To what extent must normative orders, above all the law, themselves change? (3) What potentials and risks does the technological transformation of normativity and law entail? How it works. Each session opens with lightning talks: max. 90 seconds and one slide per poster; questions are taken at the posters rather than in the plenary. Day 1 (German, 5 November): pitch session 4:15-4:35 PM, poster session from 4:35 PM into the Apéro riche. Day 2 (English, 6 November): pitch session 11:20-11:40 AM, poster session 11:40 AM-12:35 PM before lunch. Posters are on display both days; your poster language determines your pitch day. Peer review and selection. Each anonymised abstract is assessed independently by two members of the review committee, with divergences discussed in the committee. Criteria: thematic fit, academic quality, originality, clarity, and potential to spark discussion in an interdisciplinary audience. All applicants receive a briefly reasoned decision by early October 2026; interdisciplinary submissions are read by reviewers from different fields. Poster. A0, portrait, printed and brought by you. Recommended: two or three key messages, body text at least 24 pt, a large self-explanatory title, and more visuals than running text - your poster should be understandable within a few minutes even when you are not next to it. Questions: lst@sot.tum.de. We look forward to your application!

items.fullDescription: About the Book Indian Cultural Heritage: Perspectives is an edited volume that invites interdisciplinary scholarship on the diverse and dynamic dimensions of India's cultural heritage. The volume welcomes original contributions exploring tangible and intangible heritage, indigenous knowledge systems, languages, literature, folklore, performing arts, architecture, material culture, cultural memory, museums, heritage conservation, digital heritage, and contemporary issues of identity, sustainability, and cultural preservation. By bringing together diverse academic perspectives, the volume seeks to advance critical understanding of India's rich cultural traditions and their continuing significance in a rapidly changing world.

In Wayward Lives , Hartman suggests that any of the minor figures can stand in for the others, not as a claim of homogeneity, but rather as a contention that their singularity can be read as paradigmatic of waywardness—in its queer heterogeneity—in general. The chorus of black femme and queer youth is thus at once a singular plurality and a plural singularity as they make beautifully riotous lives within the enclosure of social death.

items.excerpt: In his book, Bioinsecurities: Disease Interventions, Empire, and the Government of Species (2016), Neel Ahuja's theory of "the body as a transitional theater of imperial warfare" explores how the control of human and nonhuman bodies proliferated the expansion of empire over the 19th century to the present.
