items.fullDescription: In his book, Bioinsecurities: Disease Interventions, Empire, and the Government of Species (2016), Neel Ahuja's theory of "the body as a transitional theater of imperial warfare" explores how the control of human and nonhuman bodies proliferated the expansion of empire over the 19th century to the present. Despite the growing hegemony of biomedical control, there have always been and continue to be significant moments of resistance and agency in which marginalized (colonized/Indigenous) communities have challenged or reformulated/redefined the concepts of body, disease, and health. This seminar seeks to foster a discussion in order to understand how the body can be read as a transnational figure of resistance and refusal both in the 19th century and today. Through various disciplines on the subjective and untold experiences of the body, health(care), and illness, we hope to shed light on the fluctuations in imperial medical frameworks and decolonial epistemology that pose alternative narratives-both realist and speculative-about biomedical discourses of health, gender and sexual normativity, disability/deficiency, hygiene, humanness, life/death. We are interested in questions such as: How are illnesses phrased, represented, imagined in marginalized communities? How is the effectiveness of care and therapies a scientific, ethical, and cultural problem? How can the medicalized body-or the body that is made into a site of changeability and "treatment"-become a speculative site entangling place, race, gender, and sexuality? This seminar welcomes papers that take on interdisciplinary approaches to literature and other forms of cultural production such as film, print culture, and music that engage with the theme from the 19th- 21st centuries across the world. We are especially interested in lesser-known materials and understudied communities. Topics of interest include but are not limited to: Narrative medicine from all types of media Bioethics Biopolitics and governmentality Mental health and literature, art and media studies Limitations of medical or pharmaceutical knowledge Medicalization of health/illness Marginalized bodies in medicinal knowledge (queer, disabled, racialized, female) Community/Immunity Pandemic and contagion Aging studies and end-of-life care, childcare/youth studies Utopia/Dystopia/Ecotopia Toxicity and Waste Trauma and memory studies Supernatural bodies, cyborg and alien "others", metamorphosis and transformation (Digital) post-life, afterlife studies, martyrdom Animal studies, Post-humanism To submit an abstract, please go to: https://www.acla.org/seminar/82ccd196-900f-482d-aac6-3b983a0957b2. Click the "Propose a Paper" button.

items.title: TALKING DIFFERENTLY: MARGINALISED WOMEN AND THE FORMS OF INTERSECTIONALITY IN SOUTH ASIA
items.excerpt: Talking Differently: Marginalised Women and the Forms of Intersectionality in South Asia Seminar at the Annual Meeting of the American Comparative Literature Association (ACLA) University of Houston, Houston, Texas 20-23 May 2027 - in person Organisers: Nandini Gayen and Tamanna Priya Deadline for paper proposals: 22 September 2026 Submit at: https://www....
items.fullDescription: Talking Differently: Marginalised Women and the Forms of Intersectionality in South Asia Seminar at the Annual Meeting of the American Comparative Literature Association (ACLA) University of Houston, Houston, Texas 20-23 May 2027 - in person Organisers: Nandini Gayen and Tamanna Priya Deadline for paper proposals: 22 September 2026 Submit at: https://www.acla.org/seminar/6b731612-c856-4a5e-91e9-5dbdd113434e Marginalised women in South Asia are read for what was done to them, far less often for what they made. This seminar asks what comparative literature can do about that. Intersectionality has become the default grammar for writing about marginalised women in the region. It arrived from a particular genealogy - Black feminist jurisprudence in the United States - into a region that had theorised compounded subordination for a century under other names: Phule on caste and women's education; Ambedkar on endogamy as the mechanism reproducing caste through control of women; Pandita Ramabai; Uma Chakravarti's Brahmanical patriarchy; Gopal Guru's claim that Dalit women talk differently; Sharmila Rege's Dalit feminist standpoint. Whether the import clarifies or flattens that inheritance is contested. Nivedita Menon argues that intersectionality serves states and donor agencies better than feminist politics; Sunaina Arya and Anandita Pan reply that the fault is citational, not conceptual. That argument has run almost entirely in social science. Our premise is that intersectionality is a diagram - a crossroads, a grid, a set of axes. Literary forms do not behave like diagrams. They work through voice, genre, meter, silence, obscenity, laughter, ritual and untranslatability. What does intersectionality look like as a reading practice rather than a taxonomy of identities? Where does form outrun the grid, and what should replace it - standpoint, assemblage, repertoire, abundance? Three provocations frame the seminar. First, the arithmetic of injury: criticism here tends to produce a tally of wounds, in which the Dalit, Adivasi, Muslim, trans, disabled or displaced woman is legible chiefly through what was done to her. Charu Gupta shows this figure has a history: in colonial Hindi reformist print the polluting "vamp" gave way to the deferential sufferer, Surpanakha displaced by Shabari, while the Dalit virangana of 1857 offered a rival image that never took. Following Gupta, Anjali Arondekar on archival abundance over loss, and Shailaja Paik on Tamasha performers who turn vulgarity into leverage, we welcome papers that read craft, expertise, pleasure and the ordinary. Second, marginality is not virtue. Tanika Sarkar's work on the Hindu wife as ground of cultural nationalism, and on women's agency inside right-wing movements, refuses to assume that subordination guarantees a critical position. We want dominant-caste women's self-writing - Rashsundari Debi's Amar Jiban - read alongside rather than apart from Dalit testimonio, and the complicities an axis model hides. Third, translation. Most of these texts do not exist in English. Bama's Karukku and Challapalli Swaroopa Rani's Telugu poems reach the Anglophone academy through an apparatus - glossary, preface, caste footnote, anthology - that turns literature into evidence. Swaroopa Rani's "Water" registers not only the village/wada line but the gradations within it, leather-worker and weaver. The grid has grids inside it, and translation is where they flatten. Topics might include, but are in no way limited to: the genre problem in Dalit women's testimonio; Dalit feminist poetry read as theory; the manufacture of the suffering woman in colonial print and the counter-archives that failed; nineteenth-century women's self-writing and its caste unconscious; women as agents of majoritarian politics; sung and seasonal repertoires as authorial economies rather than folklore; Adivasi women's poetry and the politics of script; landays and Afghan women's oral forms; testimonial method in Kashmir; plantation labour and memory in Sri Lanka; Muslim women and the meme as a genre of gendered communal violence; trans and hijra life-writing at the caste intersection; devadasi, Tamasha and courtesan archives read for abundance; caste in North America and Gulf labour circuits; translation as method. We invite papers on any South Asian language, region, period or diaspora. Researchers and Faculty Members at every career stage are welcome, including independent researchers and those working outside the Anglophone academy, and papers that argue against the seminar's premises are equally welcome. To submit: proposals go through the ACLA portal, not to the organisers directly. Visit https://www.acla.org/seminar/6b731612-c856-4a5e-91e9-5dbdd113434e and use the "Propose a Paper" button. Current ACLA membership is required. Deadline 22 September 2026. We'd like to have you in person, please mention your preferred mode- ONLINE/IN PERSON along with the abstract. Enquieres: nandinigayen006@gmail.com; tamanna0602@gmail.com

items.title: ACLA SEMINAR: Becoming Monster: Representation and Rights
items.excerpt: American Comparative Literature Association IN-PERSON 2027 Annual Meeting (May 20-23, 2027), Houston, Texas Organizers: Dr. Julia Chan (Lingnan University) Fatma Betul Ciftci (Lingnan University) One is not born a monster; the monster is produced. From Beowulf to Ruthven to Dracula to cyborgs, 'monster' is a cultural construction, a humanly-produced non-h...
items.fullDescription: American Comparative Literature Association IN-PERSON 2027 Annual Meeting (May 20-23, 2027), Houston, Texas Organizers: Dr. Julia Chan (Lingnan University) Fatma Betul Ciftci (Lingnan University) One is not born a monster; the monster is produced. From Beowulf to Ruthven to Dracula to cyborgs, 'monster' is a cultural construction, a humanly-produced non-human. This seminar invites scholars to discuss the monster both as a literary figure and as the representation and construction of a cultural and political identity. Through this, it aims to explore the question of where, why, and how monsters are produced, and what these monsterized creatures "show" about the communities that "produce" them. The seminar discusses how theory, from Freud's "the uncanny" to Cohen's "monster theory" to Creed's "monstrous feminine," can help us understand monsterization. The monsterized body is pushed outside the category of the "human" and thus outside the status of a rights-bearing subject. In this respect, monsterization begs the question of rights. This seminar aims to understand and make visible how the process which "produces" the Other as a monster, works in relation to rights. In Of Monsters and Migrants, Peter Arnds traces this process through Carl Schmitt's concepts of sovereignty and the "state of exception" and Agamben's biopolitics: to monsterize the migrant, the stranger, the refugee allows one to push them outside the protection of the law. As Arnds shows, the question of who - and what - monsterizes is therefore also the question of who is, or is not, recognized as a rights-bearing subject. The second focus of the seminar is the reclamation of the monster. Susan Stryker's "My Words to Victor Frankenstein Above the Village of Chamounix" identifies the trans body with Frankenstein's creature. It reverses the accusation of the "unnatural," constructed body and transforms the words "monster" and "creature" into terms of power reclamation, self-representation, and resistance. The monster is not only a position produced by the powerful but also one that can be reclaimed by those who are monsterized. What else can we see in monsters beyond the gendered or racial Other? We encourage scholars working in different areas-literary studies, television, film and anime studies, law and human rights theory, postcolonial and critical race theory, queer and trans theory-to offer new definitions of, and reflections on, the category of the monster. We invite papers around the following questions: How does the monster negotiate who counts as "human" and who counts as a subject of human rights? What social, political, or legal aspects make a body a monster? What strategies do those who are monsterized use to reclaim their representations and rights? How do different media construct the relationship between monsters and rights? Submit your paper title and abstract through the ACLA submission portal on the ACLA website by September 22, 2026, and note that you must be logged in to see the "Propose a Paper" button. Link for the seminar: https://www.acla.org/seminar/43ce7d31-1cb1-46b8-a8a2-6d34614d1e5e

items.title: The Poverty of Literature
items.excerpt: American Comparative Literature Association 2027 Annual Meeting University of Houston May 20-23 The Poverty of Literature Organizer: Gabriel Quigley, University of Victoria (gabrielquigley@uvic.ca) How does literature represent poverty? Is poverty available for representation? The title of this seminar is taken from Marx's The Poverty of Philosophy, which...
items.fullDescription: American Comparative Literature Association 2027 Annual Meeting University of Houston May 20-23 The Poverty of Literature Organizer: Gabriel Quigley, University of Victoria (gabrielquigley@uvic.ca) How does literature represent poverty? Is poverty available for representation? The title of this seminar is taken from Marx's The Poverty of Philosophy, which, in turn, subverts Proudhon's The Philosophy of Poverty. In it, Marx critiques the approach taken by Proudhon and other anarchist, communist, or socialist "theoreticians" who assume that economic categories exist independently of history. According to Marx, "so long as they look for science and merely make systems, so long as they are at the beginning of the struggle, they see in poverty nothing but poverty, without seeing in it the revolutionary, subversive side, which will overthrow the old society." A similar critique might be leveled at today's writers and critics: when literature and literary criticism engage with poverty at all, do they merely reduce it to an ahistorical economic category? What forms of reification, alienation, and exploitation does the literary assumption that poverty is available for representation produce? This seminar asks what literature owes to people experiencing poverty. At a time when 847 million people live in extreme poverty-95% of whom are in the Global South-it seeks to bring together research on the representation, history, and ontological status of poverty. Unlike Marx's "theoreticians," who "see in poverty nothing but poverty," scholars analyzing poverty through other frameworks-such as ethical demand, affective complexity, geopolitical disparities, aesthetic fetishization, and state failure-are strongly encouraged to submit abstracts. Papers may respond to such questions as: how should poverty be represented, if at all? Beyond an economic category, can poverty be conceived as an aesthetic, metaphysical, or phenomenological category? How is the concept of poverty entangled with conceptions of lack, deprivation, or destitution? How does the global distribution of poverty reflect the ongoing injuries of imperialism, colonialism, neocolonialism, globalization, and ecological catastrophe? Possible topics: - Poverty and realism; poverty and genre - The ethics of speaking for the poor - Testimony, life writing, and first-person accounts of poverty - Poverty and racial capitalism - Postcolonial and decolonial frameworks for poverty - Poverty and ecological catastrophe; climate precarity - Poverty and intersectionality (race, gender, sexuality, disability) - "Poverty porn," sentimentality, and voyeurism - Working-class literature and labor - Poverty in the Global South; imperialism and uneven development - Urban and rural poverty as literary landscapes - Homelessness and houselessness - Poverty and the archive - Poverty and affect: shame, solidarity, rage - The literary canon and class; institutional gatekeeping - Austerity, welfare, and the state in literature - Migration, displacement, and border crossing - Literature and human rights - Poverty as aesthetic, metaphysical, or phenomenological category - Poverty and ontology; being, lack, and deprivation - Bare life and destitution ACLA Seminar Description can be accessed here: https://www.acla.org/seminar/63e1eb87-fe99-49c9-aac0-517ccf904102. ACLA Paper Submission link: https://www.acla.org/cfp/2b603883-5d9b-44ae-a485-c732ba80d4bf/submit-paper. Papers can be submitted until September 22, 2026 .

items.fullDescription: Inclusive teaching and digital accessibility are two important concepts that align with Universal Design for Learning (UDL) principles; they move away from "retrofitting" (i.e., fixing a problem after a student struggles) toward a "proactive” design (e.g., building a system that works for everyone from the start). Inclusive teaching is a pedagogical framework that focuses on designing a learning environment where every student (regardless of race, gender, socioeconomic status, or learning style) feels valued and has an equal opportunity to succeed. Whereas digital accessibility is a technical standard that ensures that digital tools, documents, and platforms are usable by everyone, regardless of ability.

items.fullDescription: What strategies can paper ephemera teach us in the digital age? This panel invites conversations by writing instructors, educators, poets, and artists exploring the work that happens at/within the margins of writing. Both literally and figuratively, we take an expansive scope to the term “margins,” imagining not only the writing that appears on the space of the printed page, but writing that would normally be scrapped, discarded, remixed, or ephemeralized. This can include digital ephemera, such as “disappearing” messages in Instagram or other communication services. At another angle: margins can also mean the liminality of writing, the furthermost edges of what’s often standard and visible.

items.fullDescription: This panel session seeks to explore the cultural fascination surrounding "The Backrooms," an internet 'creepypasta' about an abandoned office building with endless corridors that became a popular YouTube series and most recently, a blockbuster horror film. What are the Backrooms? Do they represent an artificial or alien intelligence attempting to simulate reality? Are they a glitch in the imperfect fabric of an unstable universe? Are they a metaphor for the subconscious, techno-paranoia, wasteland necrocapitalism, corporate control, or the internet itself? Or is this all just a retelling of the Greek myth of the Labyrinth for a Gen Z audience?

items.fullDescription: This roundtable discusses the convergence of literary expression and digital activism as means of empowering a community. The shift of passive representation to active agency in the 21st century can be common in the digital space where the local knowledge is stored and disseminated. We discuss how marginalized groups, namely Dalit writers and activists, have used digital humanities to evade authoritarian gatekeepers and develop transnational solidarities. This session welcomes people to talk about how online spaces can be seen as a form of regenerative space where the testimonios of Dalit can be heard, transforming the world into a supportive space of collective action and literary insurgency.

items.fullDescription: Recent scholarship in autobiography and life writing has expanded beyond traditional literary forms to encompass a wide range of practices through which individuals narrate, perform, and negotiate their identities. As scholars such as Sidonie Smith and Julia Watson have argued, life writing constitutes not merely the representation of a life but a dynamic process through which identities are constructed, mediated, and made visible within specific social and cultural contexts. Consequently, autobiography has evolved into an interdisciplinary field of inquiry encompassing visual art, graphic narratives, performance, body art, digital media, and other forms of self-representation.

Drawing on the centrality of dialogue in literary and dramatic traditions, this panel reimagines conversational form as a site of constraint-based experimentation, where meaning emerges through the collision of discourses that would not ordinarily coexist. Rather than focusing on artificial intelligence as a technological subject, this session treats AI-assisted generation as a formal device for producing estranged adjacency between voices, genres, and epistemologies.

items.fullDescription: On January 19, 2022, Sheila Heti published the first of ten weekly installments of “A Diary in Alphabetical Order” in The New York Times. items.fullDescription: Bhāratīya Jñāna Paramparā , another name for Indian Knowledge Systems (IKS), is a comprehensive body of knowledge which has been accumulated over millennia. Indian Knowledge Systems encompasses philosophy, mathematics, astronomy, medicine (Ayurveda), government, ecology, the arts, and sustainable living. It is based on books such as the Vedas , Upanishads, Puranas , and treatises like the Arthashastra , Charaka Samhita , and Sushruta Samhita . This Knowledge systems place a strong emphasis on interconnection, moral behaviour, and harmony with the natural world - principles embodied in ideas such as Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam (the world is one family).

items.fullDescription: Abstract In the United States, our lives are marked by an abundance of convenience. From fresh produce year-round to two-day shipping, convenient choices feel soft, easy, and frictionless, as they have specifically been engineered to feel. Until relatively recently, it has been possible to maintain a cultural and systemic sense of alienation that makes the cost of our convenience invisible to us—to localize all of the necessary precarity and exploitation for convenience “somewhere else,” (often in the Global South) and then to ignore it.

items.title: When Lives Do Things: Lives as Archives
items.excerpt: As Sidonie Smith and Julia Watson argue, “autobiographical storytelling is a performative act through which narrators construct rather than simply describe selves.” In recent times, “life writing” has become a familiar term in literary and cultural studies, encompassing a range of written texts, including autobiographies, biographies, letters, memoirs, sl...
items.fullDescription: As Sidonie Smith and Julia Watson argue, “autobiographical storytelling is a performative act through which narrators construct rather than simply describe selves.” In recent times, “life writing” has become a familiar term in literary and cultural studies, encompassing a range of written texts, including autobiographies, biographies, letters, memoirs, slave narratives, prison narratives, captivity narratives, travel narratives, confessionals, conversion narratives and even in recent times, personal diaries. However, rather than remain transparent records of lived experience, life writings actively shape identities, produce historical knowledge, preserve cultural memory, and intervene in social and political worlds.

items.fullDescription: The guiding thread of this panel develops around a curious remark by Jacques Rancière that would seem to amend a classically Aristotelian thesis: “man is a political animal because he is a literary animal,” the fundamental condition of which is the “excess of words” constitutive of the human animal’s politicalness. Literature (or poetry) has long been placed in close proximity to politics, as we find in Plato’s Republic , where philosophy and literature—and, more generally, philosophy and politics—turn out to be perennial adversaries.

items.fullDescription: Panel Proposal for the NeMLA Convention, Newport, RI, March 6–9, 2027 Planetary crises—climate change, toxic pollution, biodiversity loss, and energy transition—are profoundly uneven in their distribution. Their material consequences are shaped by infrastructures of class, race, colonial histories, state power, and global capitalism. Increasingly, literary, artistic, and cultural texts across the world foreground these asymmetries, framing ecological crisis not only as environmental catastrophe but as a question of justice: Who breathes polluted air? Who profits from green transformation? Who consumes melting ice? Who bears the social and environmental costs of planetary change?

This panel invites papers that examine collaborative relationships among students, near-peers, tutors, and faculty that form in and around writing instruction and beyond, with particular interest in work that attends to the unexpected: encounters, connections, and forms of growth that arise when pedagogy exceeds the transactional to become genuinely communal. Papers might address-for example-embedded tutoring or near-peer mentoring in composition; teaching-and-learning communities (communities of practice) among faculty, tutors, and students; writing or Gen Ed programs at HSIs, HBCUs, or open-access institutions; the relationship between first-year instruction and identity transformation; intergenerational writing communities and alumni engagement; or the challenges that AI poses to authentic intellectual and creative development. Empirical, theoretical, and reflective approaches are welcome, as is work that bridges composition pedagogy, approaches to general education, and literary (or other forms of) community-building.

items.fullDescription: "Did I request thee, Maker?": Contemporary Cyborgs and Androids and Their Pre-Modern Antecedents Contemporary speculative fiction is saturated with androids, cyborgs, artificial intelligences, and technologically engineered forms of sentience. Yet the fantasy of constructed or quasi-human life long predates modern computing and robotics. Classical and pre-modern literature repeatedly imagines artificial beings, animated matter, virtual persons, mechanical servants, enchanted automata, and forms of life that blur the boundary between the human and the non-human. This panel invites papers that place contemporary representations of manufactured or technologically mediated beings in dialogue with their classical or pre-modern antecedents. Possible pairings might include science fiction, film, television, comics, anime, or video games alongside texts from antiquity through the early modern period. What conceptual, philosophical, theological, or aesthetic frameworks for artificial life emerge in pre-modern literature? How do earlier traditions of animation, embodiment, enchantment, or mechanical simulation anticipate contemporary debates surrounding AI, consciousness, labor, gender, race, affect, or personhood? While Frankenstein remains a central touchstone for discussions of artificial life-and itself invokes Paradise Lost as part of that genealogy-this panel is especially interested in less frequently discussed genealogies and archives. What ancestors to the android or cyborg might be found in Ovid's Metamorphoses, the works of Shakespeare, medieval romance, alchemical traditions, Jewish mysticism, Islamic philosophy, Buddhist narrative traditions, or other non-Western pre-modern texts? Possible topics may include automata and animated objects; artificial or manufactured bodies; alchemy, magic, and technological imagination; pre-modern theories of mind, soul, and consciousness; race, gender, and constructed embodiment; virtuality, simulation, and illusion; labor and mechanical life; monstrosity and the posthuman; game studies and worldbuilding; and theological or philosophical anxieties surrounding creation itself.

items.fullDescription: In the definition given by Podnieks, matrifocal literatures are written and narrated by mothers in the first-person or limited third-person voice, rendering maternal identity and experience from subjective perspectives. Such narratives (re)value the significance and meaning of maternal figures in cultural, social, and national arenas, and often contest or negotiate traditional ideologies of the “good” mother as self-sacrificing, nurturing, and sexless with her antithesis, the “bad” mother. In the last few years, we have seen the rise of matrifocal writings published to break taboos about previously silenced reproductive experiences, create a sense of community, support, and care, and, overall, empower people.

items.fullDescription: In her resolute commitment to telling stories about Black life without the white gaze, Toni Morrison articulated a model of community empowerment grounded in local knowledge, intra-communal collaboration, and the self-reflexive narration of Black worlds. While Morrison remains one of the most visible public advocates of this aesthetic and ethical orientation, practices of Black worldmaking across African and diasporic literatures have long exceeded mere response to anti-Blackness. Even under conditions structured by racial violence, coloniality, displacement, and social rupture, Black communities have continually generated modes of life, relation, memory, and imagination that assert the possibility of worlds otherwise.

items.fullDescription: Haryanvi Dalit theatre occupies a highly marginalised position within the broader landscape of Indian theatre. It may aptly be described as “the marginalised among the marginalised,” as it has remained largely excluded from both mainstream theatre studies and Dalit cultural historiography. Haryanvi Dalit Swang theatre was active long before the Dalit Panther Movement, but it received little attention due to its lack of publication and translation into English. This book seeks to recover, document, and critically examine the neglected legacy of Haryanvi Swang, with particular emphasis on its Dalit traditions and practitioners, thereby contributing to a more inclusive understanding of Indian theatrical heritage.

items.fullDescription: Philip Kan Gotanda’s play Yankee Dawg You Die centers a conflict between two Asian American actors. The aging Vincent Chang built his career playing bumbling Japanese soldiers and one-dimensional Asian stereotypes in classic Hollywood. He’s confronted by the up-and-coming Bradley Yamashita, who insists that Asian (American) characters should be played with dignity and accuracy. The heart of the play is an ambivalence about Asian (American) representation and whether viewers should sympathize with Chang for taking the only acting jobs available or with Yamashita in his condemnation of the racist roles—or with both.

items.fullDescription: TITLE: Language Learning Beyond the Classroom: Virtual Exchanges, Platforms, and AI MODALITY: Hybrid: The session will be held in-person but a few remote presentations may be included. CHAIRS: Liana Ewald (Massachusetts Institute of Technology), Dagmar Jaeger (Massachusetts Institute of Technology) ABSTRACT: This session explores the growing role of virtual exchanges, commercial platforms, and AI-mediated interactions in language, literature, and culture courses. In recent years, many instructors have experimented with new ways of connecting students with speakers, authors, and communities beyond the classroom: Teletandem exchanges, Zoom conversations with writers and artists, commercial conversation platforms, and AI conversation partners. These exchanges can open up forms of communication and cultural contact that are difficult to create in a traditional classroom, especially for students who may not have access to study abroad or regular interaction with speakers from other linguistic and cultural contexts. At the same time, these tools raise important questions. What kinds of communities do these exchanges create? What changes when conversation becomes mediated through platforms or AI? How do students respond to the differences between speaking with another person and interacting with an AI system designed to simulate one? What happens when intercultural exchange becomes something organized and mediated by commercial companies, especially when those relationships may at times raise questions about inequality or exploitation? The session is especially interested in presentations grounded in classroom experience, as well as broader reflections on the pedagogical and theoretical questions raised by these forms of virtual and AI-mediated exchange. Possible topics include current and emerging forms of virtual exchange, AI-mediated interaction, commercial platforms, the changing relationship between human and technological forms of communication, and the pedagogical, cultural, and ethical questions these developments may raise in the years ahead. DESCRIPTION: This session explores the growing role of virtual exchanges, commercial platforms, and AI-mediated interaction in language, literature, and culture courses. It welcomes presentations on classroom experiences, emerging technologies, and the practical, cultural, and ethical questions these forms of exchange may raise.

items.title: Decolonization, Digital Sphere, and Empowered Communities
items.location: Rhode Island · Salve Regina University in Newport,
items.excerpt: The digital infrastructure in today's world mirrors the colonial administrative structure with its control over data, policing user's behavior, and pushing narratives for the majoritarian political power. The global tech giants have as much sway in geopolitics as the global leaders themselves. Previously the conditions of colonization created an unequal e...
items.fullDescription: The digital infrastructure in today's world mirrors the colonial administrative structure with its control over data, policing user's behavior, and pushing narratives for the majoritarian political power. The global tech giants have as much sway in geopolitics as the global leaders themselves. Previously the conditions of colonization created an unequal economic infrastructure that marginalizes the local communities, and even after independence from the colonial power, the trade relations remain that of a colonial appendage. Similarly, the upkeep of the digital sphere is not without its economic and environmental hazards. Anibal Quijano (1928-2018) a Peruvian sociologist, talks about the plight of this expansion for resources in his book, On the Coloniality of Power. He says: …the contemporary scientific community, insists on destroying the conditions for life on the planet. So, both the movement of the most subjugated people in this world, those who would not be able to exist if they sold their means of subsistence, and those who realize that if all this comes to an end no one will be able to survive, come together in a shared analysis. 359 He stresses on the role of the communities who've resisted the colonial and postcolonial measures to protect their land, water, and air over the years. It shows how the communities have more of a lateral structure which allows for debate and discussions as opposed to the hierarchy of the colonial administrative infrastructure. This panel seeks to garner discourse around the digital world's ambivalent nature of enhancing global communications and generating jobs at the cost of endangering local communities. Questions, challenges, and possible solutions for a community-oriented resistance will be among the many concerns discussed at this panel. Submit on NeMLA's website: Submit an Abstract

items.fullDescription: This panel invites papers on the topic of (re)vision-retelling, translating, adapting, re-seeing-literature in ways that engender community empowerment. There are myriad ways to revisit literary texts through new iterations, and it is often through the act of retelling and recrafting that subversive narratives are formed and new communities forged. This panel will explore how retelling a narrative shapes understandings of an original text, the community from which it was created, and the community into which it is being called forth. How can translation produce new entry points for readers into "foreign" texts, cultures, and languages? How might the adaptation of literature foster community across disciplines, ages, cultures, genders, and species? How might an author reconfigure a historical and/or popular narrative for a new audience, and to what end? How might shifting a narrative into a new genre, form, or medium become a subversive, interpretative act? We invite papers that address the questions listed above, but also other innovative explorations into the topic of re-seeing literature for community empowerment.

items.fullDescription: Conference: 2-4 December 2026, in Gdansk, Poland and online CALL FOR PAPERS: In our modern world, which some have argued to be disjointed while immersing itself ever deeper in crisis, the turning back to "the olden days" and the ensuing nostalgia constitute anoticeable phenomenon, both individually (the memory of biography) and collectively (the memory of history). Another important - and equally noticeable - phenomenon is the longing for something vague, indefinite or never existent. Hence, during our interdisciplinary conference we would like to concentrate on the phenomena of nostalgia and melancholy. We are interested in all expressions of longing forthe past, from the reassuring and action-propelling ones to those which paralyze us, leading to despair and utter dejection. We aim to explore the experience of nostalgia and melancholy in its multifarious manifestations: psychological, social, historical, cultural, philosophical, religious, economic, political, artistic, and many others. We will also devote considerable attention to how these phenomena appear and transform in artistic practices: literature, film, theatre, and visual arts. This is why we invite researchers representing various academic disciplines: anthropology, history, psychology, psychoanalysis, sociology, politics, philosophy, economics, law, literary studies, theatre studies, film studies, memory studies, nostalgia studies, migration studies, consciousness studies, dream studies, gender studies, postcolonial studies, medical sciences, psychiatry, cognitive sciences, design, project management and other disciplines. Different forms of presentations are encouraged, including case studies, theoretical investigations, problem-oriented arguments, and comparative analyses. We will be happy to hear from both experienced scholars and young academics at the beginning of their careers, as well as students. items.title: Reading the Earth: Geology, Memory, and Relational Poetics
items.excerpt: Across contemporary literary and cultural studies, increasing attention has been devoted to the ways in which geological matter shapes cultural imagination, environmental memory, and literary form. Rocks, minerals, fossils, sediments, ruins, and other more-than-living material formations are no longer understood merely as settings or symbols, but as archi...
items.fullDescription: Across contemporary literary and cultural studies, increasing attention has been devoted to the ways in which geological matter shapes cultural imagination, environmental memory, and literary form. Rocks, minerals, fossils, sediments, ruins, and other more-than-living material formations are no longer understood merely as settings or symbols, but as archives of deep time, environmental change, historical violence, and planetary entanglement. This panel invites papers exploring how literature engages with the Earth as a site of memory, relation, and meaning-making. We are particularly interested in approaches that examine geological formations, landscapes, material traces, planetary archives, and sedimented histories as participants in literary and cultural processes rather than passive backdrops to human experience. Possible topics include geologies of memory; deep time and literary temporality; environmental trauma and material archives; fossils, ruins, and traces; sacred landscapes and earth-based imaginaries; extraction, waste, and environmental justice; posthumanist and new materialist approaches to literature; relational poetics; and the intersections of geology, ecology, and cultural memory. We welcome contributions addressing literary and cultural texts from any historical period, linguistic tradition, or geographical region, as well as comparative and transnational perspectives. The session will be held in-person but a few remote presentations may be included. Please clearly indicate in your submission whether you wish to participate in person or remotely. All abstract submissions must be submitted through the NeMLA portal https://cfplist.com/nemla/Home/S/22630. Please note that the submission window for individual abstracts officially opens June 15 and closes September 30.

In fact, ever since the outbreak of the American Revolution in 1765, through the French and the Haitian Revolutions throughout the 1790’s, all the way to 1848, the year that de-politicized Charles Baudelaire (according to his letter from May 5, 1852 to Narcisse Ancelle), literary production seems to have been inseparable from the process of building after and thinking social revolution.

items.fullDescription: Call for Proposals NeMLA's 58th Annual Convention - "Empowering Communities" March 6-9, 2027 | Salve Regina University, Newport, Rhode Island Roundtable Title: Writing and Wellbeing: A New Urgency for Human-Centered Composition Pedagogies Primary Area / Secondary Area: Rhetoric & Composition / Pedagogy & Professional Modality: In person only Chair: Miranda Lutyens, University of Massachusetts Amherst College is a time of excitement and novelty, but it can also bring about anxiety and uncertainty. Those unsettling emotions have been on an upward trend in recent years, with a host of factors - the fallout of the pandemic, social media's curation of idealized lives, and existential fears relating to climate change, generative AI, and political turmoil - raising concerns about the wellbeing of students. The college writing classroom has a long history of offering compassion through creative (and even countercultural) approaches to teaching and learning. This included affirming the rights of linguistically marginalized students to their own language, as well as efforts to keep struggling writers in school to keep them out of the Vietnam War. As we collectively face new urgencies, this roundtable session invites participants to share research projects and instructional practices that consider college writing classrooms as affective and embodied spaces. Recognizing concerns such as instructors' emotional labor and under-resourced writing programs, the session primarily focuses on putting forward innovative approaches to making writing instruction responsive to students' experiences in increasingly uncertain times. Insights gained from critical teacher research on human-centered pedagogies are particularly welcome, as are contributions from all levels of writing instruction, including first-year composition, writing in the disciplines, writing support for graduate students etc. The goal of this roundtable is for both participants and attendees to leave with expanded perspectives on how the college writing classroom might offer students more pleasure and new possibilities - to reimagine a more salutary relationship to writing, to engage with the written word in more personally meaningful ways, and to gain a greater awareness of themselves and others. The roundtable also aims to offer practical strategies for enacting - or at least experimenting with - new classroom practices. Submission Deadline: September 30, 2026 Please submit abstracts via the NeMLA portal: https://cfplist.com/nemla/Home/S/22547 Convention information can be found here: https://www.nemla.org/convention.html

items.fullDescription: Esta sessão explora como comunidades historicamente marginalizadas pelo colonialismo, racismo, desigualdade e exclusão epistêmica mobilizam a educação, a cultura, a língua, a memória e a ação coletiva como formas de empoderamento e transformação social. Fundamentada no pensamento decolonial e em abordagens interdisciplinares críticas, a sessão examina como essas comunidades desafiam as estruturas coloniais que continuam a moldar a produção de conhecimento, as práticas institucionais e a representação cultural no mundo contemporâneo. O painel acolhe contribuições que investiguem as interseções entre decolonialidade, educação, justiça epistêmica, resistência cultural e agência comunitária em diversos contextos geográficos e históricos. Os tópicos podem incluir, entre outros, pedagogias decoloniais, ensino superior e desigualdade social, produção de conhecimento baseada na comunidade, linguagem e poder, diáspora e identidade, memória e resistência, exclusão racializada, epistemologias indígenas e africanas, perspectivas feministas e interseccionais, migração, mídia e ativismo cultural. Ao abordar o tema da convenção, "Empoderando Comunidades", esta sessão busca criar um espaço interdisciplinar para discutir como comunidades marginalizadas reivindicam voz, visibilidade e autonomia por meio da educação, práticas culturais e formas alternativas de conhecimento. A sessão incentiva pesquisadores das áreas de estudos literários, estudos culturais, educação, ciência política, sociologia, estudos pós-coloniais, estudos africanos e campos afins a contribuírem com perspectivas inovadoras sobre as possibilidades de futuros decoloniais e empoderamento coletivo.

items.fullDescription: I want to be accepted by society…live in a world I don't have to hide in…make choices without being in constant fear of them destroying me or the ones I care about." (Ada, liberated TanakX5 robot, on her hopes and dreams. Alex + Ada, Book 11) Many contemporary and recent speculative fiction texts interrogate the questions of "making kin" with companion species, including the companions humans might engineer and build to keep us company. In her Staying with the Trouble, Donna Haraway proposes reknitting the current order to address Capitalocene-generated problems of overpopulation and overconsumption. To survive, humans must extend their care and loyalty to other inhabitants of our shared planet, and co-construct knowledge -sympoeisis-with them. Haraway includes part-biological cyborgs in the potential so-called symbionts with whom humans should co-exist, but does not expressly include fully non-biologic, mechanical partners in her analysis. Yet, as part of the thought experiment enacted by speculative fictions of manufactured fellow beings, Haraway's prescription might be expanded to encompass sentient partners whom humans engineer and manufacture to keep themselves company. This roundtable invites papers interrogating speculative fiction solutions for expanding kinship relations to sentient non-biologic companions, whether embodied robots, virtual companions, or other. In other words, how does a particular creator of an imagined world envision expanding Haraway's Chthulucene era of "oddkin" to included fully artificial as well as natural companion species? And how do these artificial companions fare, that is, are the humans in their worlds able to embrace their right to equal standing and accord them rights?

items.title: Beyond Hegemony: Masculinities in World and Comparative Literature
items.excerpt: This panel examines how literary and cultural texts from diverse global traditions imagine masculinity not merely as an individual identity but as a relational and communal practice. In an era marked by migration, political polarization, social fragmentation, environmental crisis, and renewed struggles for collective empowerment, narratives of masculinity...
items.fullDescription: This panel examines how literary and cultural texts from diverse global traditions imagine masculinity not merely as an individual identity but as a relational and communal practice. In an era marked by migration, political polarization, social fragmentation, environmental crisis, and renewed struggles for collective empowerment, narratives of masculinity have become central sites through which communities negotiate belonging, responsibility, vulnerability, and resistance. While dominant models of masculinity have often been associated with hierarchy, authority, nationalism, and exclusion, contemporary world literatures increasingly depict alternative masculinities grounded in care, ethical responsibility, emotional openness, solidarity, and collective survival. Such representations challenge inherited structures of power while opening new possibilities for community formation and social transformation. This panel invites comparative and transnational approaches that explore how literary texts, films, cultural narratives, and other expressive forms construct, critique, or reimagine masculinities within local and global communities. Particular attention may be given to how gender intersects with race, class, migration, coloniality, religion, ecology, technology, and cultural memory in shaping collective identities and practices of empowerment. Situated within the broader concerns of World Literature and Comparative Literature, this session seeks to foster dialogue across regions, languages, and traditions while investigating how masculinities participate in the creation-or disruption-of empowered communities. We welcome papers addressing, but not limited to: Comparative constructions of masculinity across world literatures Masculinity and migration, diaspora, or displacement Literary representations of fatherhood, mentorship, and communal responsibility Masculinities in Global South literatures Masculinity and environmental or ecological communities Masculinity, memory, and post-conflict reconstruction Queer and non-hegemonic masculinities in world literature Masculinity and cultural resistance under authoritarian regimes Masculinity, religion, and collective belonging Masculinity and affect in contemporary global fiction

It is hoped that we can bring a fresh critical light to this pivotal moment in world history. Too often, scholarly reflection on the Great War tends to focus military activity and various aspects of masculine...
items.fullDescription: Our session examines the importance of women as fictional characters, authors, and purveyors of legacies associated with the Great War of 1914-1918. It is hoped that we can bring a fresh critical light to this pivotal moment in world history. Too often, scholarly reflection on the Great War tends to focus military activity and various aspects of masculine performance. We would like to use a wider lens for our discussion of the Great War. Please note the very wide range of perspectives in this seminar: authors, characters, and context. More precisely, our reconsideration of the works, authors, and legacies of the Great War includes three directions: first, the examination of women appearing as fictional characters in this normally male-oriented thematic area; second, reflection on women writers, artists, and filmmakers engaged in representing the Great War; finally, establishing historical continuities deriving from the relationship between women and the Great War. The flexible methodology of this session includes the examination of novels, poems, paintings, photography, film, documentaries, memoirs, and memorials. A few suggestions for interpretative directions: · Recent critical directions on topics relating to women and the Great War · Non-European, global writing on the Great War · Themes of colonialism, migration, class, public health, punition, sexual violence, and race · The inclusion of documentary, archival, and any relevant internet materials · Presentations on "Women, New England, and the Great War" · The involvement of women in medical and public health issues during the Great War · Women in the Great War as represented in museums, local, national, and global media.

items.title: The Classroom as Counter-Archive: Place-Based Pedagogies of Community Empowerment
items.location: Salve Regina University. Newport, Rhode Island · NEMLA
items.excerpt: Education is an ideal means of empowerment, for it enables students to take ownership of the historical and personal archives that stand for their communities. This panel regards the classroom as a privileged site of such empowerment-particularly for students from immigrant families-and seeks proposals on how to equip them to become active agents in produ...
items.fullDescription: Education is an ideal means of empowerment, for it enables students to take ownership of the historical and personal archives that stand for their communities. This panel regards the classroom as a privileged site of such empowerment-particularly for students from immigrant families-and seeks proposals on how to equip them to become active agents in producing their own interpretations of the cultural and spatial memory they share with their forebears. We draw inspiration from courses in which students articulate their personal, familial, and communal relationships with the tangible and intangible spaces of the city they inhabit: from their own homes to the streets they traverse daily, the buildings, neighborhoods, and monuments they encounter, and the individual and social practices that animate them. Setting their lived experience against the historical archives that purport to represent them, students produce analytical descriptions of urban space. Their work collectively assembles a shared repository of cultural memory - a "counter-archive" that weaves together place-based learning, immigration histories, and autobiographical narrative. In classrooms of diverse composition, this work empowers along more than one path. Immigrant students illuminate the place of their communities within the urban social fabric, while others discover-in their own projects and in those of their classmates-insights that transform how they perceive the city and their own identities in relation to it. We invite educators across languages, periods, and disciplines to share pedagogical projects and activities-assignments, archives, community-engaged work, digital repositories, creative and testimonial writing-that treat teaching as a practice of empowerment. We especially welcome contributions that reflect on the theory of change behind their work: when does a classroom project produce agency, and how do we know?

items.fullDescription: Call fort submissions "Conversations with the Dead: Excavation as Re-vision" Chair: Edvige Giunta, Kean University The session invites presentations of prose, poetry, and/or hybrid writing that “turn” to the dead—not for the purpose of elegiac reminiscence but to unsettle or dismantle notions of chronology, inheritance, and other forms of linear, unidirectional connection between the living and the dead. Writers who turn to the dead find that that past transforms the present through the very process of excavation: communities are remade in the turning. This session will examine what that practice looks like across genres such as intergenerational memoir, speculative memoir, investigative essays, and personal rewritings of myths.

items.fullDescription: As part of this year's NeMLA's inquiry into "Empowering Communities," this panel focuses on how women writers, filmmakers, and artists from the French-speaking world represent human labor. From the French Black Code that codified the conditions of enslaved labor to neo-colonial economic structures that fuel migration patterns, human labor in colonial, post-colonial, and neo-colonial contexts not only manifests systems of coercion and emancipation, but also serves as a measure of individual and collective empowerment. This panel welcomes contributions that examine representations of human labor from any historical period in the French-speaking world. It seeks to support dialogue that investigates how women from the Francophone world stage, reappropriate, and interrogate the many forms of human labor that impacted and continue to influence peoples in the Francophone world. Possible topics include but are not limited to questions of gender, memory, empowerment, economic structures, the environment, family, migration, and reparative justice. Please note that this is an in-person panel. Abstracts are due September 30, 2026, and can be submitted through the NeMLA portal at this link: https://cfplist.com/nemla/Home/S/22673 Contact Lisa Connell (lconnell@westga.edu) with questions about the panel.

items.title: Resisting from the Edge: Marginal Characters and Collective Empowerment
items.location: Salve Regina University, Newport, RI · NeMLA
items.excerpt: This panel invites papers that examine the agency of marginalized characters in literary, visual, audiovisual, and artistic productions from the French?speaking world across any historical period. Artistic works offer numerous examples of figures who maintain an ambivalent relationship to their communities. Because of their social or ethnic origins, their...
items.fullDescription: This panel invites papers that examine the agency of marginalized characters in literary, visual, audiovisual, and artistic productions from the French?speaking world across any historical period. Artistic works offer numerous examples of figures who maintain an ambivalent relationship to their communities. Because of their social or ethnic origins, their divergent perspectives, or their transgression of established norms, certain characters find themselves pushed to the margins of social, familial, or professional groups. While such exclusion may appear to weaken those who experience it, this panel asks whether marginalization might also function as a source of strength. Can marginality become a generative position? Do marginalized individuals succeed in forming new communities that enable them to confront stigma and ultimately overcome it? This discussion seeks to shift our understanding of the place occupied by marginalized individuals and groups in fictional narratives. By considering the networks of solidarity that emerge among marginalized subjects, the panel explores what lies beneath their presumed inferiority, inviting critical attention to what is hidden, erased, or rendered invisible within dominant narratives. More importantly, we will examine how marginalized communities may become empowering spaces of resistance, mutual support, and hope. Drawing on approaches from cultural studies, postcolonial theory, sociolinguistics, and intersectionality, this session seeks to understand how literary, visual, audiovisual, and artistic narratives stage the tensions between marginality and belonging, strength and vulnerability. Proposals engaging with environmental humanities, posthumanism, Indigenous studies, as well as diaspora and migration studies are strongly encouraged. We also welcome submissions drawing on gender and queer studies, memory and trauma studies, digital humanities, or other interdisciplinary frameworks within the humanities. We welcome proposals of 250-300 words, in French or English, submitted by September 30.

items.title: Ecologies of Attention: Literature and Pedagogies of the More-than-Human
items.excerpt: Today's ecological problems demand not only ecological awareness but also a fundamental rethinking of the human-nature relationship with the more-than-human world. Increased climatic change, species extinction, ecological degradation, and planetary instability. Challenge anthropocentric assumptions where humans are seen as separate from, superior to, or s...
items.fullDescription: Today's ecological problems demand not only ecological awareness but also a fundamental rethinking of the human-nature relationship with the more-than-human world. Increased climatic change, species extinction, ecological degradation, and planetary instability. Challenge anthropocentric assumptions where humans are seen as separate from, superior to, or sole interpreters of nature. This panel invites papers that explore how literature, storytelling, environmental humanities, and creative pedagogies might cultivate "ecologies of attention" within teacher education and educational spaces. Rather than approaching nature as a passive object of study or a resource for human learning, the session seeks to examine how literary and cultural texts unsettle human-centered ways of knowing and open possibilities for relational, more-than-human pedagogies. How might literature invite future educators to engage with ecological interconnectedness, multispecies agency, and nonhuman forms of intelligence, communication, and temporality? What pedagogical possibilities emerge when teachers and learners encounter forests, rivers, plants, animals, weather systems, and landscapes not as background settings, but as active participants within shared ecological worlds? How can educational practices move beyond extractive or instrumental approaches to environmental learning toward forms of attentiveness, reciprocity, care, and ethical coexistence? The panel is particularly interested in pedagogical and creative engagements that explore how literary and speculative texts reshape ecological imagination and challenge anthropocentric assumptions within teacher education, curriculum studies, literacy practices, and environmental pedagogy. Possible topics include, but are not limited to: Ecocriticism and teacher education Pedagogies of the more-than-human Literature and ecological attentiveness Climate fiction and environmental pedagogy Multispecies storytelling and relational learning Posthumanism and educational philosophy Ecological imagination in literacy education Biosemiotics, ecological communication, and pedagogy Plant studies, animal studies, and arboreal thinking in education Indigenous ecological knowledge and decolonial pedagogies Eco-poetry, speculative fiction, and climate narratives in the classroom Slow pedagogies, ecological temporality, and relational learning Environmental ethics and pedagogies of coexistence Creative-critical approaches to ecological teaching and learning Affective responses to climate anxiety, grief, and ecological uncertainty The curriculum, sustainability, and more than human relationality are explored. Reading practices that decenter the human subject. Ecological storytelling and pedagogies oriented towards the future. The session invites interdisciplinary, theoretical, pedagogical, creative-critical, and practice-based contributions from scholars, educators, teacher educators, creative writers, and Researchers in the fields of literature, education, environmental humanities, and cultural studies and related fields. Papers engaging works such as The Overstory, How I Became a Tree, The Ministry for the Future, The Grapes of Wrath, Climate Fiction, eco-poems, speculations, and Environmental media are particularly welcome, although not restricted to these texts. Submission Guidelines Please submit: An abstract of 250-300 words A short bio-note (100 words) Institutional affiliation (if applicable) Please send submissions to: mussaratshahid@fccollege.edu.pk

items.title: Reframing Relevance: Sustaining the Humanities in Specialized Academic Contexts
items.location: Newport, RI · Northeast Modern Language Association Conference
items.excerpt: As some institutions restructure academic priorities in response to various pressures in higher education, the Humanities can face contraction, marginalization, or elimination. These challenges are intensified at specialized universities, meaning institutions oriented toward fields such as STEM, health sciences, business, etc., where Humanities courses ar...
items.fullDescription: As some institutions restructure academic priorities in response to various pressures in higher education, the Humanities can face contraction, marginalization, or elimination. These challenges are intensified at specialized universities, meaning institutions oriented toward fields such as STEM, health sciences, business, etc., where Humanities courses are often kept to general education requirements and could be perceived as peripheral to students' professional training. Within such environments, Humanities faculty must navigate not only broader disciplinary challenges but also institutional cultures that may misunderstand or underappreciate the field's contributions. This roundtable invites faculty working in specialized institutional contexts to reflect on how they sustain and advocate for the Humanities amid these pressures. How do instructors articulate the intellectual, ethical, and professional value of Humanities study to students primarily focused on career-focused pathways? What pedagogical or curricular strategies have proven effective in demonstrating relevance to disciplines such as engineering, nursing, or business? Alternatively, how have faculty members built collaborations with colleagues across fields to integrate Humanities perspectives into specialized curricula? Participants will also consider how they engage multiple audiences-students, faculty peers, and administrators-to communicate the significance of Humanities education. By sharing concrete strategies, institutional experiences, and models of interdisciplinary partnership, this discussion aims to highlight adaptable approaches for maintaining the visibility and importance of the Humanities in specialized settings. Ultimately, the roundtable seeks to reassert the Humanities as essential to professional education. This roundtable is part of the Northeast Modern Language Association conference, which will take place between March 6-9, 2027 in Newport, RI. Hybrid: The session will be held in-person but a few remote presentations may be included. 250-word abstracts for participation in this roundtable are welcome, and they can be submitted through this website: https://cfplist.com/nemla/Home/login

items.fullDescription: Call For Papers - NeMLA 2027 Panel -- Supporting the Well-Being of Students and Instructors in a Transitional Time Northeast MLA 2027: March 6-9, 2027 Panel Title: Supporting the Well-Being of Students and Instructors in a Transitional Time Modality: Virtual Only: All presentations will be delivered via Zoom regardless of whether the presenters are in-person Format: 3-4 presentations/papers, 15-20 minutes per presenter The past few years - which could be described as part of a larger cultural, political, and economic flash point -- have created true challenges for higher education. This transitional time has put pressure on all parties of our postsecondary community, as seen in the reported mental health challenges of undergraduates and the high rates of burnout amongst faculty and support networks in the sector (Mowreader; Pourasadollahi and Vincenti; Liu). In addition to these post-pandemic stressors, a host of broader concerns are also impinging on the postsecondary environment (see "The Trends Report" for one discussion). How can we empower our community - defined through instructors, students, and/or support services -- during such a transitional moment? This session will create a dialogue that touches on any of the following: -discussions/studies of interventions and/or articulations of already established practices in supporting the well-being of students and/or instructors; -the reflections of students, instructors, and/or support networks on the challenges of and responses to our contemporary moment. These challenges can include: the impact of budget cuts on postsecondary contexts, the fallout of declining academic freedom in the classroom, the impact (positive or negative) of Gen AI on the well-being of our community, the discord between instructor expectations and the reality of students. items.fullDescription: Palestine and the Challenge to German Studies Northeast Modern Language Association (NeMLA) annual convention Newport, Rhode Island March 6-9, 2027 Submission Deadline: 30 September 2026 through the NeMLA portal: https://cfplist.com/nemla/Home/S/22528 Recent work in and around German Studies (Younes and Al-Taher; El Bulbeisi; Özyürek; Moses; Salehi) argues that the erasure of Palestinian identity in Germany is tied to deeper national tensions: How the country remembers its past, how it talks or avoids talking about race, what kinds of political speech are treated as acceptable, and how it confronts histories of imperialism and genocide. Moreover, scholars (Thompson and Tuzcu; Ragab; Daher) have documented how major institutions in Germany have been engaged in a wave of repression of ethnic minority communities, targeting Palestinians, other people of color, and Jewish anti-Zionists. This scholarship demonstrates how such pressures influence which voices, histories, and political positions are treated as legitimate within the field of German Studies, and which ones are marginalized. This panel invites contributions that explore how German Studies has begun or has struggled to engage with the significance of Palestine and Palestinian life, not only in contemporary German culture, politics, and literature, but within the discipline's own structures. While scholarship on Holocaust memory culture, as well as on multidirectional memory and migrant memory archives, has broadened the field's understanding of how Holocaust memory circulates and how migrant communities navigate its demands, recent work, such as articles by Catlin, Kundnani, and Rosenbrück in the New German Critique special issue "German Memory Politics at a Crossroads" (2026) provides evidence of the limits of these frameworks and the political pressures that shape them. Rather than challenge the centrality of Holocaust memory itself, this panel aims to examine how it is mobilized to foreclose other histories of violence, displacement, and coloniality, and how this foreclosing makes it difficult to integrate anti-imperialist, antiracist, and decolonial approaches that would situate Germany within broader histories of imperialism, colonial violence, and genocide. Palestine makes these dynamics visible by revealing how debates about memory shape disciplinary boundaries, how racialization and political speech determine scholarly legitimacy, and how exclusions are reproduced even within critical frameworks. This panel welcomes contributions that examine where Palestine appears, where it is actively excluded, and how these patterns expose German Studies' unresolved tensions around race, German colonial histories, and the politics of knowledge production. The goal of this panel is to open a conversation about how German Studies might expand beyond memory-centered approaches toward more globally attuned, anti?imperialist, and decolonial analytical frameworks. Topics include but are not limited to: · Intersectional decolonial feminist frameworks and praxes · Critiques of white Western imperial feminism · "Pinkwashing" and "homonationalism" to justify colonial violence and dehumanize Indigenous communities · The role of anti-Palestinian racism in mainstream anti-immigrant backlash and far-right political actors · Scapegoating of Muslims as the new Nazis in the theory of "imported anti-Semitism" (Özyürek) · Germany's colonial and neocolonial relationships to the broader region of West Asia · Integrating Palestinian perspectives into pedagogy, curriculum, and study abroad advising · Courses and lesson plans that include the Nakba and its continuity · German Studies and BDS/academic boycott · The "Historikerstreit 2.0" and attacks on "postcolonialism" · The history of East German solidarity with Palestinians · Student and faculty support in campus organizing for Palestine solidarity, and institutional and departmental barriers Abstracts: Please submit 300-word abstracts by 30 September 2026 though the NeMLA portal: https://cfplist.com/nemla/Home/S/22528 For questions, please contact the panel organizer Maria Grewe (mgrewe@jjay.cuny.edu).

items.fullDescription: If you've taught older literature recently, you've probably heard students ask the question "Why am I reading this?" They've got a point. Why should we read Shakespeare's plays, or Paradise Lost , or (god-forbid) "The Rape of the Lock"? We might be able to coax students into reading a Jane Austen novel or even Huckleberry Finn because they are still part of our cultural imagination, but it's less easy to coax students into reading Beowulf or Tom Jones -texts that are less familiar in form and content. As we jettison the canon and the timeless truths of literature, what do we expect reading older texts will give our students that they wouldn't otherwise understand? How do we explain our reasoning to students about why they should read texts from earlier literary periods? How do we present these earlier periods (or periodization) and their culture and ideas as relevant to our undergraduate students in our English, writing, or humanities programs? Or is relevance the problem? How might we redefine older literature in our classes, or what we (can) do with these texts? I'm particularly interested in position papers that take into consideration practical pedagogical and theoretical concerns: arguments about curricula, course development or assignments that do different things with this literature. Papers are welcome on any kind of literature/texts or periods prior to 1800.

items.fullDescription: From its founding ideals framing rights as tied to individuals to many of the ‘myths that made America,’ such as the self-made man, ideas of individualism are deeply entrenched in the culture of the United States. Yet at the same time, the US has also always understood itself as a particular community: as a city upon a hill, a melting pot, a more perfect union. As such, the United States has been established on a seeming paradox, forming ‘out of many, one.’ More recently, this previous consensus has become increasingly brittle, with fragmentation, polarization, hyper-individualism, and loneliness on the rise—as some would argue: again.

items.fullDescription: Despite the international prominence of Stanisław Lem and, more recently, Andrzej Sapkowski's The Witcher , Polish science fiction and speculative literature remain strikingly underrepresented in English-language scholarship. Existing criticism tends to orbit a small number of canonical figures and a handful of frequently revisited texts, leaving a rich, historically complex tradition, spanning censorship-era political allegory, post-1989 transformation, contemporary literary crossover, and a distinct national cinema largely unexamined outside of Polish-language scholarship.

items.fullDescription: "That Sounds Funny": CFP for ALA "Music and the American Literary Imagination" symposium The American Humor Studies Association (AHSA) invites submissions for a proposed panel for the American Literature Association (ALA) 2027 symposium "Music and the American Literary Imagination," to be held January 28-30, 2027, in Nashville, TN. For hundreds of years, humor has been an indelible element of American popular music as well as literature. This AHSA-sponsored, non-guaranteed panel seeks proposals that consider the connections between American humor, American music, and American literature. We invite submissions on any genre, period, or place, including papers that explore the fuzzy boundaries of what it means to be "American." We are especially interested in presentations that examine humor practices in the American South; for example, proposals might consider the use of humor in Southern rap, children's author Shel Silverstein's role in shaping the "outlaw country" sound, or the recent rise of right-wing "humorists" in Nashville. Together, the presentations constituting this panel will explore the pitfalls and possibilities of the imbrication of music, humor, and American literary culture. Please send a 250-word abstract and a brief biography by October 15, 2026, to AHSA Vice President Benjamin Schwartz at bs8959@princeton.edu. All panel participants must be AHSA members before the ALA conference opens on January 28, 2027. The Constance Rourke travel award is available for graduate students on a panel. The award varies between $100 - $300 (depending on AHSA funds and the number of applicants) to help defray the cost of attending conferences with AHSA-sponsored panels. We also remind everyone that AHSA has in place a mentoring program to help emerging scholars prepare an essay for publication. Presenting at ALA can be the first step to being published.

items.fullDescription: European Comic Art Special Issue 'Francophone Graphic Narratives / Bande dessinée: Authority and Resistance' European Comic Art invites proposals for a special issue on 'Francophone Graphic Narratives/Bande dessinée: Authority and Resistance'. This issue will examine how francophone graphic narratives engage with, challenge, and reimagine authority in its many forms - political, cultural, institutional, and aesthetic - and how they forge practices of resistance and dissent. The bande dessinée is a medium that subverts hierarchies and blurs boundaries. Long regarded as the lowly offspring of literature and the visual arts, comics have since been legitimised by scholars and artists demonstrating their capacity to engage with complex sociohistorical, political, and cultural topics. This 'Ninth Art' now occupies an increasingly important place in university classrooms, academic publications, and public discourse alike. Its multimodal features - panel layout, gutters, framing, braiding, and complex interplay between text and image - allow comics to stage and challenge authority in formally distinctive ways. This aesthetic vantage point makes comics a powerful medium through which to bring displaced, excluded, and silenced narratives into view. From Chantal Montellier's impressive four-decade oeuvre of political cartoons and graphic novels contesting racism, misogyny and totalitarianism to Jessica Oublié's Peyi an nou , which provides a counternarrative to state discourse on the BUMIDOM, the bande dessinée has often served to undercut official rhetoric. This special issue of European Comic Art seeks articles that examine how Francophone bandes dessinées engage with dominant institutions and discourses from theoretical and pedagogical perspectives. How do comics represent power and powerlessness? How do they respond to hierarchies that exist in various settings and communities? How do they decentre and challenge 'standard' language practices? Finally, how might comics be used pedagogically to help foster students' critical thinking skills and question institutional, political, and social discourses? Possible topics include, but are not limited to: Migration Ecocriticism Social justice and political activism Gender and sexuality Comics and memory studies Class, labour, and economic inequality Pedagogy and second language acquisition Nationalism, cosmopolitanism, and globalization Colonial legacies, decolonial resistance/critique Monolingualism, multilingualism, and language politics Official histories, counter archives, and silenced narratives Humour, parody, satire, and subversion Submission Guidelines Please submit a 500-word abstract with a short biographical note to Liana Pshevorska at lpshevorska@wesleyan.edu and Valentina Denzel at vdenzel@msu.edu by October 15, 2026. Informal inquiries are welcome. Decisions will be communicated in November 2026. The deadline for submitting full manuscripts is February 28, 2027. Articles should be in English, approximately 8,000 words, including images, notes, and bibliography. Contributors may include up to four images, which will be factored into the overall length of the article. Each image will be counted as approximately three-quarters of a printed page, based on an estimate 400 words per page. Please note that authors are responsible for obtaining copyright permission for all included images. Documentation of permissions should be submitted alongside the manuscript.
