items.excerpt: Call for Papers: NANO: New American Notes Online (ISSN: 2160-0104) Special Issue 18: Exploring the Boundary Waters of the Blue Humanities Special Issue Guest Editors: Eric Denbang Kunkuri and Dana Van Kooy Deadline: 16 October 2026 Publication: spring/summer 2027 Full CFP Details: https://nanocrit.com/index.php/home/cfp-plus-submissions-new The creative a...
items.fullDescription: Call for Papers: NANO: New American Notes Online (ISSN: 2160-0104) Special Issue 18: Exploring the Boundary Waters of the Blue Humanities Special Issue Guest Editors: Eric Denbang Kunkuri and Dana Van Kooy Deadline: 16 October 2026 Publication: spring/summer 2027 Full CFP Details: https://nanocrit.com/index.php/home/cfp-plus-submissions-new The creative and scholarly work being done in the blue humanities has deepened our turn towards exploring waterways and boundary waters. The currents circulating through the blue humanities flow into and from myriad disciplines, including anthropology, biology, decolonial studies, feminist/queer studies, geography, history, indigenous studies, literature, music, performance studies, philosophy, and the visual arts. The cultural and theoretical inlets being carved out by work in the blue humanities have proven generative in terms of developing a distinctive metaphor-laden language, analytic methods like Kamau Brathwaite's theory of "tidalectics," and new ways of submerging ourselves in both historical and unprecedented questions about the water that is in and, as Rachel Carson notes in her famous title, "around us." For this special issue, we invite submissions of traditional and multimodal essays of up to 5,000 words (excluding works cited) that explore the boundary waters of the blue humanities. We encourage essays focused on narratives as well as submissions that explore art installations and other medial forms that address the boundary waters circulating around and through the blue humanities. Topics may include but are not limited to the following: Boundary waters that divide and connect nations, classes, and/or ecological zones Mythic, cinematic, and visual narratives of how humans and/or nonhumans are "held," migrate, or are moved through watery littorals Critical explorations like those associated with "tidalectics," a term that comes from Kamau Brathwaite, who proposed an alternative framework for literary and political engagement that is grounded in the rhythm of waves and the cyclic ebb and flow of tides "Portraits" of littoral space(s) in literature, history, myth, the visual arts, and theatrical and musical performances Exploring the significance of physical, structural, and emotional vulnerabilities and instabilities within littorals, shoals, or port cities Hydrological infrastructure (colonial, postcolonial, urban, rural) associated with port cities, canal locks, and dams Relational undercurrents that speak to our ways of submerging ourselves into the watery worlds that surround us Traditional water ways: ways of being with or "holding" water The role of inland waterways in routing stories and/or facilitating/impeding human and nonhuman migrations Exploring the agency of oceans and rivers in sustaining capitalist and imperial economies and their alternatives Water's many forms (snow, ice, fog, rivers, oceans) and ways "water" facilitates connection and/or imposes isolation How waterways-"paths" of water and ways of being with water-lead us to new or alternative futures Scenes of erosion that expose lost or forgotten histories Please direct questions to the special issue editors: Eric Denbang Kunkuri [edkunkur@mtu.edu] and Dana Van Kooy [drvankoo@mtu.edu] For questions about the use and disclosure of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools, please see NANO's AI Statement (https://nanocrit.com/index.php/Journal-Information) Please use the Submission Form on top left of the CFP page: https://nanocrit.com/index.php/Submissions/Submission-Form NANO: New American Notes Online is a free, open-access, peer-reviewed journal. NANO does not charge for submission, review, or publication. It is indexed in the MLA International Bibliography, GALE, ProQuest, and DOAJ.

items.fullDescription: The rise of the superhero is one of the most significant cultural developments of the twentieth and twenty-first centuries. Since the debut of Superman in Action Comics #1 (April 18, 1938), superheroes have evolved from colorful comic-book figures into powerful global symbols that shape conversations about politics, morality, identity, technology, gender, race, mythology, trauma, and resistance. What began with the imaginative vision of Jerry Siegel (writer) and Joe Shuster (artist) has expanded into a worldwide phenomenon spanning comics, film, television, literature, gaming, digital media, and academic discourse.

items.fullDescription: TRANSPOSITIONES Journal for Transdisciplinary and Intermedial Culture Studies / Zeitschrift fu?r transdisziplinäre und intermediale Kulturforschung, ISSN 2749-4128 (print), 2749-4136 (online), Vol. 6, No. 2 (2027) Call for Papers Thematic focus of the issue: Earth / Sediment / Trace: Geologies, Material Memories, and the More-than-Living World Across the environmental humanities, increasing attention has been devoted to the geological dimensions of culture and the cultural dimensions of the Earth. Geohumanities, critical mineral studies, energy humanities, environmental justice scholarship, and related fields have opened new perspectives on extraction, sedimentation, toxicity, waste, material memory, and deep time. At a moment marked by accelerating ecological transformations and growing awareness of the material infrastructures that sustain contemporary life, geological matter has emerged as a crucial site for rethinking history, memory, environment, and cultural imagination. Rather than treating the Earth as a passive backdrop to human activity, recent scholarship has approached rocks, minerals, soils, fossils, sediments, and other material formations as archives of planetary processes, environmental change, cultural memory, and political conflict. Questions of resource extraction, environmental justice, and slow violence increasingly intersect with inquiries into deep temporalities, material traces, sacred landscapes, and the long afterlives of human and more-than-human actions. This issue invites contributions that explore how literature, art, media, philosophy, religion, and cultural practices engage with geological matter, deep time, sedimented histories, and the material conditions of planetary life. We especially welcome work that investigates the cultural significance of rocks, minerals, fossils, soil, waste, ruins, and other forms of more-than-living matter, while also addressing questions of environmental justice, resource extraction, toxicity, and slow violence. We welcome analyses of literary, philosophical, historical, and cultural texts from a wide range of regions and traditions, including comparative and transnational perspectives. Topics may include: • geohumanities and geological imagination; • earth, stone, sediment, dust, and soil; • lithic ecologies and critical mineral studies; • deep time, planetary temporalities, and environmental history; • extractivism, mining, resource conflicts, and energy humanities; • environmental justice and slow violence; • toxic landscapes and contaminated environments; • waste, ruins, landfills, and material afterlives; • fossils, paleontology, and material histories of life; • material memory, archives, traces, and sedimented histories; • sacred geographies, holy mountains, stones, and pilgrimage landscapes; • archaeology, antiquarianism, and the materialities of the past; • textual strata, sedimented knowledge, and epistemic layers; • geological trauma, memory, and post-catastrophic landscapes; • petrofiction, climate fiction, and environmental storytelling; • artistic and literary engagements with earth materials; • relations between living and non-living matter; • fungi, decomposition, and processes of material transformation; • posthumanist, new materialist, and decolonial approaches to geology and the earth. Proposals comprising a 250-word abstract in English or German and a brief biographical note should be sent to: transpositiones@uw.edu.pl by October 20, 2026. A final decision regarding abstract acceptance will be made by October 31. Deadline for submitting completed manuscripts: February 28, 2027. The issue is expected to be published in the autumn of 2027.

items.fullDescription: Call for Chapters Proposals Submission Deadline: July 17, 2026 Full Chapters Due: October 30, 2026 Submission Date: October 30, 2026 Introduction This edited collection features scholarly voices with attention to horror in its transmedia representations, including film, literature, comics, art, branding, and more. Chapters give attention to the ways that fans take up the realities and ideas presented in horror, the affordances of the genre, and participation in this network of storytelling. The reactions of readers/viewers/fans, the decisions of creatives, the presentation of ideas within particular forms of media, and more form elements of the researched conversation in this volume. Objective This collection seeks to advance conversation about the theoretical functions of horror across media including notions of adaptation and literary/literacy-based choices in the work. This includes, but is not limited to, design structures, cultural influences, the role of lore, (re)considerations of the monstrous, embodiment in the genre, sub-genre considerations, and more. Target Audience This book is intended for academics in media, literacy, literature, communication, and interdisciplinary fields. Students enrolled in courses in these fields can benefit from this knowledge as they pursue courses of study and further academic work in these disciplines. Recommended Topics Emotional and Philosophical Reactions to Horror Media Themes and Interactions across Media Representations in the Genre Adaptation Processes/Decisions/Designs in Horror across Media Studies of Narrative and Response/Interpretation Recent Trends/Movements in Horror Theoretical Approaches to Horror Composition/Representation Analysis of Race, Gender, Class in Horror Considerations and Reconsiderations of the Monstrous Author/Creator Decisions and Purposes in the Genre/across Media Horror Character and Author/Director Studies Critical and Analytical Work on Embodiment in Horror Critical and Analytical Examinations of Cultural Stories in the Genre The Role of Lore/Mythology in Horror Studies of Writing/Creating Processes in the Genre Fandom Communities, Fan Fiction, Cosplay, and Other Responses Submission Procedure Researchers and practitioners are invited to submit on or before July 17, 2026, a chapter proposal of 1,000 to 2,000 words clearly explaining the mission and concerns of his or her proposed chapter. Authors will be notified by July 31, 2026 about the status of their proposals and sent chapter guidelines.Full chapters of a minimum of 10,000 words (word count includes references and related readings) are expected to be submitted by October 30, 2026, and all interested authors must consult the guidelines for manuscript submissions at https://www.igi-global.com/publish/contributor-resources/before-you-write/ prior to submission. All submitted chapters will be reviewed on a double-anonymized review basis. Contributors may also be requested to serve as reviewers for this project. Note: There are no submission or acceptance fees for manuscripts submitted to this book publication, Theory and Practice in Horror Transmedia Fandom and Creation. All manuscripts are accepted based on a double-anonymized peer review editorial process. All proposals should be submitted through the eEditorial Discovery® online submission manager. Publisher This book is scheduled to be published by IGI Global Scientific Publishing, an international academic publisher of the "Information Science Reference", "Medical Information Science Reference", "Business Science Reference", and "Engineering Science Reference" imprints. IGI Global Scientific Publishing specializes in publishing reference books, scholarly journals, and electronic databases featuring academic research on a variety of innovative topic areas including, but not limited to, education, social science, medicine and healthcare, business and management, information science and technology, engineering, public administration, library and information science, media and communication studies, and environmental science. For additional information regarding the publisher, please visit https://www.igi-global.com. This publication is anticipated to be released in 2027. Indexing Information for Prospective Authors IGI Global Scientific Publishing meets the criteria for inclusion in major indexing services such as Scopus; however, it is important to note that all indexing decisions are made independently by these services. IGI Global Scientific Publishing books are selectively indexed by the indexing organization after publication. Indexing cannot be guaranteed for any book prior to publication, and the indexing organization has complete control over the final selection and timeline. items.fullDescription: What is the real difference between speaking with nature and speaking for it? Is eco-centric thought a universally shared ideology, or does it develop in reaction to historical, philosophical, and socio-cultural contexts? In what way do the fundamental principles of Indian ecology vary from prevailing Western structures? These essential inquiries delineate the parameters of Ramachandra Guha’s Speaking with Nature: The Origins of Indian Environmentalism (2024), which effectively contests the notion that environmentalism is a unidirectional phenomenon dictated by Western influence. This view posits that the rest of the world, particularly the Global South, lacks eco-conscious awareness because it is ‘too poor to be green’.

items.fullDescription: Black Performing Arts: Sound, Movement, Image, Text Submission Deadline: October 31, 2026 The Black Performing Arts Area provides a scholarly forum to share research pertaining to Black performance across expressive forms. Broadly defined, the area focuses on all forms of performing and visual arts, including all musical genres, theatrical performance and performance art, performance elements in visual art, and connections between different Black expressive forms. In all these contexts we are interested in investigating where aesthetic technique and embodiment merge across Black diasporic expressivity. The panels on Black Performing Arts: Sound, Movement, Image, Text will showcase interdisciplinary discussions of cultural identity, art, religion, ritual, power, image, representation, symbols and their meaning, and the social processes and systems that influence and inform the innovation, production, regulation, and consumption of Black performing arts. Additionally, we invite research that examines the role of Black music within society, how Black performing and visual arts might be read intersectionally with attention to race, class, gender, and sexual identity, and the relationship between Black performing arts and their broad political and economic context. For the 2027 conference, we are particularly interested in research that explores the rich history of Black performance in Boston and New England, and for papers that connect to the conference's broad theme, "Revolutions and Revisions in Popular Culture." items.fullDescription: The Mystery & Detective Fiction Area of the Popular Culture Association invites proposals for the annual conference in Boston, Massachusetts, March 24-27, 2027, to be held at the Boston Marriott Copley Place (110 Huntington Ave., Boston, MA). The deadline for submission is October 31, 2026. This year's PCA conference theme is "Revolutions & Revisions in Popular Culture." Presenters in Mystery & Detective Fiction are invited to consider how their work might engage with questions of transformation, reinterpretation, innovation, resistance, adaptation, or cultural change. Theme-related proposals are welcome but not required, and all submissions relevant to the area will receive full consideration. We seek proposals from researchers, academics, graduate students, and independent scholars for scholarly discussions on all aspects and periods of mystery and detective fiction. Interdisciplinary approaches are strongly encouraged. We ask that proposals extend existing scholarship in new directions and avoid plot summary or review. Proposals should have a clear and focused argument that can be developed adequately in a 15-minute presentation. For the 2027 conference we are actively looking for submissions that would work as joint panels with the True Crime Area. We encourage topics that explore the mutual influence and exchange between True Crime and Mystery/Detective Fiction. You may indicate in your proposal if you would like your paper to be considered for a joint panel; even if not accepted for a joint panel, your abstract will be considered for our regular Mystery and Detective Fiction programming. Some possible topics for the 2027 conference: ? Boston-area mystery/detective/crime fiction/TV series/films-such as novels by George V. Higgins, Robert B. Parker, Hank Phillippi Ryan, Dennis Lehane; TV shows like City on a Hill, Spenser for Hire; films like The Departed, Mystic River, etc. ? Fiction re-imagining real-life crime events in Boston/nearby area, such as novels/film/TV about Fall River's Lizzie Borden, Boston's Whitey Bulger, etc. ? Subgenres, such as hardboiled detective fiction, eco-detective fiction, neo-noir, etc. ? The role of AI in detective/mystery fiction as theme or character ? Depictions of older characters as detectives or criminals ? Generic hybridity-detective/mystery crossed with horror, sci-fi, romance, dystopia ? Authors or texts featuring characters identifying with marginalized or historically excluded communities and their literary, social or political impact within the genre ? Transnational and global crime fiction ? Analysis of specific authors and/or time periods, including relevant tropes ? Adaptation of mystery and detective fiction in film, television, theatre, computer games, etc. Submission Process Please submit your 250-300 word abstract through the PCA conference's submission portal. The deadline for submissions is October 31, 2026. If you are a first-time presenter in our area, please identify yourself with a note after your abstract: First-time presenters in Mystery & Detective Fiction are eligible for the Earl Bargainnier Award. To propose a panel, please submit individual presentations, then email the area chair with a request to be considered as a panel. The PCA/ACA requires a minimum of four papers per panel. In your email, name all participants and briefly explain the thematic link between your papers. About Us: The Mystery & Detective Fiction Area of PCA/ACA is dedicated to recognizing and promoting the scholarly study of all aspects of mystery and detective fiction, and to fostering an inclusive community for early-career scholars, adjuncts, grad students, and independent scholars, as well as established academics. Each year we also sponsor the George N. Dove Award for outstanding contributions to the serious study of crime fiction. We invite members and presenters to participate in our annual group dinner at the national conference and to join us at the annual business meeting, where we set the area's course for the next year. Finally, please send all inquiries to Marla Harris (mhcrocombe@gmail.com).

items.excerpt: The Routledge Handbook of Hip Hop and Sport, Culture, and Activism Call for Chapters Description: The Routledge Handbook of Hip Hop and Sport, Culture and Activism addresses the critical need for a comprehensive academic survey of Hip Hop's connection to sport as a preeminent sociological and political force among Millennials and Generation Z. items.fullDescription: The Routledge Handbook of Hip Hop and Sport, Culture, and Activism Call for Chapters Description: The Routledge Handbook of Hip Hop and Sport, Culture and Activism addresses the critical need for a comprehensive academic survey of Hip Hop's connection to sport as a preeminent sociological and political force among Millennials and Generation Z. This handbook maps the emerging critical terrain where Hip Hop intersects with the sports-industrial complex, digital activism, and the persistent structures of racial capitalism and white supremacy. As the culture enters its second half-century, it serves as an emergent space for self-expression and identity formation, both to hegemonic and counter-hegemonic ends. The leading objectives of this volume are to delineate how Hip Hop's relationship with sport provides narrative resources for youth to explore their social realities in the context of late-stage capitalism and its bedfellows: white supremacy and patriarchy. This handbook explores both the route and roots of Hip Hop expression through the lens of the African diaspora and the historical relationship between Black expressive history and social movements. This handbook is also interested in the ways in which Hip Hop's relationship with sport can be oriented both towards liberation and political conservatism, particularly in the context of Hip Hop's historical and presentist embrace of Donald Trump and his representative movements. This project aims to both engage Hip Hop's historical relationship with sports (professional and amateur) as well as its contemporary shifts,such as the institutionalization of breaking in the 2024 Olympics and the rise of representation activism in major sports leagues (NBA, NFL) that create new tensions between cultural authenticity and corporate appropriation. It is intended to define the current state of theory and establish a foundation for future scholarship across the interdisciplinary fields of hip-hop studies, sport management, and Africana studies. Since this project is a handbook and not an anthology, the chapter topics have already been pre-selected by the editors. However, we encourage submissions that engage the specific areas of expertise of each contributor, and the contributor is welcome to interpret the proposed topics according to their own research and experience. The targeted audience for this handbook are advanced high school students and undergraduates, so chapters should be written with this audience in mind. We invite abstract submissions from Hip Hop practitioners, sport sociologists, scholars, graduate students, postgraduate researchers, and early career researchers. Details for Submission: Abstracts of 250-300 words for the chapters listed below must be submitted by October 31st, 2026. Microsoft Word or PDF formats will be accepted. When submitting your abstract, please include your name, affiliation, email address, title of chapter, and short biography (100 words). Authors will be notified of their acceptance by November 30th, 2026. Full chapters of 4,000-6,000 words (including references) are due by April 30th, 2027. For further questions, contact Dr. Micah J. Dobson (mjdobson92@gmail.com ) and Dr. Tyler Bunzey (tylerbunzey@gmail.com). Table of Contents Section 1: Hip-Hop: A Cultural Politic Chapter 1: The Context of Hip-Hop's Roots and Routes in the Early 1970s Chapter 2: Political Movements that Impacted Hip-Hop's Foundation Chapter 3: Hip-Hop's Formal Political Movements like "Rock the Vote" Chapter 4: Hip-Hop and Moral Panic Section 2: Hip-Hop Generating Identity Chapter 5: Hip-Hop and Generational Identity in the "Post-Racial" Era Chapter 6: Obama, Neoliberalism, and Hip-Hop Mainstream Partisan Politics Chapter 7: From "FDT" to Kodak Black: Hip-Hop's Complicated Relationship with Trump Chapter 8: Hip-Hop and the Black Lives Matter Movement Chapter 9: "Alright" and Social Protests Against Police Brutality Section 3: Hip-Hop and the Sports-Industrial Complex Chapter 10: A History of the Relationship Between Hip-Hop and Sport Chapter 11: Subculture to Spectacle: The Evolution of Breaking and Olympic Institutionalization Chapter 12: Ice Cube, The Big Three, and Mogul "Activism" Chapter 13: Jay-Z and the Problematics of the Roc Nation-NFL Partnership Section 4: Representing: Hip-Hop and Sport Chapter 14: The Politics of Aesthetics: Street Fashion, the Tunnel Walk, and Racialized Pleasure Chapter 15: Generational Agency: From Michael Jordan's Brand to LeBron's "Representation Activism" Chapter 16: The WNBA and Queering Hip-Hop Aesthetics Chapter 17: Hip-Hop Dance as Art and Sport

items.fullDescription: PCA Annual Conference, March 24-27, 2027: Boston, Massachusetts The Collecting and Collectibles Area invites proposals exploring how "collecting" has become an embodiment of the economic, political, environmental, and digital precarities that shape contemporary popular culture. Collecting now operates as a dynamic source for epistemic production, constantly redefining how popular culture is constructed, construed, mediated, valorized, historicized, and even contested. The 2027 PCA conference theme is "Revolutions & Revisions in Popular Culture." Presenters in Collecting and Collectibles Area are invited to consider how their work might engage with questions of transformation, reinterpretation, innovation, resistance, adaptation, or cultural change. Theme-related proposals are welcome but not required, and all submissions relevant to the area will receive full consideration. We welcome contributions that integrate practice-based, collaborative, comparative, transnational and cross-cultural approaches and involve innovative methods, community engagement, public and digital humanities to address topics including, but not limited to: --Emerging Technologies of Collecting: AI and collecting cultures, virtual archives, NFTs and blockchain collectibles, social media collecting communities, online marketplaces and economies, smart museums, mixed- reality collections, and AI-enabled smart twins of museums --Participatory Collecting Culture: Gaming memorabilia and sports collections, comic books, manga, anime, and graphic novels, fan archives, and exclusive/ limited editions --Popular Media collecting: Film and television memorabilia, music and vinyl records, cassettes, CDs, concert and artist-branded merchandise, celebrity memorabilia, fast-food promotional premiums, licensed toys, action figure and doll sets, LEGO, and theme park merchandise -- Heritage and Transcultural collecting: counter archives and collectibles, indigenous collections, digitality and heritage preservation, migration and portable collectibles, cultural diplomacy collections -- Crisis Collecting: Climate change and at-risk collections, pandemic collecting, trauma and collecting, sustainable and ethical colleting, resilient collections, commemorative coins and medals, satirical magazines, post-collapse souvenirs, war memorabilia -- Consumer Culture and Collecting: Auctions and collector markets and communities, investment collecting, branding and nostalgic collecting, resale platforms -- Materiality of Collecting: household collectibles, stamps, travel souvenirs, and their digital adaptations We welcome individual papers, complete panels, creative presentations, and interdisciplinary collaborations. Scholars, independent researchers, graduate students, and undergraduate students are encouraged to submit. Membership in the PCA is needed to submit a proposal. items.title: New Approaches to Teaching the Gothic
items.excerpt: Diane Long Hoeveler and Tamar Heller's Approaches to Teaching Gothic Fiction: British and American Traditions (MLA Options for Teaching) was published in 2003; Anna Powell and Andrew Smith's Teaching the Gothic (Palgrave) was published in 2006. While both texts are excellent guides for teachers of the Gothic, quite a lot has happened in the twenty years s...
items.fullDescription: Diane Long Hoeveler and Tamar Heller's Approaches to Teaching Gothic Fiction: British and American Traditions (MLA Options for Teaching) was published in 2003; Anna Powell and Andrew Smith's Teaching the Gothic (Palgrave) was published in 2006. While both texts are excellent guides for teachers of the Gothic, quite a lot has happened in the twenty years since these texts appeared, not the least of which was a Gothic-infused global pandemic and the insidious rise of artificial intelligence in daily life. Academics today are and have been teaching the Gothic at a time when the world's problems - rising fascism, global conflict, climate change, the devaluation of Higher Education, among many others - make the world itself seem downright Gothic. This collection will seek to provide updated reflections, evaluations, and strategies on teaching the Gothic and utilising or creating Gothic pedagogy in the contemporary moment and beyond. Courses on or including the Gothic are taught in a wide variety of venues within and outside academia; settings include community colleges, traditional undergraduate programmes, graduate programmes, community centres, prisons and reformatories. Classrooms themselves vary greatly, from giant lecture halls to small upper-level seminars to fully online virtual spaces. Students of the Gothic come from all ages and backgrounds, and include native speakers of English and students acquiring English later in life. These contexts, venues, and audiences present different challenges for the instructor, and require unique approaches to make for successful learning experiences. We are seeking contributions from a range of scholars at different ranks and types of institutions (as well as outside of them) to present a broad understanding of the diversity of how we study and teach the Gothic today, and to provide new directions for the future. We already have interest from an academic press. Potential topics might include but are not restricted to one or a mixture of the following: Teaching the Gothic in the midst of a crisis (e.g. pandemic, war, from a distance or physically within such spaces) Teaching the Gothic outside of the university / in non-traditional settings Challenges of AI to teaching the Gothic The use of various digital platforms in teaching / student research Gothic and the archives in contemporary times What texts (and which editions) absolutely must be on any Gothic syllabus (and why)? Gothic forms (teaching beyond traditional formats, for instance) Gothic theory as pedagogy (in times of crisis particularly) Syllabus organizational strategies and rationales: Chronological? Thematic? Canon? Decolonizing the Gothic syllabus Preparing for and managing class discussions about violence, sexual violence, trauma, discrimination, or other tough topics that arise in the Gothic? Strategies for teaching a Gothic course for an audience unfamiliar with the Gothic / unfamiliar with academia / non-traditional students. Gothic and public engagement / school outreach Opportunities for service learning / personal and professional development in the Gothic course Creative forms of assessment in the Gothic classroom Neurodivergence and the Gothic Designing assignments with AI in mind Cancel culture and the Gothic Co-editors Bridget Marshall (University of Massachusetts, Lowell) and Jen Baker (University of Warwick, UK) seek abstracts of 300-500 words for chapters which will demonstrate innovative approaches to teaching the Gothic or engaging with or creating new Gothic pedagogies, particularly situated within recent contexts. We are open to a variety of forms, including case studies, reflective essays, theoretically informed essays, and other formats that can best showcase pedagogical insights. If your proposed essay includes samples of work by students/participants we will require written permissions before publication. Please also include a brief professional bio of 300 words (max) with your abstract. Please send your abstract and bio by 10 November 2026 to Bridget_Marshall@uml.edu and J.Baker.5@warwick.ac.uk We are happy to answer questions at the same address.

items.fullDescription: About the Series Dramatis Personae is an annual cycle of interdisciplinary, outreach-oriented conferences dedicated to exploring theatre through the lenses and tools of the human and social sciences. Each edition takes a specific theme as a point of convergence for researchers from different fields (anthropology, sociology, psychology, education, philosophy, political science, organisational studies and other fields of the human sciences), inviting them to approach theatre not merely as the exclusive object of theatre studies, but as a privileged site where the great questions of human experience become visible, are tested, and are transformed. Dramatis Personae is born from the collaboration between Officine Teatrali, a centre for theatre research and studies, WakeUp, association for social promotion, and Antropolis, a cultural association for scientific outreach. Thanks to the sponsorship of the Municipality of Vanzago, this annual event takes place in the splendid setting of the Sala degli Affreschi at Palazzo Calderara. Theme of the First Edition There is a kind of knowledge that does not pass through words. It is transmitted through gesture, learned through imitation and contact, deposited in muscle, in breath, in the posture one assumes before another. It is the knowledge theatre has always carried, and which the human sciences have come to recognise as one of the fundamental ways in which human beings inhabit the world and hand it down. The first edition of Dramatis Personae chooses this borderland as its theme: bodies that know. Bodies that act, that teach without teaching, that carry within them collective memories and invisible competences. Bodies of actors who build stage presence through a training that is also a transformation of the self. Bodies that cross ritual thresholds, bodies that suffer and resist, bodies that work, that care, that lead. Thematic Areas Proposals are invited that engage with one or more of the following areas, each of which takes the stage as its point of observation and opens onto dialogue with one or more disciplines of the human and social sciences. 1. The Stage as a Laboratory of Embodied Knowledge Body techniques, habitus, tacit knowledge: stage presence as a form of knowledge that resists verbal transcription. 2. Theatre and Ritual: Bodies Crossing Thresholds Continuities and ruptures between ritual and theatrical forms, liminality, technologies of the collective body. 3. The Body on Stage as a Site of Power Bodily normativity on stage and beyond it: gender, disability, migration, exclusion and resistance. 4. The Stage as Pedagogical and Transformative Practice Theatre as an instrument of formation: of the actor, of the spectator, of communities. 5. Bodies on Stage that Testify and Resist Documentary theatre, theatre of memory, theatre of war: the body as witness. 6. The Performer's Body in the Digital Age Presence, liveness and technological mediation: what happens to the body when the stage becomes dematerialised. 7. The Body that Works, the Body that Cares, the Body that Leads The transfer of the performer's embodied competences into organisational, clinical and educational contexts. Proposals that, while not falling precisely within one of these areas, engage originally with the general theme of the edition are equally welcome. Submission Guidelines Contributions may be submitted by researchers (doctoral candidates, postdoctoral fellows, faculty members, independent scholars) in the human and social sciences, and by theatre professionals with a reflective disposition toward their own practice. Proposals must include: title of the contribution abstract (maximum 400 words), specifying the theoretical framework, method, and relevance to the theme of the edition a maximum of 5 keywordsa brief biographical note for the author(s) (maximum 150 words), with institutional affiliation, if any indication of the relevant thematic area (one or more of those listed above) Proposals may be submitted in Italian or in English. Conference presentations will last 15 minutes, followed by discussion. Selection Process Proposals will undergo an anonymous peer review process, conducted by a joint scientific committee composed of scholars from theatre studies and the human and social sciences. Between a minimum of four and a maximum of eight contributions will be selected, forming the presentations of the conference day, possibly distributed across two sessions. Deadlines Phase Date Deadline for submission of proposals: 30 october 2026 Notification of selection results: 30 november 2026 Submission of final texts for publication: 11 jenuary 2026 Conference day: 6 february 2027 Publication Contributions selected and presented at the conference will be considered for scientific publication in a dedicated volume, subject to a further peer review process on the complete texts. Programme Structure The event takes place at Palazzo Calderara and opens with a performance, serving as an introduction to this year's theme. This is followed by selected academic presentations, organized into one or two sessions. The afternoon is dedicated to hands-on workshops and concludes with a group reflection session. items.excerpt: The Southern Humanities Conference, 2027 Call for Papers Conference Theme: Divergence, Convergence, Emergence Knoxville, TN, January 28-31, 2027 The Southern Humanities Conference offers an opportunity for scholars, artists, writers, musicians, performers, and humanists of all kinds to share their knowledge, research, work, and experiences in an interdisc...
items.fullDescription: The Southern Humanities Conference, 2027 Call for Papers Conference Theme: Divergence, Convergence, Emergence Knoxville, TN, January 28-31, 2027 The Southern Humanities Conference offers an opportunity for scholars, artists, writers, musicians, performers, and humanists of all kinds to share their knowledge, research, work, and experiences in an interdisciplinary, welcoming, and engaging intellectual space. For 2027 our conference theme will be "Divergence, Convergence, Emergence." Divergent thinking is a hallmark of creative endeavors ranging from the visual and performative arts to scientific inquiry. It can also signify a transgression of a custom or standard, or even a social more or behavioral norm, through contravention or subversion of what others consider "ordinary" or "natural." On the other hand, the benefits of group diversity are undeniably numerous and valuable in education, collaboration, and problem-solving. Convergent thinking can help triangulate resolutions to mysteries in historical systems and literary plot structures, among other questions. Convergence can also be considered a precursor to meaningful communal and cooperative social and cultural interactions. The notion of emergence-a phenomenon in which novel, unpredictable, and sometimes unexpected outcomes arise from a constellation of interactions between simpler underlying elements-provides a way of understanding origins and evolutions of phenomena that interest the analytical and imaginative mind. Emergence is also often associated with the concept of synthesis and the idea that the whole can be greater than the sum of its parts. The intersections of (and interstices between) emergence, divergence, and convergence serve as the stimulus for our collective conversation in Knoxville and offers us a platform for appraising the world around us. The Southern Humanities Conference invites proposals for papers on any aspect of the theme "Divergence, Convergence, Emergence" broadly conceived. Our conference themes are meant to be inspiring and prompt reflection, not limiting. The topic is interdisciplinary and invites proposals from all areas of study, as well as creative pieces including but not limited to performance, music, art, and literature. Customary paper and full panel proposals are invited, as are ones for creative presentation formats like roundtables and demonstrations. Moreover, the Southern Humanities Conference welcomes proposals from teachers and professionals outside the academy, as well as from scholars in the early stages of their academic careers. Please note that the name of our organization simply reflects its having been founded in the U.S. South; no presenter is expected to present anything "southern," though southern topics are also welcomed. Conference attendees come from all over the United States, Canada, and overseas. SUBMISSION GUIDELINES: Please submit proposals of 300-500 words through our website at www.southernhumanities.org (preferred), or by email sent to Brett Bebber at southernhumanities@gmail.com. Proposals are due by December 1, 2026, but are accepted and reviewed on a rolling basis. We are currently planning to meet for an in-person conference in Knoxville. Conference registration fees for the 2027 Conference will be $195 for students and retirees and $250 for academic faculty and other professionals. CONFERENCE AWARDS: Two awards of up to $300 are available to help mitigate the costs of travel to the conference. The Kathryn M. Reynolds award is for first- or second-time presenters, and Bennie D. Ussery award is for the best proposed paper from a graduate student. A third award, the Mark Ledbetter and Susan Cumings Award, offers registration remission for up to four graduate students. If you would like to be considered for one of these awards, please indicate which award(s) in your proposal. Those interested in being considered for either award should submit their proposals by October 31, 2026.

items.excerpt: Faster than society gathers wisdom: Video games and/as speculative Fiction (McFarland, Studies in Gaming Series) Editor: Marc A. Ouellette, Old Dominion University (mouellet@odu.edu) While video games are not at all underexplored as dystopic works, they have not as yet been considered in terms of their speculative visions of a dystopian future. Still, gam...
items.fullDescription: Faster than society gathers wisdom: Video games and/as speculative Fiction (McFarland, Studies in Gaming Series) Editor: Marc A. Ouellette, Old Dominion University (mouellet@odu.edu) While video games are not at all underexplored as dystopic works, they have not as yet been considered in terms of their speculative visions of a dystopian future. Still, games offer plenty of instances of the corrupt national leaders, divisions, sexism, and rank profiteering one finds in novels like Atwood's ubiquitous tale, games afford players an opportunity to enact and participate in the rebuttal. Thus, the panel seeks to look at games as predictive, speculative versions of dystopian fiction, while offering a means of demonstrating that video games, current and past, are indeed a substantial part of the present and the future of literature. For example, Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas, a video game released in 2004 is not only a dystopic fiction, its game world, its story, its characters, and its in-game cultural productions can be read quite easily as anticipating and predicting the first (and indeed the second) Trump-eras. Not only are there anti-immigrant screeds, the game also includes Russia owning the president, deep racial divisions, and comments used by verbatim by contemporary conservative politicians. Brabazon, Redhead, and Chivaura (2018) cite the need for consumers to refer to previous iterations of dystopic fiction as a means of making sense of a "dystopic present" (2). They cite the rise of popularity of Orwell's 1984 (1949), Lewis's It Can't Happen Here (1935), and of course Atwood's The Handmaid's Tale (1985). Intriguingly, just before Atwood was preparing to release a sequel, Classics scholar Michael Zimm (13 Aug. 2019) proclaimed that video games were finally worthy of study alongside historical texts like the Illiad and the Odyssey. Here, an under-examined point highlights the ways games, like original recitations (and unlike film remakes) of Greek epics, make the audience participants as well as witnesses. The rise of populism, "forever wars," and authoritarianism has inspired commentators to seek literary works for analogues, but not yet video games. Thus, the collections will provide an opportunity for scholars to turn to two frequently disregarded forms, video games and spec fiction, to make sense of a "cataclysmic present." While games offer plenty of instances of the corrupt national leaders, divisions, sexism, and rank profiteering one finds in novels like Atwood's tale, games afford players an opportunity to enact and participate in the rebuttal. Thus, the collections seeks to look at games as predictive, speculative versions of dystopian fiction, while offering a means of demonstrating that video games, current and past, are indeed a substantial part of the present and the future of literature. As a corollary, then, the volume will offer other games that quite clearly resonate as depictions of dystopic literature that predict and help us make sense of later events and outcomes. Indeed, the fact that games allow players to participate in these outcomes makes them a powerful literary form to add to the roster of speculative fiction and predictive dystopic texts. Suggested Topics and Lines of Inquiry We invite proposals for chapters that address video games as speculative fiction, dystopic literature, or predictive texts. Possible topics include (but are not limited to): Political Simulation: Corruption, failed governments, or populist demagoguery in games and series Media and Spectacle: Analysis of in-game media, news broadcasts, or propaganda Fantasy sports and sporting fantasies Racial and Social Division: How games simulate, critique, or perpetuate racial, class, or ethnic divisions Adaptations and alterations of classic, medievalist, or other period pieces Techno-Libertarianism/Randian Critique: Critical readings of games that address objectivism, tech oligarchs, or utopian experiments gone wrong. Gender and Sexism: Speculative visions of gender roles, reproductive politics, or institutional sexism in dystopian game worlds. Player Agency and Rebuttal: The ways ludic participation (e.g., player choice, procedural rhetoric) allows players to resist or enact dystopian systems. The Speculative Past: Chapters addressing how historical fiction games function as speculative fiction (e.g., alternative histories & steampunk worlds) Post-Apocalyptic Games: Analyzing games as commentaries on environmental collapse, resource wars, and social breakdown. We invite scholars from multiple disciplines to submit abstracts (300-500 words) by 18 Dec. 2026, with completed papers due 15 May 2027. Please send abstracts and inquiries to mouellet@odu.

items.fullDescription: In her book Bodyminds Reimagined , Sami Schalk asks us “What might it mean to imagine disability differently?” (2) Her work, situated in the exploration of black speculative fiction, engages with (dis)ability studies and black feminism to gesture toward a reimagining of what Margaret Price termed the ‘bodymind’, a concept predicated on “the enmeshment of the mind and body.” (5) How might this enmeshment be understood in the context of chronic conditions, themselves experienced as a direct result of climate change and biomedical violence? Is the planet - made sick by extractive capitalism and anthropogenic action as Shukla, Settee, Lincoln and others claim - now existing in a state of (dis)ability?

items.fullDescription: How is everyone doing? At a routine meeting of the Editorial Board of this journal in March 2026, this innocuous question erupted into disquiet, tension, unease. Speaking from vastly different parts of the world, there was an unmistakable sense of a planet slipping beyond available comprehension and unplugging us from work and life routines. As wars in the Middle East expand and fires spread from apartment blocks reduced to rubble to bombed oil refineries and shipping corridors, profound geopolitical, personal, even psychic rifts leave us grasping for the language and feel of the moment, the falling apart of things, the zeitgeist of an endangered now.

items.fullDescription: The advancement of artificial intelligence has transformed humanities research and education, deepening computation’s influence on scholarly practice and everyday life. From the early era of “humanities computing” in the 1970s to the rise of “computational humanities” over the past decade, this trajectory highlights the enduring—and expanding—role of computation in shaping inquiry across the humanities. These intersections are especially visible in interdisciplinary work. As T. S. Eliot observes, “Immature poets imitate; mature poets steal; bad poets deface what they take, and good poets make it into something better, or at least something different.” The same spirit can illuminate how methods and tools migrate across fields.

items.fullDescription: XXV Congreso Internacional sobre Nuevas Tendencias en Humanidades, Universidad de Split, Croacia, 30 de junio - 2 de julio de 2027. Fundada en 2003, la Red de Investigación de Nuevas Tendencias en Humanidades pone a su disposición un foro que aúna el interés por las tendencias en humanidades tradicionalmente establecidas, al tiempo que desarrolla prácticas innovadoras en el ámbito de las humanidades y configura un escenario de cara al futuro de estas. El XXV Congreso Internacional sobre Nuevas Tendencias en Humanidades invita a presentar investigaciones que aborden los siguientes temas anuales y el tema destacado de 2027: Tema destacado 2027 - Archipiélagos de significado: las humanidades en un mundo lleno de mundos Tema 1: Humanidades comprometidas, ciudadanía y cultura democrática Tema 2: Lenguaje, poder y construcción de sentido Tema 3: Literatura, narrativa e imaginación cultural Tema 4: Tecnologías de la comunicación: IA, medios de comunicación e interpretación Tema 5: Lugar, comunidad y futuros sostenibles

items.fullDescription: XXXIV Congreso Internacional sobre Aprendizaje, Universidad Aristóteles de Tesalónica, Grecia, 7-9 de julio de 2027. Fundada en 1989, la Red de Investigación de Aprendizaje se reúne en torno a un interés común por el aprendizaje ?en sus vertientes tanto formal como informal? abarcando todos sus niveles: desde el aprendizaje durante la primera infancia, pasando por el periodo escolar, enseñanza secundaria y universitaria, hasta la educación para adultos que se desarrolla en las diferentes poblaciones y ámbitos laborales. El XXXIV Congreso Internacional sobre Aprendizaje invita a presentar investigaciones que abordan los siguientes temas anuales y el tema destacado de 2027: Tema destacado 2027 - Educación democrática en la era de la IA: Diversidad y alfabetización para la IA Tema 1: Futuros democráticos del aprendizaje Tema 2: Diversidad crítica e inclusión Tema 3: Aprendizaje práctico de la IA Tema 4: Gobernanza y ética en la educación
